meta.licence_note: Control ids here are OUR OWN numbering; the MCSB control-family prefixes (IM-, PA-, NS-, DP-, LT-, AM-) are cited as identifiers. Every title, objective, procedure, evidence rule, verdict rule and remediation is our own writing, derived from Microsoft's public Azure/Graph API documentation. Microsoft publishes its own crosswalks from MCSB to CIS, NIST SP 800-53, ISO 27001 and PCI DSS, so a compliance mapping cites Microsoft's mapping rather than one we invented. No benchmark prose is reproduced.

controls.title: Every holder of a privileged directory role is challenged for a second factor at sign-in
controls.objective: MCSB IM-6 and PA-2 rest on the same premise: a password alone must never produce an administrative session. An account holding Global Administrator, Privileged Role Administrator, User Administrator, Application Administrator or any other role that can grant permissions is one phished password away from tenant ownership, so a second factor must be enforced for that population by tenant policy rather than left to each administrator's preference.
controls.procedure: Entra ID reaches this outcome through one of two mutually exclusive mechanisms, so establish which is live before reading anything else. `az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/policies/identitySecurityDefaultsEnforcementPolicy'` returns `isEnabled`; while security defaults are enabled no Conditional Access policy can be in the enabled state, although disabled policy objects may still exist, so read this flag first and interpret every policy body against it. If security defaults are off, list Conditional Access policies with `az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/identity/conditionalAccess/policies'` and re-request `@odata.nextLink` until a response carries none — `az rest` performs exactly one HTTP request and never follows paging. Per policy record `state`, `conditions.users.includeRoles/excludeRoles/includeUsers/excludeUsers/includeGroups/excludeGroups`, both `conditions.applications.includeApplications` and `conditions.applications.excludeApplications`, `conditions.clientAppTypes`, `grantControls.operator`, `grantControls.builtInControls` and `grantControls.authenticationStrength.id`. Then build the real administrator population starting from the licence-independent plane: `roleManagement/directory/roleAssignments?$expand=principal` returns every active directory-role assignment in any tenant, whereas `roleAssignmentScheduleInstances` and `roleEligibilityScheduleInstances` are Privileged Identity Management surfaces that require Entra ID P2. Read all three and reconcile them, treating an empty PIM collection in an unlicensed tenant as 'PIM not in use', never as 'no administrators'. Expand every assignment whose principal is a group through `/groups/{id}/transitiveMembers`, and expand each `excludeGroups` entry the same way, because an exclusion is evaluated against membership at sign-in rather than against the group id you recorded. Finally read `reports/authenticationMethods/userRegistrationDetails` (`isAdmin`, `isMfaRegistered`, `isMfaCapable`, `methodsRegistered`) to expose administrators who would be blocked by the policy or who would satisfy it with a weak method.
api: next='https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/identity/conditionalAccess/policies'; : > ca_all.json; while [ -n "$next" ]; do az rest --method GET --url "$next" > page.json; jq -c '.value[]' page.json >> ca_all.json; next=$(jq -r '."@odata.nextLink" // empty' page.json); done
controls.evidence: The `isEnabled` value of the security-defaults policy; the full JSON body of each Conditional Access policy that claims to cover administrators, keyed by policy `id` and `displayName`, with `state`, the whole `conditions.users` object, `conditions.applications.includeApplications` and `excludeApplications`, `conditions.clientAppTypes`, `grantControls.operator`, `grantControls.builtInControls` and `grantControls.authenticationStrength.id` quoted verbatim; the resolved list of privileged-role principals (object id, UPN or service principal name, role `displayName` and template id) annotated with which collection it came from — `roleAssignments`, `roleAssignmentScheduleInstances` or `roleEligibilityScheduleInstances`; the transitive membership of every excluded group and every group-carried assignment; the `isMfaRegistered`/`methodsRegistered` row per administrator; and the HTTP status of every Graph call, so that a 403 is visible as a collection failure rather than an empty result.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when either (a) `isEnabled` on the security-defaults policy is true; or (b) at least one Conditional Access policy satisfies all of the following simultaneously: `state` == 'enabled' (both 'enabledForReportingButNotEnforced' and 'disabled' fail); `conditions.users.includeRoles` contains the role template id of every privileged role that has at least one active or eligible holder, or `conditions.users.includeUsers` == ['All']; `conditions.applications.includeApplications` == ['All'] and `conditions.applications.excludeApplications` is empty; `conditions.clientAppTypes` == ['all']; and the grant cannot be satisfied without a second factor, meaning either `grantControls.authenticationStrength.id` is non-null with `grantControls.builtInControls` empty, or `grantControls.builtInControls` contains 'mfa' and either `grantControls.operator` == 'AND' or `builtInControls` == ['mfa']. In addition, the intersection of {active ∪ eligible privileged-role principals, expanded transitively through any group} with {`excludeUsers` ∪ transitive members of `excludeGroups` ∪ holders of `excludeRoles`} must be empty apart from the emergency-access object ids evidenced under 1.6. Any Graph call that returns 403, or any collection whose last page still carried an `@odata.nextLink`, makes the result INCONCLUSIVE and never PASS.
controls.remediation: Create a Conditional Access policy targeting the directory roles rather than a hand-maintained user list, with `conditions.users.includeRoles` set to every privileged role template id in use, `conditions.applications.includeApplications` == ['All'] and no application exclusions, `conditions.clientAppTypes` == ['all'], and `grantControls.authenticationStrength` pointing at the phishing-resistant strength so that SMS and voice cannot satisfy it. If any other grant control is combined with it, set `grantControls.operator` to 'AND' so a compliant device alone cannot stand in for the second factor. Deploy in report-only first, read the impact from the sign-in logs, then set `state` to 'enabled'. Keep the exclusion list to the two emergency-access accounts and nothing else, expand and re-verify those exclusions on a schedule, and add a second policy requiring a compliant or hybrid-joined device for the same population if MCSB IM-7 conditional access on device state is in scope.
controls.caveat: Six false passes. (1) `state` == 'enabledForReportingButNotEnforced' is report-only — the policy body reads as perfect and enforces nothing, so a check that only asserts a matching policy object exists passes a tenant with zero enforcement. (2) `grantControls.operator` == 'OR' with `builtInControls` == ['mfa','compliantDevice'] lets a compliant device alone produce an administrative session with a password; matching on the presence of 'mfa' in the array is therefore not sufficient. (3) `excludeGroups` names a group id, not people; a dynamic group whose membership rule quietly matches most administrators empties the policy without changing the policy, so every exclusion must be expanded through `/groups/{id}/transitiveMembers` at assessment time. (4) `roleAssignmentScheduleInstances` and `roleEligibilityScheduleInstances` require Entra ID P2 and return empty or 403 without it, which reads as an empty administrator population and therefore as nothing to check; `roleManagement/directory/roleAssignments` is the licence-independent view of active assignments and must be the baseline, while `/directoryRoles` is worse still because it only returns roles that have been activated in the tenant. An eligible Global Administrator excluded from the policy is a password-only path to tenant ownership that neither the directoryRoles view nor an unlicensed PIM query will show. (5) Graph and ARM are separate control planes with separate authorisation: a service principal that can read every subscription through ARM typically holds no Graph application role, so all Conditional Access and role calls return 403 while `az account show` succeeds — record the status code, because a 403 rendered as an empty array is a silent pass. (6) Legacy per-user MFA state (`/beta/users/{id}/authentication/requirements`, `perUserMfaState`) is a different mechanism — 'enforced' there does not satisfy a Conditional Access rule, and neither mechanism is reached by the legacy protocols covered in 1.3. `userRegistrationDetails` needs an Entra ID P1 licence and AuditLog.Read.All or Reports.Read.All; a 403 there is a collection error to record, not evidence of clean registration.

controls.title: Any account that can reach the Azure control plane must present a second factor
controls.objective: MCSB IM-6 and IM-7 extend beyond named administrators: a Contributor on one subscription, a guest with a Reader role, or a service account signing in with a password can all drive the Azure Resource Manager control plane. Every human identity able to authenticate to the portal, the CLI, PowerShell or the ARM API must be covered by a strong-authentication policy, otherwise the strength of the administrative control in 1.1 is bounded by the weakest non-administrative account that can still touch resources.
controls.procedure: Enumerate every Conditional Access policy, re-requesting `@odata.nextLink` until it is absent, and identify those whose `conditions.applications.includeApplications` is either ['All'] or contains the Windows Azure Service Management API application id 797f4846-ba00-4fd7-ba43-dac1f8f63013, and whose `conditions.users.includeUsers` is ['All'] with `conditions.users.includeGuestsOrExternalUsers.guestOrExternalUserTypes` covering B2B collaboration guests. Record `state`, `grantControls` and the complete exclusion set. Establish the population that must be covered from three sources rather than one: internal members via `users?$select=id,userPrincipalName,userType,accountEnabled,onPremisesSyncEnabled&$top=999` paged to exhaustion, guests via the same collection filtered on `userType eq 'Guest'` with `$count=true` and the `ConsistencyLevel: eventual` header that advanced queries require, and every principal holding an Azure RBAC assignment anywhere in the estate from an Azure Resource Graph query over `authorizationresources` run at management-group scope rather than against whichever subscription happens to be current. Resource Graph returns at most 1000 rows per request, so page with `--first`/`--skip` until a short page is returned. Read registration reality from `reports/authenticationMethods/userRegistrationDetails` (`isMfaCapable`, `methodsRegistered`) and, where per-user MFA predates Conditional Access in the tenant, sample the beta endpoint `users/<id>/authentication/requirements` for `perUserMfaState` — there is no bulk listing for it, so sampling is the only option and must be declared as such. Read `policies/crossTenantAccessPolicy/default` for `inboundTrust.isMfaAccepted`. Then judge, account by account, whether each exclusion is a documented exception or an unmanaged gap.
api: az extension add --name resource-graph 2>/dev/null; az extension show --name resource-graph --query version

next='https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/users?$select=id,userPrincipalName,userType,accountEnabled,onPremisesSyncEnabled,creationType&$top=999'; : > users_all.json; while [ -n "$next" ]; do az rest --method GET --url "$next" > page.json; jq -c '.value[]' page.json >> users_all.json; next=$(jq -r '."@odata.nextLink" // empty' page.json); done; wc -l users_all.json

az graph query -q "authorizationresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.authorization/roleassignments' | project subscriptionId, principalId=tostring(properties.principalId), principalType=tostring(properties.principalType), roleDefinitionId=tostring(properties.roleDefinitionId) | distinct principalId, principalType" --management-groups <tenant-root-mg-id> --allow-partial-scopes --first 1000 --skip 0
controls.evidence: The `state`, `conditions.users`, `conditions.applications` and `grantControls` of each policy claimed to provide tenant-wide coverage; the enumerated account population split into members, guests and service accounts with their object ids, together with the page count proving the enumeration ran to exhaustion; the distinct principal id list holding any Azure RBAC assignment from the Resource Graph query, with the management-group scope it was run at and whether `--allow-partial-scopes` suppressed any scope; the per-account `isMfaCapable`/`methodsRegistered` rows; the `inboundTrust` object from the cross-tenant access policy; and, for every exclusion, the named business justification and owner the client supplied.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when all of the following hold. (a) At least one Conditional Access policy has `state` == 'enabled' and requires MFA or an authentication strength — `grantControls.authenticationStrength.id` non-null, or `builtInControls` containing 'mfa' with `operator` == 'AND' or `builtInControls` == ['mfa'] — for `conditions.users.includeUsers` == ['All'] over `conditions.applications.includeApplications` == ['All'], or at minimum over an `includeApplications` list containing 797f4846-ba00-4fd7-ba43-dac1f8f63013. (b) `conditions.users.includeGuestsOrExternalUsers.guestOrExternalUserTypes` includes B2B collaboration guests, or `includeUsers` == ['All'] with no guest exclusion. (c) Every object id in the union of `excludeUsers` and the transitive members of `excludeGroups` appears as a row in the client-supplied exception register file, each row carrying a named owner and a review date not in the past. (d) Every excluded object id is absent from the distinct principal list returned by the Resource Graph role-assignment query, or is one of the emergency-access accounts evidenced under 1.6. A partial Resource Graph result, an unpaged user enumeration, or a missing exception register makes the control INCONCLUSIVE rather than PASS.
controls.remediation: Move the tenant to a single all-users, all-apps policy requiring an authentication strength rather than several application-specific policies that overlap unpredictably. Retire per-user MFA state in favour of Conditional Access so that one mechanism governs, since the two evaluate independently and the legacy state does not satisfy a policy grant. For non-human accounts that currently sign in with a password, replace the password flow with a managed identity or a workload identity federation credential (see 1.11) so the account no longer needs an MFA exception at all, and delete the exclusion once it is unused. Where B2B guests hold Azure RBAC assignments, either set `inboundTrust.isMfaAccepted` to false so the guest must perform MFA against your tenant, or accept the partner's factor explicitly in writing.
controls.caveat: Manual because only a human can decide which populations may legitimately sit outside the policy: a directory-synchronisation service account, a kiosk identity and a break-glass account are all defensible exceptions, while a developer's second account and a shared team login are not, and the API returns all four identically — nothing in the object model records intent, ownership or a compensating control, so the exception register has to come from the client and be reconciled by a person. Four concrete traps. (1) Report-only policies (`state` == 'enabledForReportingButNotEnforced') satisfy every structural test and enforce nothing. (2) B2B guests may satisfy your MFA requirement with a factor performed in their own tenant when `crossTenantAccessPolicy` `inboundTrust.isMfaAccepted` is true — the guest is covered on paper by a control you cannot audit and did not configure, so record the inbound trust setting alongside the verdict. (3) The Graph `users` collection pages at 100 by default and `az rest` issues one request and does not follow `@odata.nextLink`, so a tenant of 5,000 users assessed from one page looks small and fully covered; page to exhaustion or declare the run inconclusive. (4) The Resource Graph query must not be left at its default scope: run at the tenant root management group, page past the 1000-row cap, and note that `--allow-partial-scopes` succeeds while silently omitting scopes the identity cannot read, so a scanning identity without a tenant-root role assignment returns a short, clean-looking principal list that misses exactly the subscriptions nobody is watching.

controls.title: Legacy authentication protocols that cannot carry a second factor are refused outright
controls.objective: MCSB IM-6 and IM-1 fail silently if a protocol exists that never reaches the policy engine. Basic-authentication clients — IMAP4, POP3, authenticated SMTP, older Exchange ActiveSync and anything Entra ID reports as 'Other clients' — submit a username and password in one shot with no capability to prompt for a second factor, which makes them the standing bypass for every MFA control in this section and the protocol of choice for password spraying.
controls.procedure: Two independent pieces of evidence are required, because a policy without traffic data cannot prove effectiveness and traffic data without a policy cannot prove intent. First establish the enforcement mechanism: read `policies/identitySecurityDefaultsEnforcementPolicy` for `isEnabled`, since security defaults themselves block legacy authentication and a tenant running them will legitimately have no blocking Conditional Access policy at all. If security defaults are off, list all Conditional Access policies paging to exhaustion and find one whose `conditions.clientAppTypes` is exactly ['exchangeActiveSync', 'other'], whose `conditions.users.includeUsers` is ['All'], whose `conditions.applications.includeApplications` is ['All'], whose `grantControls.builtInControls` contains 'block', and whose `state` is 'enabled'. Record its exclusion set and, from `auditLogs/directoryAudits`, the date it was last modified. Second, query the sign-in log for real legacy traffic over the retained window, covering both event types: v1.0 `auditLogs/signIns` returns interactive sign-ins unless the filter opts into others, so run the legacy-client filter once plainly and once combined with `signInEventTypes/any(t: t eq 'nonInteractiveUser')`, paging through `@odata.nextLink` each time, and record `status.errorCode`, `conditionalAccessStatus`, `userPrincipalName`, `clientAppUsed` and `ipAddress` for every row. A successful legacy sign-in (`status.errorCode` == 0) after the policy's last modification date is the disproof of the policy. Bound the negative result by reading `subscribedSkus` to establish whether sign-in log retention is 7 days or 30.
api: az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/auditLogs/signIns?$filter=createdDateTime ge <iso8601-30-days-ago> and (clientAppUsed eq %27IMAP4%27 or clientAppUsed eq %27POP3%27 or clientAppUsed eq %27Authenticated SMTP%27 or clientAppUsed eq %27Other clients%27 or clientAppUsed eq %27Exchange ActiveSync%27)' --query 'value[].{t:createdDateTime,upn:userPrincipalName,app:clientAppUsed,ca:conditionalAccessStatus,err:status.errorCode,ip:ipAddress}'

az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/auditLogs/signIns?$filter=(signInEventTypes/any(t: t eq %27nonInteractiveUser%27)) and createdDateTime ge <iso8601-30-days-ago> and (clientAppUsed eq %27IMAP4%27 or clientAppUsed eq %27POP3%27 or clientAppUsed eq %27Authenticated SMTP%27 or clientAppUsed eq %27Other clients%27)' --query 'value[].{t:createdDateTime,upn:userPrincipalName,app:clientAppUsed,err:status.errorCode}'

next='https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/auditLogs/signIns?$filter=clientAppUsed eq %27Other clients%27&$top=999'; : > legacy.json; while [ -n "$next" ]; do az rest --method GET --url "$next" > page.json; jq -c '.value[]' page.json >> legacy.json; next=$(jq -r '."@odata.nextLink" // empty' page.json); done

az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/auditLogs/directoryAudits?$filter=activityDisplayName eq %27Update conditional access policy%27&$top=100' --query 'value[].{t:activityDateTime,by:initiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName,target:targetResources[0].displayName}'
controls.evidence: The security-defaults `isEnabled` value; the blocking policy's `id`, `displayName`, `state`, `conditions.clientAppTypes`, `conditions.users`, `conditions.applications.includeApplications` and `grantControls` quoted from the Graph response, with the last-modification timestamp from `directoryAudits`; every sign-in row returned by both the interactive and the non-interactive legacy-protocol filters, with `createdDateTime`, `userPrincipalName`, `clientAppUsed`, `conditionalAccessStatus`, `status.errorCode` and `ipAddress`, plus the page count proving each query ran to exhaustion; and the tenant SKU list establishing the sign-in log retention window that bounds the negative result.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when either (a) `isEnabled` on the security-defaults policy is true, or (b) a Conditional Access policy has `state` == 'enabled', `conditions.clientAppTypes` == ['exchangeActiveSync','other'] exactly, `conditions.users.includeUsers` == ['All'], `conditions.applications.includeApplications` == ['All'] and `grantControls.builtInControls` containing 'block', with no exclusions other than the emergency-access object ids from 1.6; AND, in both cases, the retained sign-in log contains zero rows across both the interactive and the non-interactive queries whose `clientAppUsed` is one of the legacy values and whose `status.errorCode` == 0. A tenant with the policy but with successful legacy sign-ins dated after the policy's last modification is PARTIALLY_MET and must name the accounts. A tenant whose `subscribedSkus` contain no Entra ID P1 or P2 SKU cannot produce a 30-day negative and is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW, not PASS; the same applies if any sign-in query ended on a page that still carried an `@odata.nextLink`.
controls.remediation: Deploy a dedicated block policy scoped to exactly the two legacy client app types, all users and all cloud apps, keeping it separate from the MFA policy so that a change to one does not silently loosen the other. Before enabling, run the sign-in queries to find which mailboxes and service accounts still use legacy protocols and migrate them to modern authentication libraries or to a managed identity. Independently, disable the protocols at the workload: Conditional Access governs authentication and not protocol availability, so authenticated SMTP must also be turned off per mailbox and organisation-wide through Exchange Online administration, which is not reachable from `az` and has to be evidenced separately.
controls.caveat: The most damaging trap here is inverted logic: for a block policy `conditions.clientAppTypes` must be exactly ['exchangeActiveSync', 'other'], because the value ['all'] would block every client including browsers. A checker written to demand 'all' marks a correct tenant as failing and, when relaxed, marks a policy scoped to browsers only as passing. Four more. (1) Conditional Access cannot switch a protocol off; authenticated SMTP to Exchange Online is governed by mailbox and organisation settings in Exchange, so a tenant that passes the policy check may still accept SMTP AUTH with a password, and that evidence cannot be gathered with the Azure CLI. (2) The Graph sign-in log retains 7 days without an Entra ID P1 or P2 SKU and 30 days with one, so zero rows can mean 'no licence' rather than 'no legacy traffic' — which is why the SKU call is part of the evidence and not an optional extra. (3) v1.0 `auditLogs/signIns` returns interactive sign-ins unless the filter explicitly opts into `signInEventTypes`, and a large share of IMAP/POP/SMTP activity is recorded as non-interactive; querying only the default event type produces an empty result set on a tenant with continuous legacy traffic. (4) `az rest` returns the first page only; a policy list truncated at page one reads as 'no blocking policy exists' and a sign-in list truncated at page one reads as 'no legacy traffic', so the same defect produces a false fail on one call and a false pass on the other. Sign-in and audit log reads require AuditLog.Read.All — a 403 must be recorded as a collection failure, since an error body parsed for `.value` yields an empty array indistinguishable from a clean log.

controls.title: The Global Administrator population is small, cloud-native, and never a single account
controls.objective: MCSB PA-1 and PA-5 pull in opposite directions on purpose. Every Global Administrator is a full tenant compromise if taken, so the population must be minimal; but a tenant with one Global Administrator is one lost phone or one departed employee away from an unrecoverable lock-out, and a tenant whose only administrators are synchronised from on-premises Active Directory hands cloud tenancy control to whoever owns the domain controller. The healthy state is a handful of accounts, all created in the cloud, all strongly authenticated, and all accounted for.
controls.procedure: Read the population from the role-management plane rather than the legacy directory-roles view, because the latter only returns roles that have been activated at least once in the tenant. Filter on the well-known role template id 62e90394-69f5-4237-9190-012177145e10 rather than on a display name, since the display name differs between APIs and localisations. Take active holders from `roleManagement/directory/roleAssignments?$filter=roleDefinitionId eq '62e90394-69f5-4237-9190-012177145e10'&$expand=principal`, which works in every tenant regardless of licence, and cross-check against `roleAssignmentScheduleInstances` where Entra ID P2 is present. Separately, and without merging the counts, list eligible holders from `roleEligibilityScheduleInstances` with the same filter. Expand every principal that is a group through `/groups/{id}/transitiveMembers`, and also read `identityGovernance/privilegedAccess/group/eligibilityScheduleInstances?$filter=groupId eq '<id>'`, because a principal who is only PIM-eligible for the group is not returned as a member yet can become one on demand. For each resolved user read `userType`, `onPremisesSyncEnabled`, `accountEnabled`, `creationType` and `userPrincipalName` from `/users/{id}`, check the UPN suffix against the verified domains from `/domains`, and read its MFA registration from `reports/authenticationMethods/userRegistrationDetails`. Finally list partner access with `tenantRelationships/delegatedAdminRelationships` and record every relationship whose `status` is 'active' together with the `roleDefinitionId` values in `accessDetails.unifiedRoles`.
controls.evidence: The full list of principals returned by the active Global Administrator query from `roleAssignments`, each with object id, resolved `userPrincipalName` or service principal `displayName` and principal type, plus the `assignmentType`, `memberType` and `endDateTime` from the schedule-instance view where the tenant is licensed for it; the separate list of PIM-eligible holders; for group-carried assignments the transitive membership of that group and its PIM-for-Groups eligible principals; per user the `userType`, `onPremisesSyncEnabled`, `accountEnabled` and `creationType` values, the verified-domain list the UPN suffix was checked against, and the `isMfaRegistered` row; and every delegated admin relationship with `status`, `endDateTime` and the `roleDefinitionId` values it conveys.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when the count of distinct principals holding an active Global Administrator assignment — taken from `roleAssignments`, with any group principal replaced by its transitive members plus its PIM-for-Groups eligible principals — is at least 2 and at most 4; every one has `onPremisesSyncEnabled` not true; every one has a UPN whose suffix appears in the tenant's verified domain list, `userType` not 'Guest', and no '#EXT#' substring; every one shows `isMfaRegistered` true in `userRegistrationDetails`; and no delegated admin relationship with `status` == 'active' carries 62e90394-69f5-4237-9190-012177145e10 in `accessDetails.unifiedRoles`. The count of PIM-eligible Global Administrators is reported alongside but never merged into the active count. A 403 on any of these collections, or a `roleAssignments` result of zero principals, is a collection failure to investigate rather than a verdict.
controls.remediation: Reduce standing Global Administrator to two dedicated cloud-only accounts used for nothing else, and move every other administrator to a role that matches their actual job (User Administrator, Application Administrator, Security Administrator) held as a PIM-eligible assignment per 1.5. If the tenant currently has one administrator, create the second emergency-access account before removing anything. Break the on-premises path by ensuring no synchronised account holds the role. Maintain a written inventory of every service principal that holds a privileged role and reconcile it at each review. Review delegated admin relationships and terminate any partner relationship that no longer corresponds to a live engagement, granting partners the narrowest unified roles rather than Global Administrator.
controls.caveat: Six traps, two of which flip the verdict in opposite directions. (1) 'Fewer is better' is wrong below two: a single Global Administrator is a finding, so the rule has a floor as well as a ceiling. (2) PIM-eligible administrators are not returned by the active-assignment query at all; a tenant reporting two standing Global Administrators while forty are eligible with self-service activation has forty administrators, so both collections must be read and reported separately. (3) A role assigned to a role-assignable group returns one principal — the group — and the naive count is off by however many members it has. A role-assignable group cannot use dynamic membership and cannot be nested, so transitive expansion is bounded, but PIM for Groups can make a principal eligible for membership without ever appearing in `/members` or `/transitiveMembers`, and that principal is a Global Administrator on demand. (4) `roleAssignmentScheduleInstances` and `roleEligibilityScheduleInstances` require Entra ID P2; in an unlicensed tenant they return empty or 403, so a check built solely on them reports zero administrators, which here reads as a fail for the wrong reason and would read as a pass in any rule phrased as 'no excessive holders'. Use `roleManagement/directory/roleAssignments` as the baseline. (5) Delegated admin relationships (the partner/CSP path) grant administrative roles from an entirely different tenant and appear in no user, group or role-member listing; a tenant that is clean by every internal measure can still be administered from outside, and from the customer side the object exposes the relationship and its roles but not a partner tenant field, so the counterparty must be confirmed out of band. (6) Filtering `groups` on `isAssignableToRole` is an advanced query: without `$count=true` and the `ConsistencyLevel: eventual` header the request fails, and an error body parsed for `.value` yields an empty list that reads as 'no role-assignable groups exist'. Judging whether a service principal holding the role belongs to a sanctioned automation is a human decision and is deliberately kept out of the mechanical PASS condition.

controls.title: Privileged roles are activated on demand and expire, rather than being held permanently
controls.objective: MCSB PA-2 asks for no standing access: a role held permanently is exploitable at any moment by anyone who compromises the account, whereas a role that must be activated with a justification, an approval and a second factor, and which expires by itself, is exploitable only inside a short window that produces an audit record. Just-in-time assignment also makes over-provisioning visible, because an eligible role nobody ever activates is an entitlement nobody needs.
controls.procedure: Confirm the tenant is licensed for the capability first with `subscribedSkus`, looking for AAD_PREMIUM_P2, EMSPREMIUM, SPE_E5 or a Microsoft Entra ID Governance SKU, since Privileged Identity Management requires Entra ID P2 and its absence changes how every empty collection below must be read. On the directory plane, list active assignments with `roleManagement/directory/roleAssignmentScheduleInstances?$expand=roleDefinition,principal` and treat a row as standing access when `assignmentType` is 'Assigned' and `endDateTime` is null; rows with `assignmentType` 'Activated' are transient activations and are counted separately. Cross-check the same population against the licence-independent `roleManagement/directory/roleAssignments?$expand=principal`, because in an unlicensed tenant the schedule collections are the ones that come back empty while the assignments still exist. List entitlements with `roleEligibilityScheduleInstances?$expand=roleDefinition,principal`. Read the activation rules with `policies/roleManagementPolicyAssignments?$filter=scopeId eq '/' and scopeType eq 'Directory'&$expand=policy($expand=rules)`, then inspect rules by id: `Enablement_EndUser_Assignment` for `enabledRules`, `Approval_EndUser_Assignment` for `setting.isApprovalRequired` and its approver list, `Expiration_EndUser_Assignment` for `maximumDuration`, and `Expiration_Admin_Eligibility` for `isExpirationRequired`. Then repeat the whole exercise on the resource plane, which is a different control plane with a different endpoint and a different credential: enumerate every subscription with `az account list --all` and every management group with `az account management-group list`, and for each scope call `roleEligibilityScheduleInstances` and `roleAssignmentScheduleInstances` under `Microsoft.Authorization` at api-version 2020-10-01, where the equivalent fields are `properties.assignmentType`, `properties.memberType` and `properties.endDateTime`. Do not rely on whichever subscription is currently selected.
api: az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/policies/roleManagementPolicyAssignments?$filter=scopeId eq %27/%27 and scopeType eq %27Directory%27&$expand=policy($expand=rules)' --query 'value[].{role:roleDefinitionId,rules:policy.rules[].{id:id,enabled:enabledRules,approval:setting.isApprovalRequired,max:maximumDuration,expreq:isExpirationRequired}}'

az role assignment list --subscription <subscription-id> --all --include-inherited --query "[?roleDefinitionName=='Owner' || roleDefinitionName=='User Access Administrator'].{principal:principalId,type:principalType,role:roleDefinitionName,scope:scope}"
controls.evidence: The SKU list establishing whether Entra ID P2 is present. Per privileged role: the list of standing assignments (`assignmentType` 'Assigned' with null `endDateTime`) with principal object id and `memberType`, reconciled against the licence-independent `roleAssignments` view; the list of eligible assignments; and the governing policy's rule objects quoted by rule id — `Enablement_EndUser_Assignment.enabledRules`, `Approval_EndUser_Assignment.setting.isApprovalRequired` with its approver list, `Expiration_EndUser_Assignment.maximumDuration`, `Expiration_Admin_Eligibility.isExpirationRequired`. Plus, for every subscription id returned by `az account list --all` and every management group name, the ARM assignment and eligibility schedule instances with `properties.assignmentType` and `properties.endDateTime`, cross-checked against `az role assignment list --all --include-inherited`; and the group eligibility instances for any role-assignable group.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when all of the following hold. (a) On the directory plane, for every privileged role, the number of rows with `assignmentType` == 'Assigned' and `endDateTime` == null is zero apart from the emergency-access object ids evidenced under 1.6. (b) On the resource plane, for Owner and User Access Administrator at every subscription id returned by `az account list --all` and every management group name returned by `az account management-group list`, the number of rows with `properties.assignmentType` == 'Assigned' and `properties.endDateTime` == null is likewise zero apart from those same object ids. (c) The governing role management policy has `Enablement_EndUser_Assignment.enabledRules` containing both 'MultiFactorAuthentication' and 'Justification', `Approval_EndUser_Assignment.setting.isApprovalRequired` == true, and `Expiration_EndUser_Assignment.maximumDuration` no longer than PT8H. (d) Every row whose `memberType` is 'Group' has been resolved through the group's membership and its PIM-for-Groups eligibility instances, and those principals are included in the counts above. A tenant whose `subscribedSkus` contain no Entra ID P2 or Governance SKU is NOT_MET on the design of standing access, not NOT_APPLICABLE and never PASS on empty collections.
controls.remediation: Convert each standing assignment to an eligible one and delete the permanent assignment afterwards — creating the eligibility without removing the assignment changes nothing. Set the role management policy for each privileged role so activation demands a second factor, a justification and an approver who is not the requester, cap the activation window at eight hours or less, and require eligibility itself to expire so entitlements are re-justified. Apply the same pattern on the resource plane for Owner and User Access Administrator at management group and subscription scope, remembering that this is configured through a separate API and does not inherit from the directory-role settings, and use PIM for Groups where a role is carried by a role-assignable group so that group membership is itself just-in-time.
controls.caveat: Timing, indirection and scope are what break this check. (1) `assignmentType` 'Activated' rows are transient: a run during a change window shows activations that are not standing access, and a run at 02:00 shows a clean tenant that is not clean, so the standing test must be `assignmentType` == 'Assigned' with a null `endDateTime`, and activation rows should be reported as usage rather than as findings. (2) Role-assignable groups defeat the whole model: a role can be eligible-only while the group carrying it has permanent members, so `memberType` 'Group' rows must be followed into the group's membership and into `identityGovernance/privilegedAccess/group/eligibilityScheduleInstances`, which requires a `$filter` on `groupId` or `principalId` and returns nothing useful without one. (3) The directory plane and the resource plane are separate products reached with separate tokens — a tenant with immaculate directory-role PIM can still have a permanent Owner on every subscription, and no Graph call will ever show it. (4) The ARM calls are scope-by-scope: iterating only the currently selected subscription, or only the subscriptions returned without `--all`, reports zero standing Owners for an estate where they exist in the subscriptions the run never visited; disabled subscriptions and management-group-scoped assignments are the usual omissions. (5) Absence of an Entra ID P2 licence makes the schedule collections return empty, which is indistinguishable from a compliant tenant unless the SKU call is part of the evidence and the licence-independent `roleAssignments` view is read alongside; treat an unlicensed tenant as a design finding, never as a pass. (6) The policy filter needs `scopeId eq '/'` with `scopeType eq 'Directory'`; a mistyped scope returns an empty rule set that reads as 'no weak rules found', and note the ARM field names differ from the Graph ones (`properties.endDateTime`, not `endDateTime`), so a parser written for one plane silently finds nothing on the other.

controls.title: Two emergency-access accounts exist, sit outside every lock-out path, and their use raises an alarm
controls.objective: MCSB PA-5 and LT-4 together: the same Conditional Access, MFA and just-in-time controls that make a tenant safe can also make it unenterable — an expired federation certificate, a deleted authentication method or a misconfigured policy can lock every administrator out at once. Two accounts deliberately exempted from those controls preserve recoverability, but because they are exempt they are the single most attractive target in the tenant, so their credentials must be escrowed and every use of them must be alerted on.
controls.procedure: Ask the client to name the emergency-access accounts before looking, then verify rather than discover — an account found by searching for exclusions is indistinguishable from an attacker's backdoor. For each named account read `users/<upn>?$select=id,userPrincipalName,userType,accountEnabled,onPremisesSyncEnabled,passwordPolicies,createdDateTime` and confirm it is cloud-native, enabled, uses a verified domain the tenant owns, and is not a mailbox-bearing everyday identity. Enumerate its registered credentials with `/users/{id}/authentication/methods`. Pull every Conditional Access policy, paging to exhaustion, and compute per policy whether the account is reached — expanding `excludeGroups` transitively — so that you can state it is excluded from all of them rather than from the ones you happened to read. Confirm its directory role with `roleManagement/directory/roleAssignments?$filter=principalId eq '<object-id>'`. Then evidence the alerting on the ARM side, which is a different control plane: the Entra diagnostic settings are a tenant-level ARM resource read with `az rest --method GET --url 'https://management.azure.com/providers/microsoft.aadiam/diagnosticSettings?api-version=2017-04-01-preview'`, not with a resource-scoped diagnostic-settings list. Confirm the SignInLogs category is enabled and note the destination workspace id. Then look for the detection in both places it can live: `az monitor scheduled-query list` in every subscription returned by `az account list --all`, and Microsoft Sentinel analytics rules under the destination workspace, since a Sentinel rule is a different resource type and never appears in the scheduled-query list. Resolve the rule's action group and its recipients. Finally read the accounts' recent sign-ins from the audit log to confirm they have not been used casually.
controls.evidence: For each named emergency-access account: the user object showing `onPremisesSyncEnabled` false, `accountEnabled` true and a UPN in a verified tenant domain; the registered authentication methods; its active directory role assignment from `roleAssignments`; the exclusion state computed against every enabled Conditional Access policy with all policy ids listed and every `excludeGroups` expansion shown; the tenant diagnostic setting showing the SignInLogs category enabled and the destination workspace resource id; the alert or analytics rule whose query text contains the account object id, quoted, together with its enabled state and its action group; the action group's resolved recipients; and the account's sign-in history over the retained window.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when exactly two accounts are named by the client and verified; both have `onPremisesSyncEnabled` not true, `accountEnabled` true and a UPN suffix in the tenant's verified domain list; both hold a permanent Global Administrator assignment in `roleManagement/directory/roleAssignments` (the deliberate exception to 1.5); for every policy with `state` == 'enabled', both object ids appear in `excludeUsers` or in the transitive membership of an `excludeGroups` entry; the set of principals excluded from every enabled policy contains those two object ids and nothing else; a tenant diagnostic setting has the SignInLogs category with `enabled` true and a non-empty workspace destination; and at least one enabled scheduled-query alert rule or Sentinel analytics rule, in any subscription returned by `az account list --all`, has query text containing both object ids and an action group whose resolved receiver list is non-empty.
controls.remediation: Create two cloud-only accounts in a verified tenant domain, assign each a permanent Global Administrator role, register a strong credential on each (ideally a FIDO2 key held in separate physical custody), and exclude both from all Conditional Access policies including future ones by putting the exclusion in the deployment template rather than the portal. Escrow the credentials in split custody with a documented retrieval process. Configure the tenant diagnostic setting to export SignInLogs to a workspace and create an alert on any sign-in by those object ids routed to an action group that pages a human, then confirm delivery by firing it. Exercise the accounts on a scheduled cadence so the credentials are known to work before they are needed.
controls.caveat: Manual because the parts that decide the outcome are not in any API: whether the credentials are genuinely escrowed, held in split custody by two different people, periodically tested, and whether the paged recipient is a person who would actually respond — an API can show a rule and a mailbox but not whether anyone reads it. Four traps, two of which produce the opposite of the intended verdict. (1) 'Excluded from every Conditional Access policy' is exactly the signature of an attacker-created backdoor account, so discovering excluded accounts and calling them break-glass inverts the control — reconcile the excluded set against a client-approved list of names and treat any additional excluded principal as a finding, not as extra resilience. (2) The exclusion is per policy, so a policy created after the review does not carry it; a tenant that passes today locks itself out on the next policy authored by someone who does not know the convention, which is why the exclusion must live in the deployment pipeline. (3) Detection can legitimately live in Microsoft Sentinel, whose analytics rules are Microsoft.SecurityInsights resources and are invisible to `az monitor scheduled-query list`; conversely, running the alert query against only the current subscription misses a rule that lives in the security subscription, so the first form produces a false fail and the second a false pass. The Entra diagnostic settings are equally easy to get wrong: they are a tenant-level ARM resource under `providers/microsoft.aadiam`, and passing that path as the `--resource` of a resource-scoped diagnostic-settings query returns nothing, which reads as 'no logging configured'. (4) An emergency-access account synchronised from on-premises defeats the purpose, since the on-premises directory is one of the failure modes being recovered from; and alert-rule existence is not alert delivery, so the action group's receivers must be enumerated — a rule pointing at an unmonitored mailbox, or one whose `enabled` is false, reads as compliant.

controls.title: External identities are invited only by approved staff and land in the restricted directory role
controls.objective: MCSB PA-3 and PA-4 govern how identities enter and leave. A guest in Entra ID is a real principal in your directory that can enumerate users, groups and applications and can be granted Azure RBAC like anyone else. If any member can invite anyone, and guests receive the default rather than the restricted directory permission set, the tenant's identity boundary is set by whichever employee last pasted an address into an invitation dialog.
controls.procedure: Everything here is on the Microsoft Graph (tenant) control plane, not ARM, so it needs a token with Graph directory-read scope — a subscription reader credential answers none of it. Read the tenant-wide settings from the authorization policy singleton: `az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/policies/authorizationPolicy'`, capturing `allowInvitesFrom`, `guestUserRoleId` and `defaultUserRolePermissions.allowedToReadOtherUsers`. The v1.0 response is a single object; older tooling and the beta path have returned a collection under `value`, so the parser must handle both shapes rather than indexing blindly. If `allowInvitesFrom` is 'adminsAndGuestInviters', the population that can actually invite is the membership of the Guest Inviter directory role, so enumerate it: `az rest --method GET --url "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/directoryRoles(roleTemplateId='95e79109-95c0-4d8e-aee3-d01accf2d47b')/members"` — an unactivated role returns 404 rather than an empty list, which is a different fact and must be recorded as such. Then read the cross-tenant access configuration, which governs B2B independently of the invitation setting — `az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/policies/crossTenantAccessPolicy/default'` for the tenant default, and `.../crossTenantAccessPolicy/partners` for every per-partner override, since a partner entry supersedes the default for that tenant. Enumerate the guest population with `az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/users?$filter=userType%20eq%20%27Guest%27&$select=id,userPrincipalName,displayName,userType,creationType,externalUserState,createdDateTime,signInActivity&$count=true' --headers 'ConsistencyLevel=eventual'` — percent-encode the spaces in the filter, since a raw space in the URL is not reliably encoded for you — and drive the pagination yourself by re-issuing `az rest` against each `@odata.nextLink`, because `az rest` returns one page and never follows it. For each guest compute the age since `createdDateTime` and the interval since `signInActivity.lastSuccessfulSignInDateTime`. Cover the non-invitation entry paths as well: list self-service sign-up flows with `az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/identity/b2xUserFlows'` and entitlement-management access packages, both of which mint external principals without an invitation. Finally check whether the population is under governance at all by listing access review definitions and their most recent instances.
controls.evidence: The `allowInvitesFrom` and `guestUserRoleId` values from the authorization policy singleton, quoted with the GUID exactly as returned, alongside `defaultUserRolePermissions.allowedToReadOtherUsers`; the Guest Inviter role membership (or the 404 showing the role is not activated) where the invitation setting delegates to it; the cross-tenant default object and every partner override with its tenant id; the enumerated guest list with object id, `creationType`, `externalUserState` ('PendingAcceptance' or 'Accepted'), `createdDateTime` and `signInActivity.lastSuccessfulSignInDateTime`, together with the number of `@odata.nextLink` pages retrieved and the final page's absence of a nextLink as proof the enumeration completed; the b2xUserFlows collection; and the access review definition covering guests with its `status` and recurrence, or its absence. Every non-200 response is recorded with its HTTP status.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when all of: `allowInvitesFrom` is 'none' or 'adminsAndGuestInviters' (the values 'adminsGuestInvitersAndAllMembers' and 'everyone' are FAIL); where it is 'adminsAndGuestInviters', every member returned by the Guest Inviter role is an enabled account with `userType` 'Member'; `guestUserRoleId` equals the restricted-guest template 2af84b1e-32c8-42b7-82bc-daa82404023b (10dae51f-b6af-4016-8d66-8c2a99b929b3 and a0b1b346-4d3e-4e8b-98f8-753987be4970 are FAIL); the cross-tenant default does not permit inbound B2B collaboration for all users and all applications, and no partner override re-opens it; the `b2xUserFlows` collection is empty or every flow returned is named in the engagement's supplied external-access inventory file; no guest is older than 90 days with no successful sign-in and no access package assignment; and a recurring access review definition whose scope selects guest users exists with `status` 'InProgress' or a completed instance whose `endDateTime` falls inside the last recurrence period. Guests for which `signInActivity` is absent from the response, and any call that returned a non-200, are REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW and block a PASS rather than counting toward one.
controls.remediation: Set `allowInvitesFrom` to 'adminsAndGuestInviters' and delegate invitation through the Guest Inviter role rather than leaving it with all members. Set `guestUserRoleId` to the restricted-guest template so guests cannot enumerate the directory. Replace ad-hoc invitations with entitlement management access packages that carry an expiry and an approver, so external access has a defined end date at creation time. Configure per-partner cross-tenant access entries for the organisations you actually work with and leave the default closed. Disable or scope any self-service sign-up flow you did not intend. Create a recurring access review over guest users with the sponsoring business owner as reviewer and auto-removal on no response.
controls.caveat: Five false passes. (1) The cross-tenant access policy has a default object and a per-partner collection, and the partner entry wins — reading only the default and finding it closed is a false pass in a tenant that opened everything for one partner tenant, so both calls are mandatory. (2) `guestUserRoleId` is a GUID, so a naive 'the value is set' check passes on a0b1b346-4d3e-4e8b-98f8-753987be4970, the member-equivalent role that gives guests the same directory read access as employees, and on the 10dae51f default which is only partially restricted; the value must be compared, not tested for presence. (3) `allowInvitesFrom` governs the invitation API only — self-service sign-up user flows, entitlement management access packages and B2B direct connect all create external principals without an invitation, so a locked-down invitation setting alongside an open sign-up flow produces guests nobody invited. (4) `az rest` issues exactly one request and does not follow `@odata.nextLink`, so a tenant with more than 999 guests silently returns the first page and a dormancy rule computed over it reports a clean, small guest population; the collector must loop on nextLink and record the page count. (5) `signInActivity` requires an Entra ID P1 licence and the AuditLog.Read.All scope, and it is omitted from the response rather than erroring when unavailable — an unlicensed tenant returns every guest with no sign-in data, so a dormancy rule that reads absent as 'recent' flags nobody and reads as compliant. Note also that the v1.0 authorization policy is a singleton object while some paths return it wrapped in `value`, and that the Guest Inviter role returns 404 when never activated, which is not the same fact as an empty membership.

controls.title: No external or guest identity holds directory privilege or subscription ownership
controls.objective: MCSB PA-1 and PA-3: an external identity is authenticated by another organisation, whose password policy, MFA enforcement, joiner-mover-leaver process and breach history are outside your control and outside your audit. Granting such an identity a privileged directory role or an Owner assignment on a subscription exports administrative control of your estate to a directory you cannot assess, and the offboarding of that person is an event you will never see.
controls.procedure: This control spans both control planes and must be run against both, with both credentials: Microsoft Graph for the tenant plane and ARM for the subscription plane. On the Entra plane, list active and eligible directory role holders from the PIM schedule collections (`roleAssignmentScheduleInstances` and `roleEligibilityScheduleInstances`, both `$expand=roleDefinition,principal`) AND from the non-PIM `roleManagement/directory/roleAssignments`, because the schedule collections require Entra ID P2 and return an error or nothing in a tenant without it. Expand any group principal transitively with `/groups/{id}/transitiveMembers`, and for each such group also read `membershipRule` and `membershipRuleProcessingState`, since a dynamic group's membership is a query result that can admit an external principal after your snapshot. Resolve each resulting user with `/users/{id}?$select=id,userPrincipalName,userType,creationType,externalUserState,identities`. On the ARM plane, answer the whole estate in one call with Resource Graph rather than looping subscriptions: `az graph query -q "authorizationresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.authorization/roleassignments' | extend pid=tostring(properties.principalId), ptype=tostring(properties.principalType), rid=tolower(tostring(properties.roleDefinitionId)), scope=tostring(properties.scope) | join kind=leftouter (authorizationresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.authorization/roledefinitions' | project rid=tolower(id), roleName=tostring(properties.roleName), roleType=tostring(properties.type), perms=properties.permissions) on rid | project subscriptionId, scope, roleName, roleType, perms, pid, ptype" --management-groups <tenant-root-mg-id> --allow-partial-scopes --first 1000 --skip 0`, incrementing `--skip` by 1000 until fewer than 1000 rows return. Keep `perms` and `roleType` in the projection so custom roles can be judged by what they grant rather than by their name. Resolve every distinct `pid` of type User or Group through `directoryObjects/getByIds` in batches of at most 1000 ids, and classify each as internal or external from `userType`, `creationType` == 'Invitation' and the `identities[].issuer` value, not from the UPN string alone.
api: az graph query -q "authorizationresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.authorization/roleassignments' | extend pid=tostring(properties.principalId), ptype=tostring(properties.principalType), rid=tolower(tostring(properties.roleDefinitionId)), scope=tostring(properties.scope) | join kind=leftouter (authorizationresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.authorization/roledefinitions' | project rid=tolower(id), roleName=tostring(properties.roleName), roleType=tostring(properties.type), perms=properties.permissions) on rid | project subscriptionId, scope, roleName, roleType, perms, pid, ptype" --management-groups <tenant-root-mg-id> --allow-partial-scopes --first 1000 --skip 0
controls.evidence: Every Resource Graph row granting a role at any scope, with `scope`, `roleName`, `roleType`, the role's action set for custom roles, `pid` and `ptype`, plus the `--skip` sequence and row counts proving the paging ran to exhaustion; the Graph resolution of each principal id showing `userType`, `creationType`, `externalUserState` and `identities[].issuer`; the directory-role holder list from the non-PIM roleAssignments collection and from both schedule-instance collections, with the HTTP status of the schedule calls so a P2-less tenant is visible as such; for every group principal, its transitive membership and whether it is dynamic (`membershipRule` present); and, for every principal id that Graph does not return, the assignment id and scope recorded as an orphaned or unresolvable assignment.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when no principal classified as external — `userType` == 'Guest', or `creationType` == 'Invitation', or an `identities[].issuer` that is neither one of the tenant's verified domains nor the tenant's own issuer (values such as 'ExternalAzureAD', 'mail', 'google.com', 'facebook.com' are external) — holds any active or eligible Entra directory role of any kind, and none holds Owner, Contributor, User Access Administrator or Role Based Access Control Administrator, nor any custom role definition whose action set contains `*` or `Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write`, at any management group, subscription, resource group or resource scope. A role assignment whose principal id is not returned by `getByIds` is a FAIL row in its own right, not ignorable noise. A group holding any of those roles whose `membershipRule` is non-empty is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW and blocks a PASS, since its membership is evaluated after the snapshot. Any Graph or Resource Graph call that returned a non-200, and any Resource Graph result flagged as partial by `--allow-partial-scopes`, blocks a PASS.
controls.remediation: Remove the external principal from the role and re-grant the access through a mechanism with an owner and an expiry: an entitlement management access package for project-based external collaborators, or a PIM-eligible assignment with an approval requirement for a partner administrator who genuinely needs it. Where an external party needs to operate resources, prefer a dedicated internal account for that engagement over a guest in a privileged role. Replace dynamic groups in privileged role assignments with assigned groups whose membership changes are auditable events. Delete every orphaned role assignment whose principal no longer exists, since re-creating a principal with the same object id restores the grant.
controls.caveat: Six traps. (1) The `#EXT#` substring is a convention, not a guarantee: a guest whose home tenant has a verified domain you also own, or one converted to a member account, has a perfectly ordinary UPN, so classification must use `userType`, `creationType` and `identities[].issuer` together. (2) `az graph query` returns 100 rows by default and silently stops there — in a real estate that is a fraction of the assignments and the query reports clean, so `--first 1000` plus `--skip` paging to exhaustion is mandatory, and `--allow-partial-scopes` succeeds while omitting scopes the credential cannot read, which must be reported rather than absorbed. (3) Resource Graph rows for a subscription do not include assignments inherited from the management group above it; an external principal made Owner at a management group is invisible in per-subscription rows and is caught only by control 1.10. (4) An assignment whose principal has been deleted still exists and still appears in Resource Graph while `getByIds` simply omits the id — and `getByIds` also omits ids the caller lacks permission to read — so treating 'principal not returned' as 'not a guest' converts the highest-risk row into a pass. (5) The PIM schedule collections require Entra ID P2; in a tenant without it they error or return nothing, and a collector that reads that as 'no privileged directory roles held' produces the cleanest possible false pass — the non-PIM `roleManagement/directory/roleAssignments` collection is the mandatory cross-check. (6) Matching privileged ARM roles by display name misses a custom role definition granting `*`, and misses a group whose dynamic membership rule (for example one keyed on a mail domain or an extension attribute) will admit guests without any role assignment ever changing.

controls.title: Subscription ownership rests with a small, group-managed set and no legacy co-administrators
controls.objective: MCSB PA-1 and PA-7: Owner on a subscription is Contributor plus the ability to grant roles, which makes it self-perpetuating — an Owner can assign Owner. Held directly by individual users it is untraceable to a role or a process; held by many it means nobody can say who can change anything; and held by a residual classic co-administrator it is full control through a plane that modern role-assignment listings do not read.
controls.procedure: Enumerate the subscription estate first from the tenant, not from the CLI's current context: `az account list --all --query "[?state=='Enabled'].{id:id,name:name,tenant:tenantId}"`, and reconcile that count against the management group tree from `az account management-group show --name <tenant-root-mg-id> --expand --recurse`, because a subscription the reader credential cannot see is absent from the first list and present in the second. Note that `az account list --all` only covers tenants the signed-in identity has actually authenticated to, so a multi-tenant estate needs `az login --tenant <id>` per tenant before the counts mean anything. Then answer the ownership question for every subscription in one Resource Graph call filtering the joined role name to Owner, User Access Administrator and Role Based Access Control Administrator, paging with `--first 1000` and an incrementing `--skip` until a short page returns. Active assignments are only half the answer: for each subscription also read the PIM eligibility plane at `https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/<id>/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/roleEligibilityScheduleInstances?api-version=2020-10-01` alongside `roleAssignmentScheduleInstances`, since an eligible Owner does not appear as a role assignment until activated. Read deny assignments at `.../Microsoft.Authorization/denyAssignments?api-version=2022-04-01`, which alter effective authority without being role assignments. For the legacy plane, query `.../Microsoft.Authorization/classicAdministrators?api-version=2015-07-01` directly and record both the result and the az CLI version, since `az role assignment list --include-classic-administrators` is deprecated in current CLI builds. Resolve every Owner principal id through Graph so the report names people and groups rather than GUIDs.
api: az graph query -q "authorizationresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.authorization/roleassignments' | extend pid=tostring(properties.principalId), ptype=tostring(properties.principalType), rid=tolower(tostring(properties.roleDefinitionId)), scope=tostring(properties.scope) | join kind=inner (authorizationresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.authorization/roledefinitions' | extend roleName=tostring(properties.roleName) | where roleName in ('Owner','User Access Administrator','Role Based Access Control Administrator') | project rid=tolower(id), roleName) on rid | project subscriptionId, scope, roleName, pid, ptype" --management-groups <tenant-root-mg-id> --allow-partial-scopes --first 1000 --skip 0
controls.evidence: Per enabled subscription: every role assignment row granting Owner, User Access Administrator or Role Based Access Control Administrator with its `scope`, `pid`, `ptype` and the Graph-resolved principal display name; the PIM eligibility and assignment schedule instances distinguishing permanent from time-bound and eligible from active ownership; the classic administrator response body with the api-version and az CLI version used to obtain it; the deny assignment objects including `isSystemProtected`; the `--skip` sequence proving Resource Graph paging ran to exhaustion; and the reconciliation of subscription counts between `az account list --all` and the recursed management group tree, with the tenants authenticated to at collection time.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, for every enabled subscription: the number of distinct principals holding Owner at subscription scope — counting active assignments and PIM-eligible assignments together — is between 1 and 3 inclusive; none of those assignments has `ptype` == 'User' (ownership is carried by an Entra group or by a PIM-eligible assignment, not by a person directly); every service principal holding Owner or User Access Administrator matches an entry in the engagement's supplied automation inventory file, with any unmatched service principal scored REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW and blocking a PASS, and no inventory file supplied meaning the control cannot PASS; the classic administrators call returns an empty collection with an HTTP 200; and the count of enabled subscriptions from `az account list --all` equals the number of subscriptions in the recursed management group tree. Any call returning a non-200, and any Resource Graph result flagged partial, blocks a PASS.
controls.remediation: Replace direct user Owner assignments with an Entra security group per subscription whose membership is governed and reviewable, and make that group's assignment PIM-eligible so ownership is activated rather than held. Reduce Owner to the minimum by moving day-to-day work to Contributor plus a narrower role for role management. Remove any residual classic co-administrator on subscriptions that still expose the legacy plane. Where an automation principal needs to create role assignments, grant Role Based Access Control Administrator with a condition constraining which roles it may assign, rather than Owner.
controls.caveat: The dominant false pass is scope, not count. (1) Resource Graph rows for a subscription do not carry assignments inherited from the management group above it, so a subscription showing two Owners can have twenty through inheritance; this control is only sound when read together with 1.10, and reading it alone is precisely how estates get missed. (2) `az role assignment list` silently defaults to the currently selected subscription and has `--include-inherited` off by default, so the obvious one-liner produces a partial answer for one subscription and reads as an estate-wide result. (3) `az graph query` truncates at 100 rows without `--first`, which in a large estate makes the Owner count look small, and `--allow-partial-scopes` returns success while omitting scopes the credential cannot read. (4) PIM-eligible Owners are not role assignments and do not appear in any roleAssignments listing until activated — a subscription can show zero active Owners and carry a dozen people who can become Owner in thirty seconds, which is the cleanest false pass in this control. (5) Deny assignments and resource locks change effective authority without appearing as role assignments, so a Blueprint or managed-application deny assignment can make an apparent Owner unable to act; effective authority is not the role list alone. (6) A subscription in the tenant that the reader credential cannot enumerate is absent from `az account list --all` entirely and reads as an estate with fewer subscriptions rather than as an incomplete collection, which is why the count reconciliation is part of the rule — and in a multi-tenant estate the list only covers tenants the identity has logged into. (7) Classic co-administrators were retired by Azure on 31 August 2024 and `--include-classic-administrators` is deprecated in current az CLI builds, so an empty result on a modern tenant is the platform default rather than proof anyone remediated anything; record the api-version and CLI version so the empty set is interpretable, and treat a CLI that drops the flag entirely as a collection gap rather than a clean finding.

controls.title: Tenant root scope and the root management group carry no standing authority
controls.objective: MCSB PA-1 and PA-7 at the top of the hierarchy. Azure RBAC inherits downward, so an assignment at the tenant root scope or at the root management group applies to every subscription, resource group and resource in the tenant, present and future, and it is invisible to anyone auditing a single subscription. The Global Administrator elevation that grants User Access Administrator at the root scope is designed to be temporary, but nothing removes it automatically, and a tenant that elevated once years ago is still carrying tenant-wide access-management rights.
controls.procedure: Establish the hierarchy first: `az account management-group list --query '[].{name:name,display:displayName}'` and then `az account management-group show --name <tenant-root-mg-id> --expand --recurse` — the root management group's name is the tenant id and it is created lazily, so a caller without access gets an error that must be recorded as an error rather than read as an empty hierarchy. Read assignments at the tenant root scope, which sits above the root management group and is where the Global Administrator elevation lands: `az role assignment list --scope '/' --query "[].{role:roleDefinitionName,principal:principalName,type:principalType,scope:scope}"`, or equivalently `az rest --method GET --url 'https://management.azure.com/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments?api-version=2022-04-01&$filter=atScope()'`; any User Access Administrator row here is a live elevation. Reading the '/' scope itself requires authority at '/', so a credential without it receives 403 — capture the status code, because an empty list and a refused read are opposite findings that look identical downstream. Then, for every management group in the tree, run `az role assignment list --scope /providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/<name> --include-inherited` — `--include-inherited` is off by default and its absence hides exactly the inheritance this control exists to find. Use Resource Graph only as a cross-check for management-group-scoped rows, never as the source for the '/' scope, and pass `--management-groups` so the query looks above subscription scope at all. Finally verify that every subscription is parented under a child management group rather than directly under the root, by comparing the `children` of the recursed root, or the `descendants` call, against the subscription list from `az account list --all`.
api: az graph query -q "authorizationresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.authorization/roleassignments' | extend scope=tostring(properties.scope) | where scope startswith '/providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/' | project id, scope, principalId=tostring(properties.principalId), roleDefinitionId=tostring(properties.roleDefinitionId)" --management-groups <tenant-root-mg-id> --allow-partial-scopes --first 1000 --skip 0
controls.evidence: The full management group tree from the recursed root call, with each group's name and its children, or the exact error returned when the root is unreadable; every role assignment returned at the tenant root scope with `properties.roleDefinitionId`, `properties.principalId` and `properties.scope` as returned, together with the HTTP status of that call so a 403 is never recorded as zero rows; the per-management-group assignment list obtained with `--include-inherited`, showing role name, principal and the scope the assignment actually lives at; the set of subscriptions whose parent is the root management group; and, for every management-group-scope assignment found, the enumerated list of subscriptions it reaches by inheritance.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when the tenant root scope '/' call returns HTTP 200 with zero role assignments — no residual User Access Administrator from a Global Administrator elevation; the root management group carries no Owner, Contributor, User Access Administrator or Role Based Access Control Administrator assignment other than principals named in the engagement's supplied platform-operations inventory file; every enabled subscription is parented under a child management group rather than directly under the root; and every management-group-scope assignment discovered is reported against the full list of subscriptions it reaches by inheritance. A 403 or any other non-200 on the '/' scope read, an error on the root management group read, or no inventory file supplied, is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW and blocks a PASS.
controls.remediation: Delete any role assignment at the tenant root scope; the Global Administrator elevation is revoked by removing the resulting User Access Administrator assignment at '/', not by waiting. Move governance assignments down from the root management group to a platform or landing-zone management group so that the root carries policy and nothing else. Parent every subscription under an intermediate management group so a future root-level assignment has a smaller blast radius and the hierarchy expresses the environment split. Where broad access-management rights are genuinely needed, grant them as PIM-eligible assignments at the narrowest management group that covers the need.
controls.caveat: This control exists because every other RBAC check in this section is scoped below it. (1) `az role assignment list` omits inherited assignments unless `--include-inherited` is passed, so the default output of the obvious command is precisely the wrong answer for a hierarchy question. (2) The root management group is created on first use and its name equals the tenant id; a caller lacking access receives an error, and a collector that turns errors into empty lists records 'no management group assignments' for a tenant that has many. (3) The tenant root scope '/' is not the root management group — they are different scopes, the elevation lands on '/', and no management-group query returns it. (4) Resource Graph does not index the '/' scope at all: an ARG predicate written as `scope == '/'` matches nothing in every tenant, elevated or not, so using ARG as the source for the elevation check produces a guaranteed and entirely silent pass. ARG also needs `--management-groups` to see above subscription scope, `--allow-partial-scopes` in large estates, and still truncates at 100 rows without `--first`. (5) Reading role assignments at '/' requires authority at '/', which most audit credentials do not have; a 403 swallowed into an empty array is the single most likely way this control reports clean on a tenant carrying a years-old elevation, so the status code is part of the evidence. (6) The Entra plane and the ARM plane remain separate: a Global Administrator with no ARM assignment looks harmless in every query here yet can re-grant themselves User Access Administrator over the whole tenant with one elevation call, so this control's PASS is conditional on the Global Administrator population controls in 1.4 and 1.5.

controls.title: Application and service-principal secrets are short-lived, current, and attributable
controls.objective: MCSB IM-8 and IM-3: a client secret on an app registration is a bearer credential that authenticates as the application with all of its permissions and no second factor, and it is routinely pasted into pipeline variables, configuration files and chat. A two-year secret is a two-year window; an expired secret still sitting on the object is evidence that credentials are added and never revoked; and a credential on an application nobody owns cannot be rotated by anyone.
controls.procedure: Read both object types, because credentials can be attached to either and only one of them is visible to the app-centric commands. For application registrations: `az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/applications?$select=id,appId,displayName,createdDateTime,passwordCredentials,keyCredentials&$top=999'`, then re-issue `az rest` against each `@odata.nextLink` until none is returned, since `az rest` fetches exactly one page. For service principals: `az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/servicePrincipals?$select=id,appId,displayName,servicePrincipalType,accountEnabled,appOwnerOrganizationId,passwordCredentials,keyCredentials&$top=999'`, paged the same way. Name the credential collections explicitly in `$select` rather than relying on the default property set of a collection GET. For every credential compute the issued lifetime as `endDateTime` minus `startDateTime` and the remaining life against the collection timestamp, and record `keyId` and `displayName` so a specific credential can be revoked without guessing. Exclude service principals whose `servicePrincipalType` is 'ManagedIdentity', whose certificates are platform-managed. For each object holding a credential, read `/applications/{id}/owners` or `/servicePrincipals/{id}/owners` so every credential has a named human accountable for it.
