Read `/applications/{id}/federatedIdentityCredentials` and record each entry's `issuer`, `subject` and `audiences` — a federated credential replaces a secret only if its subject actually pins one workload, so the values are evidence, not a checkbox. Cross-read the directory audit log for credential-management activity to distinguish rotation from accretion, percent-encoding the spaces in the filter value.
controls.evidence: For every application and Application-type service principal: the object id, `appId`, `displayName`, and each credential's `keyId`, `displayName`, `startDateTime` and `endDateTime` exactly as returned, with the computed issued lifetime in days and whether it is already expired at the collection timestamp; the owners collection for each credential-bearing object; every federated identity credential with its `issuer`, `subject` and `audiences` verbatim; the directory audit rows showing when credentials were last added, annotated with the log retention window in force for the tenant; and the number of `@odata.nextLink` pages retrieved for each collection, with the absence of a nextLink on the last page as proof the enumeration completed.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when no application registration and no Application-type service principal holds a passwordCredential or keyCredential whose `endDateTime` minus `startDateTime` exceeds 180 days; none holds a credential whose `endDateTime` is earlier than the collection timestamp; every credential-bearing object returns at least one owner whose `accountEnabled` is true; and every federatedIdentityCredential returned has a non-wildcard `subject` and an `issuer` matching an entry in the engagement's supplied workload-federation inventory file. Service principals with `servicePrincipalType` == 'ManagedIdentity' are excluded from the lifetime rule. An application whose only credentials are federated credentials satisfies the secret-lifetime rule but is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW, not PASS, until its `issuer`/`subject`/`audiences` triple has been matched to a documented workload. Any collection whose paging did not terminate on a nextLink-free page blocks a PASS.
controls.remediation: Replace client secrets with workload identity federation where the workload runs somewhere that can issue a token (GitHub Actions, Kubernetes, another cloud) by adding a federatedIdentityCredential whose subject pins the exact repository, branch, environment or service account, and deleting the secret; and with a user-assigned managed identity where the workload runs in Azure — neither has a secret to leak or rotate. Where a secret is unavoidable, issue it for no more than 180 days, store it in Key Vault rather than in pipeline configuration, and automate rotation. Delete every expired credential rather than leaving it in place, and assign at least two owners to every application so rotation is never blocked on one person.
controls.caveat: The cleanest-looking false pass in this section comes from projection: `passwordCredentials` and `keyCredentials` must be named in `$select` on a collection GET, and the obvious unqualified `GET /applications` can return every application with no credential arrays at all, so the control reports a spotless tenant. Six more. (1) Credentials can be attached to the service principal as well as to the application, and the app-centric `az ad app` commands never show them — an attacker who adds a secret to the service principal is invisible to an application-only check. (2) `az rest` does not follow `@odata.nextLink`, so any tenant with more than 999 applications or service principals is assessed on its first page; `az ad app list` without `--all` has the same effect. (3) Managed identity service principals carry platform-rotated certificates that trip a naive lifetime rule and are not findings; filter on `servicePrincipalType`. (4) An expired credential is not harmless — it evidences a process that adds and never revokes, and the secret value may still be live in a pipeline variable or a repository — so scoring only unexpired credentials understates the finding. (5) Treating 'no secrets, only federated credentials' as an automatic pass is the inverted false pass: a federated credential whose subject is a wildcard or a broad claim (an entire GitHub organisation, any branch, any Kubernetes namespace) is a standing, unrotatable path to authenticate as that application, strictly worse than a 180-day secret. (6) `directoryAudits` retains roughly 30 days on P1/P2 and about 7 on the free tier, so an empty audit result means the window expired, not that no credential was ever added — never read it as evidence of a clean rotation history. Note finally that the issued lifetime, not the remaining lifetime, is the thing being measured: a two-year secret issued last week has plenty of remaining life and is still a two-year secret.

controls.title: Every application registration and enterprise application has a live, internal owner
controls.objective: MCSB IM-3, PA-3 and AM-1: an application registration with no owner is an identity nobody is responsible for — its permissions are never reviewed, its secrets are never rotated, and when it eventually breaks or is abused there is no one to ask. Ownership is also a privilege in its own right, because an owner can add a credential to the application and thereafter authenticate as it, inheriting every permission it holds, which makes a guest or a low-trust service principal listed as owner a privilege escalation path rather than good hygiene.
controls.procedure: Enumerate applications and service principals with `$top=999` and explicit `@odata.nextLink` following as in 1.11, then read owners per object: `az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/applications/<object-id>/owners?$select=id,displayName,userPrincipalName,userType,accountEnabled'` and the same path under `/servicePrincipals/`. Both must be read: the owners of an application registration and the owners of its enterprise application (service principal) are separate collections, and an application with an owner routinely has an ownerless service principal object carrying the tenant consent. Do not substitute `$expand=owners` on the collection, which caps the expanded collection and truncates without an error. Exclude Microsoft's own first-party service principals by filtering on `appOwnerOrganizationId` equal to the Microsoft services tenant f8cdef31-a31e-4b4a-93e4-5f571e91255a, and exclude `servicePrincipalType` == 'ManagedIdentity', whose lifecycle is bound to the Azure resource that owns it — for those, record the owning resource id from `alternativeNames` instead. Classify each owner by object type first: a user owner is acceptable only when `accountEnabled` is true and `userType` is 'Member'; a service principal owner has no `userType` at all and must be reconciled against the automation inventory rather than failed on a null. Throttle deliberately — honour `Retry-After` on 429 and keep concurrency low — and record any object whose owners call returns 429, 403 or any other non-200 as a collection error, never as an object with no owners.
controls.evidence: A row per application registration and per non-Microsoft, non-managed-identity service principal, carrying object id, `appId`, `displayName`, `createdDateTime`, and the owners collection with each owner's object id, `@odata.type`, `userPrincipalName`, `userType` and `accountEnabled`; the explicit list of objects returning zero owners; separately, every object whose owners call failed, with the HTTP status and any `Retry-After` observed, so unreadable objects are never conflated with ownerless ones; the `allowedToCreateApps` value from the authorization policy; and the page counts for both collection enumerations.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every application registration and every service principal that is neither Microsoft first-party (`appOwnerOrganizationId` == f8cdef31-a31e-4b4a-93e4-5f571e91255a) nor a managed identity returns at least one owner that is either a user with `accountEnabled` true and `userType` 'Member', or a service principal matching an entry in the engagement's supplied automation inventory file; and no owner is a user whose `userType` is 'Guest' or whose `accountEnabled` is false. Objects whose owners could not be read, and service principal owners with no inventory entry, are REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW and block a PASS. Enumerations that did not terminate on a nextLink-free page block a PASS.
controls.remediation: Assign at least two owners — ideally the members of a team-owned group rather than one individual — to every application registration and enterprise application, and make ownership a required field in whatever process creates them. Remove guest and unnecessary service principal owners, since ownership confers the ability to mint credentials for the application. Retire applications that nobody will claim rather than assigning a nominal owner: an unclaimed application holding tenant permissions is a standing risk, and deleting it is the only remediation that reduces it. Set `allowedToCreateApps` to false (see 1.14) so new ownerless applications stop appearing.
controls.caveat: Five ways this check lies. (1) The owners collection requires one call per object, so a tenant with a few thousand applications will hit Microsoft Graph throttling; a 429 handled by moving on yields an empty owners array indistinguishable from a genuinely ownerless application, and the finding count then depends on how fast the collector ran. Honour `Retry-After`, record every non-200, and exclude those objects from the verdict. (2) `$expand=owners` on the collection is the obvious optimisation and it truncates the expanded collection silently, so an application with many owners can come back looking ownerless — the result is not trustworthy for a verdict either way. (3) Microsoft first-party service principals legitimately have no owner and there are hundreds in any tenant; failing to exclude them buries real findings in noise, while excluding them by display name rather than by `appOwnerOrganizationId` also excludes any third-party application that happens to be named similarly. (4) Application and service principal owners are distinct collections, so checking only `/applications` passes a tenant whose consented enterprise applications — the objects that actually hold the granted permissions — have no owner at all. (5) A service principal listed as owner returns no `userType`, so a rule written as `userType == 'Member'` fails it on a null and a rule written as `userType != 'Guest'` passes it silently; owner type must be branched on the object type, and a service principal owner is a credential-minting path that has to be reconciled against the automation inventory rather than waved through. Note also that `az rest` returns a single page, so a large tenant is otherwise assessed on its first 999 objects.

controls.title: Application permissions amounting to tenant takeover are held only by an approved inventory
controls.objective: MCSB PA-1, PA-7 and IM-3 applied to non-human identities. A handful of Microsoft Graph application permissions are equivalent to owning the tenant: one lets an application assign directory roles, one lets it grant itself any other permission, and one lets it add a credential to any other application and then act as that application. An application holding any of them is an administrator that never signs in, is not covered by the Conditional Access policies written for people, and is usually not on anyone's list of administrators.
controls.procedure: Bind the right credential first, because this control lives on the tenant plane and not the subscription plane: confirm a Microsoft Graph token is obtainable for the assessing identity with `az account get-access-token --resource-type ms-graph`, and note that authorisation for every call below comes from Graph permissions (Directory.Read.All, Application.Read.All, RoleManagement.Read.Directory) which Azure RBAC does not grant — an identity that is Owner on every subscription can still be refused here. Resolve the Microsoft Graph resource service principal and read its own permission catalogue, so app-role ids are mapped to names from the tenant's own data rather than from a hardcoded table: `az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/servicePrincipals(appId=%2700000003-0000-0000-c000-000000000000%27)?$select=id,appRoles'`. Then list every application-permission grant issued on it with `az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/servicePrincipals/<graph-sp-object-id>/appRoleAssignedTo?$top=999'`, reading `@odata.nextLink` from each response and re-issuing `az rest --method GET --url '<next link>'` in a loop until the property is absent, and join `appRoleId` to that catalogue for the permission name and `principalId`/`principalDisplayName`/`principalType` for the holder. Repeat the same pair of calls for every other resource service principal that carries privilege in the tenant — Office 365 Exchange Online (appId 00000002-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000), Office 365 SharePoint Online (00000003-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000) and the Windows Azure Service Management API (797f4846-ba00-4fd7-ba43-dac1f8f63013) — because a permission held on those is entirely invisible to a Graph-only sweep. Separately list delegated grants with `az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/oauth2PermissionGrants?$top=999'`, paging the same way, and flag every row whose `consentType` is 'AllPrincipals', which applies to every user in the tenant. Enumerate the service principals that hold a directory role from the active assignment collection, `roleManagement/directory/roleAssignments?$expand=principal`, and where Privileged Identity Management is licensed add `roleEligibilityScheduleInstances` so principals that are eligible but not currently activated are counted too. Finally join every principal id collected against the Azure RBAC results from 1.9, because a service principal holding Owner or User Access Administrator on the resource plane is the ARM-side equivalent of the same capability. Present the joined list to the client and obtain, in writing, the approved inventory with an owner and a business purpose per application.
api: az rest --method GET --url '<value of @odata.nextLink from the previous response, repeated until the property is absent>'
controls.evidence: The Microsoft Graph service principal's `appRoles` catalogue mapping each `id` to its `value`; every `appRoleAssignedTo` row across every page with `principalId`, `principalDisplayName`, `principalType` and the resolved permission name, together with proof that the final page carried no `@odata.nextLink`; the same for each additional resource service principal enumerated, and an explicit list of which resource service principals were and were not swept; every `oauth2PermissionGrants` row whose `consentType` is 'AllPrincipals', with `clientId`, `resourceId` and the full `scope` string; the service principals holding a directory role, taken from the active assignment collection and, where licensed, the eligibility instances; the cross-referenced service principals holding Owner or User Access Administrator from 1.9; the Graph token's audience and the permissions the assessing identity itself holds, so a permission-filtered enumeration is visible rather than inferred; and the client's written approved inventory naming each application, its owner and its purpose.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when all four hold. (a) Every principal holding one of the escalation-grade Microsoft Graph application permissions — RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory, AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All, Application.ReadWrite.All, Directory.ReadWrite.All, PrivilegedAccess.ReadWrite.AzureADGroup, or any other write permission over roles, applications or directory objects — is a member of the client's written approved inventory and that entry names an owner and a purpose. (b) Every grant whose `consentType` is 'AllPrincipals' over the same scope set is likewise in that inventory. (c) No service principal outside the inventory holds a directory role or holds Owner or User Access Administrator on the resource plane. (d) Every collection enumerated terminated on a response with no `@odata.nextLink`, and no call returned 403. A run failing (d) is inconclusive and must not be recorded as PASS.
controls.remediation: Reduce each application to the least permission that supports its function — most tools that ask for Directory.ReadWrite.All need one specific write scope or only read access — and prefer a scoped role assignment or a resource-specific consent over a tenant-wide application permission. Where a governance or migration tool genuinely needs an escalation-grade permission, give it a dedicated application with a named owner, a federated (workload identity) credential rather than a client secret, and an inventory entry with a review date. Revoke tenant-wide delegated grants and re-consent per user or per group. Alert on the directory audit events that add an app role assignment to a service principal or add a credential to an application, since granting a permission to an application is the quietest privilege escalation available on the tenant plane.
controls.caveat: Manual because no API distinguishes a legitimate governance tool from an attacker's application: someone must supply and vouch for the approved inventory, and an application added last week by a Global Administrator looks exactly like one added last week by whoever compromised them. The concrete traps. The escalation set is not one permission and clearing three of four is not a partial pass — AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All lets an application grant itself anything, Application.ReadWrite.All lets it add a credential to any other application and become it, and RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory lets it assign Global Administrator, so any one alone is full compromise capability. App role ids must be resolved from the resource service principal's own `appRoles` collection, because the same GUID means a different permission on a different resource and a hardcoded table drifts. `appRoleAssignedTo` and `oauth2PermissionGrants` are paged and `az rest` does not follow `@odata.nextLink`, so a single call silently returns the first page and an unpaged sweep of a large tenant reads as a short, clean list. Enumerating directory-role holders only from the PIM schedule collections is the sharpest false pass here: `roleAssignmentScheduleInstances` and `roleEligibilityScheduleInstances` reflect PIM-managed assignments and need an Entra ID P2 licence, so in a tenant without PIM they return an empty collection that reads as 'no service principal holds a directory role' — read the active `roleManagement/directory/roleAssignments` collection and treat PIM as an addition, never a substitute. Graph is a different control plane from ARM with a different authorisation: a script that catches the 403 and continues records an empty result as compliance, so an authorisation failure must be a hard error, not an empty set. Delegated grants live in a separate collection and a tenant-wide grant of a broad delegated scope is equivalent to the application permission the moment an administrator signs in to that application. App-only tokens are not subject to the Conditional Access policies written for users, so 'CA covers our admins' is not a compensating control for any of this. Directory audit retention is 7 days without a premium licence and 30 with one, so an absent audit row proves nothing about when a permission was granted. Finally, permissions on Exchange, SharePoint and the ARM plane are outside the Graph call entirely, so a PASS is only as complete as the list of resource service principals actually enumerated — that list belongs in the evidence.

controls.title: Ordinary users can neither consent to applications nor create their own app registrations
controls.objective: MCSB PA-7 and IM-3 on the default user role. If any user can consent to an application, a single convincing consent prompt gives an attacker-controlled application a durable OAuth grant to that user's mail, files and directory data — a credential-free account takeover that survives a password reset and is unaffected by MFA, because the grant is a separate artefact from the password. If any user can register applications, the tenant accumulates identities outside the ownership and credential controls in 1.11 and 1.12.
controls.procedure: Read the tenant's authorization policy singleton with `az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/policies/authorizationPolicy'` and record `defaultUserRolePermissions.permissionGrantPoliciesAssigned`, `defaultUserRolePermissions.allowedToCreateApps`, `defaultUserRolePermissions.allowedToCreateSecurityGroups`, `defaultUserRolePermissions.allowedToCreateTenants` and `defaultUserRolePermissions.allowedToReadOtherUsers`. The consent setting is nested inside `defaultUserRolePermissions`, so a query written against a top-level property name returns null and a checker that reads null as 'no grant policy assigned' reports the most permissive tenant as compliant. Each assigned value is a policy id carrying its grant-type prefix, for example `ManagePermissionGrantsForSelf.microsoft-user-default-low`; strip the prefix before looking the policy up, since the policy resource id is the bare `microsoft-user-default-low`. Treat `ManagePermissionGrantsForSelf.microsoft-user-default-legacy` as unrestricted user consent rather than as a restriction, even though a policy is assigned. For any assigned value that is not the built-in low-risk one, resolve what it actually permits: `az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/policies/permissionGrantPolicies/<policy-id>/includes'` and read each condition's `permissionClassification`, `resourceApplication`, `permissionType`, `clientApplicationsFromVerifiedPublisherOnly` and `clientApplicationIds`, then read `/excludes` as well, because a condition set is includes minus excludes and reading only one half misstates the effective policy. Then confirm a live path exists for legitimate requests rather than a dead end, with `az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/policies/adminConsentRequestPolicy'`, checking `isEnabled` and a non-empty `reviewers`. Finally enumerate who holds Application Developer, Application Administrator and Cloud Application Administrator: resolve each role's id from `roleManagement/directory/roleDefinitions` by display name, then list `roleManagement/directory/roleAssignments?$filter=roleDefinitionId eq '<id>'&$expand=principal`, adding the PIM eligibility instances where that licence exists — those roles carry application creation and consent rights independently of the default user role, and a restriction on the default role does not touch them.
controls.evidence: The authorization policy singleton exactly as returned, including the whole `defaultUserRolePermissions` object rather than a hand-picked subset, so that an absent key is distinguishable from a false value; where any non-built-in grant policy is assigned, that policy's `includes` and `excludes` condition sets in full; the admin consent request policy with `isEnabled` and the `reviewers` collection; the resolved role definition ids and the full membership of Application Developer, Application Administrator and Cloud Application Administrator including PIM-eligible holders; the count of per-user consent grants outstanding; and the recent consent audit rows showing who has been consenting and to what.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when all of the following are literally true in the returned JSON. `defaultUserRolePermissions.permissionGrantPoliciesAssigned` is present and is either an empty array or contains only `ManagePermissionGrantsForSelf.microsoft-user-default-low`, compared case-insensitively after prefix normalisation. `defaultUserRolePermissions.allowedToCreateApps` is boolean false. `defaultUserRolePermissions.allowedToCreateSecurityGroups` is boolean false. `adminConsentRequestPolicy.isEnabled` is true and `reviewers` has at least one entry. The combined membership of Application Developer, Application Administrator and Cloud Application Administrator, including PIM-eligible holders, is empty or wholly contained in the client's named administrator list. Any of those keys being absent or null, or any call returning 403, makes the run inconclusive rather than PASS.
controls.remediation: Set the default user role's assigned permission grant policies to the empty list to disable user consent entirely, or to the built-in low-risk policy where the business needs self-service for low-impact permissions from verified publishers. Set `allowedToCreateApps` and `allowedToCreateSecurityGroups` to false. Enable the admin consent workflow and name reviewers who will actually respond within a working day, otherwise the restriction is routed around rather than obeyed. Trim Application Developer and Cloud Application Administrator to the people who need them and move them behind time-bound activation. Review the existing per-user grants in `oauth2PermissionGrants` and revoke those to applications nobody recognises, because disabling future consent does not revoke a single past grant.
controls.caveat: Four things read as compliant and are not. (1) The property path: the consent setting is `defaultUserRolePermissions.permissionGrantPoliciesAssigned`, and a query aimed at a top-level name that does not exist on the v1.0 resource returns null — which a naive checker scores as 'no policy assigned, therefore consent disabled', turning the most permissive tenant into a pass. Assert the key is present before evaluating it, and note that the v1.0 endpoint returns a single object while the beta endpoint returns a collection under `value`, so a path written against beta yields null here for the same reason. (2) Policy identity: a custom permission grant policy has an arbitrary display name, so 'a restrictive-sounding id is set' proves nothing — resolve `includes` and `excludes`, and treat a condition whose `resourceApplication` is 'any' or which omits `clientApplicationsFromVerifiedPublisherOnly` as broad regardless of its name. The built-in `microsoft-user-default-legacy` is the classic instance: a policy is assigned, the setting looks configured, and it permits consent to anything. (3) The role plane: `allowedToCreateApps` false does not constrain anyone holding Application Developer, which grants application creation independently and is routinely handed to development teams, and Application Administrator and Cloud Application Administrator can consent on behalf of the tenant. If those holders are enumerated through `/directoryRoles` rather than `/roleManagement/directory`, a role that has never been activated in the tenant has no `directoryRole` object at all and the call returns nothing — an absence that reads as zero members. (4) No retroactive effect: every grant consented to before the setting was hardened is still live in `oauth2PermissionGrants`, so a tenant that fixed the policy last month can still be carrying an attacker's grant from last year. Finally, this is the tenant control plane — Graph permissions govern these reads and Azure RBAC does not, so an under-permissioned assessor gets 403s that must fail the run rather than produce empty evidence.

controls.title: No network security group admits the public internet to SSH
controls.objective: Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark NS-1 and NS-2 require administrative planes to be reachable only from known networks. An inbound rule whose source is the internet and whose destination port range covers TCP/22 exposes every NIC and every subnet that network security group is bound to, turning SSH into a directly brute-forceable perimeter service that no host-level hardening compensates for.
controls.procedure: Bind identity and scope first: `az account show` to record the tenant and subscription, and `az account list --all --query "[?state=='Enabled'].{id:id,tenant:tenantId}"` to establish the full subscription set. Azure Resource Graph answers only for subscriptions present in the current login context, so a tenant with subscriptions linked to a second Entra ID directory needs a second `az login --tenant <id>` and a second sweep, and a query run without `--subscriptions` inherits whatever the local context happens to hold. Then answer the estate in one call with `az graph query` (install once with `az extension add --name resource-graph`), expanding `properties.securityRules` and normalising both the singular and plural source and port fields. Treat these source values as internet: `*`, `0.0.0.0/0`, `::/0`, `any`, the service tag `Internet`, and any prefix with a `/0` mask, all case-insensitively; then, client-side, union the expanded source prefixes per rule and test whether the union covers the public address space, because a pair such as `0.0.0.0/1` and `128.0.0.0/1` is the whole internet without matching any literal in the list. Treat protocol `Tcp` and `*` as in scope. Treat destination port `*` as covering everything, and otherwise split each range on the hyphen and test containment numerically, since `0-65535` and `1-1024` contain 22 without the characters '22' appearing. Ignore `properties.defaultSecurityRules`, which are the platform's own entries and not operator configuration. Because a single query that returns only Allow rules cannot establish whether a lower-numbered Deny shadows them, run a second query that returns every inbound rule on each candidate network security group ordered by `priority`, and compute first-match-wins evaluation over that complete set client-side. Corroborate on running hosts with `az network nic list-effective-nsg --name <nic> --resource-group <rg>`, and check separately for Azure Virtual Network Manager security admin rules, which are evaluated ahead of network security groups and are returned by the virtual network's `listNetworkManagerEffectiveSecurityAdminRules` operation rather than by the effective-rules view. Finally, list NICs that carry a public IP but have no network security group on either the NIC or its subnet, and record each such public IP's SKU, because an unfiltered NIC is only closed by default when the address is Standard SKU.
api: az graph query --first 1000 --subscriptions <sub1> <sub2> -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/networkSecurityGroups' | mv-expand rule = properties.securityRules | extend p = rule.properties | extend srcs = iff(array_length(p.sourceAddressPrefixes) > 0, p.sourceAddressPrefixes, pack_array(tostring(p.sourceAddressPrefix))) | extend prts = iff(array_length(p.destinationPortRanges) > 0, p.destinationPortRanges, pack_array(tostring(p.destinationPortRange))) | mv-expand src = srcs to typeof(string) | mv-expand prt = prts to typeof(string) | where tostring(p.direction) =~ 'Inbound' and tostring(p.access) =~ 'Allow' | where tostring(p.protocol) in~ ('Tcp','*') | where src in~ ('*','0.0.0.0/0','::/0','any','internet') or src endswith '/0' | extend lo = toint(split(prt,'-')[0]), hi = toint(iff(array_length(split(prt,'-')) > 1, split(prt,'-')[1], split(prt,'-')[0])) | where prt == '*' or (lo <= 22 and hi >= 22) | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, nsg = name, ruleName = tostring(rule.name), priority = toint(p.priority), src, prt, protocol = tostring(p.protocol), nsgId = id" -o json
az graph query --first 1000 --skip 1000 -q "<the same query, repeated while the response's count equals --first or skip_token is populated>" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/networkSecurityGroups' | where id in~ (<candidate nsg ids from the previous query>) | mv-expand rule = properties.securityRules | extend p = rule.properties | where tostring(p.direction) =~ 'Inbound' | project id, ruleName = tostring(rule.name), priority = toint(p.priority), access = tostring(p.access), protocol = tostring(p.protocol), src = p.sourceAddressPrefix, srcs = p.sourceAddressPrefixes, prt = p.destinationPortRange, prts = p.destinationPortRanges, dst = p.destinationAddressPrefix, subnets = properties.subnets, nics = properties.networkInterfaces | order by priority asc" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/networkInterfaces' | mv-expand ipc = properties.ipConfigurations | where isnotempty(tostring(ipc.properties.publicIPAddress.id)) | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, nic = name, nicNsg = tostring(properties.networkSecurityGroup.id), subnetId = tostring(ipc.properties.subnet.id), pip = tostring(ipc.properties.publicIPAddress.id), id" -o json
controls.evidence: For each offending rule: the subscription id, resource group, network security group name and full ARM resource id, the rule name and numeric priority, and the raw `direction`, `access`, `protocol`, `sourceAddressPrefix` plus `sourceAddressPrefixes`, and `destinationPortRange` plus `destinationPortRanges` values exactly as returned, recording an empty plural array distinctly from a populated one. Alongside each, the complete priority-ordered inbound rule list for that network security group, so the shadowing decision is reproducible from the evidence rather than asserted. Record the group's `properties.subnets` and `properties.networkInterfaces` arrays, and for NICs carrying a public IP with no group on either the NIC or its subnet, the public IP resource id, its literal address and its SKU. Record the graph response's `count`, `total_records`, `result_truncated` and `skip_token` fields and the list of subscriptions actually swept, so a truncated or permission-filtered enumeration is visible in the evidence rather than inferred.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, across every enabled subscription in every tenant in scope, no network security group has an effective inbound Allow rule whose source resolves to the public internet, whose protocol is Tcp or any, and whose destination port range numerically contains 22 after first-match-wins priority ordering has been applied over the complete inbound rule set; and no NIC carrying a public IP is left with no network security group on either the NIC or its subnet unless that public IP is Standard SKU. A run in which `result_truncated` is true, `count` is below `total_records`, `skip_token` is populated and unfollowed, `--allow-partial-scopes` was used, or the swept subscription list is shorter than `az account list --all` returns, is inconclusive and must not be recorded as PASS.
controls.remediation: Narrow the rule to the operator source with `az network nsg rule update --nsg-name <nsg> --resource-group <rg> --name <rule> --source-address-prefixes <admin_cidr>`, or delete it with `az network nsg rule delete` and reach the host through Azure Bastion, a site-to-site or point-to-site VPN, or an ExpressRoute-attached private path. Where interactive SSH is only occasionally needed, replace the standing rule with Just-in-Time VM access (control 2.5) so the opening is time-boxed, scoped to the requester's address and audited. Attach a group with an explicit deny to any NIC or subnet that currently has none.
controls.caveat: Seven ways this returns a clean result on an exposed estate. (1) `az graph query` returns 100 rows unless `--first` is given, caps at 1000 per page, and needs `--skip` or the returned skip token to continue; a silent truncation reads as a clean estate, so reconcile `count`, `total_records` and `result_truncated` every run. (2) Resource Graph shows only what the caller holds Reader on and is eventually consistent, so an under-privileged or freshly-run sweep returns an artificially short set; and `--allow-partial-scopes` converts a scope failure into a partial answer with no error, which is the most convenient false pass available here. (3) A rule may leave `sourceAddressPrefix` null and populate `sourceAddressPrefixes`, and likewise `destinationPortRange` against `destinationPortRanges`; code reading only the singular form misses the plural rule entirely. (4) A range such as `0-65535` contains 22 without the string '22' appearing, and a source pair of `0.0.0.0/1` with `128.0.0.0/1` is the whole internet without matching any literal wildcard, so both tests must be numeric or CIDR-aware rather than string equality. (5) The absence of a group is not automatically safety. Inside a group the platform's own deny rule at priority 65500 ends the chain, but a NIC or subnet with no group attached has no such chain: a Standard-SKU public IP is closed to inbound until a rule allows it, whereas a Basic-SKU address, or a VM behind a Basic load balancer, is reachable with nothing filtering it — so 'no network security group' must be resolved against the public IP SKU, not waved through. A group attached to nothing is still a finding, because it will be attached eventually. (6) Azure Virtual Network Manager security admin rules are evaluated before network security groups and can allow traffic a group would deny; they are not shown by `az network nic list-effective-nsg`, so a clean group result does not prove the traffic is blocked until the virtual network's effective security admin rules have been read from their own operation. (7) `az network nic list-effective-nsg` fails on a deallocated VM, so a stopped fleet cannot be corroborated this way and its configuration verdict stands alone.

controls.title: No network security group admits the public internet to Remote Desktop
controls.objective: Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark NS-1 and NS-2 again: an inbound rule sourced from the internet and covering TCP/3389 leaves every Windows host behind that network security group one credential guess or one pre-authentication Remote Desktop vulnerability away from compromise, and it is the most reliably scanned port on Azure's public address space.
controls.procedure: Identical traversal to control 2.1 with the port changed, run over the same subscription set derived from `az account list --all` and with the same paging discipline. Expand `properties.securityRules` in a single `az graph query`, normalise `sourceAddressPrefix` against `sourceAddressPrefixes` and `destinationPortRange` against `destinationPortRanges`, and keep inbound Allow rules whose source is `*`, `0.0.0.0/0`, `::/0`, `any`, the `Internet` service tag or any prefix with a `/0` mask, whose protocol is `Tcp`, `Udp` or `*`, and whose destination port range numerically contains 3389. Split the result: TCP and wildcard protocol drive the verdict, UDP/3389 is reported as an accompanying observation, because Remote Desktop has a UDP transport on the same port number. As in 2.1, the Allow-only result cannot establish shadowing on its own, so fetch every inbound rule on each candidate group ordered by `priority` and apply first-match-wins client-side before concluding anything. Corroborate on running hosts with `az network nic list-effective-nsg`, which merges the subnet group with the NIC group, and read Azure Virtual Network Manager security admin rules from the virtual network's own effective-rules operation, since they are evaluated first and are not part of the effective network security group view. Where Just-in-Time VM access is in use, expect a high-priority deny on 3389 plus short-lived allow rules scoped to a requester address; capture the rule's description and creation time so a time-boxed opening is not written up as a standing one, and so a standing rule is not excused as a Just-in-Time artefact.
api: az graph query --first 1000 --subscriptions <sub1> <sub2> -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/networkSecurityGroups' | mv-expand rule = properties.securityRules | extend p = rule.properties | extend srcs = iff(array_length(p.sourceAddressPrefixes) > 0, p.sourceAddressPrefixes, pack_array(tostring(p.sourceAddressPrefix))) | extend prts = iff(array_length(p.destinationPortRanges) > 0, p.destinationPortRanges, pack_array(tostring(p.destinationPortRange))) | mv-expand src = srcs to typeof(string) | mv-expand prt = prts to typeof(string) | where tostring(p.direction) =~ 'Inbound' and tostring(p.access) =~ 'Allow' | where tostring(p.protocol) in~ ('Tcp','Udp','*') | where src in~ ('*','0.0.0.0/0','::/0','any','internet') or src endswith '/0' | extend lo = toint(split(prt,'-')[0]), hi = toint(iff(array_length(split(prt,'-')) > 1, split(prt,'-')[1], split(prt,'-')[0])) | where prt == '*' or (lo <= 3389 and hi >= 3389) | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, nsg = name, ruleName = tostring(rule.name), priority = toint(p.priority), src, prt, protocol = tostring(p.protocol), descr = tostring(p.description), nsgId = id" -o json
az graph query --first 1000 --skip 1000 -q "<the same query, repeated while count equals --first or skip_token is populated>" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/networkSecurityGroups' | where id in~ (<candidate nsg ids>) | mv-expand rule = properties.securityRules | extend p = rule.properties | where tostring(p.direction) =~ 'Inbound' | project id, ruleName = tostring(rule.name), priority = toint(p.priority), access = tostring(p.access), protocol = tostring(p.protocol), src = p.sourceAddressPrefix, srcs = p.sourceAddressPrefixes, prt = p.destinationPortRange, prts = p.destinationPortRanges, subnets = properties.subnets, nics = properties.networkInterfaces | order by priority asc" -o json
controls.evidence: The offending rule object as returned by the graph query or by `az network nsg show`: rule name, numeric priority, description, direction, access, protocol, both source fields and both destination-port fields verbatim, plus the group's ARM resource id, resource group and subscription id, and the subnets and network interfaces it is associated with taken from `properties.subnets` and `properties.networkInterfaces`. Include the full priority-ordered inbound rule list for that group so the shadowing conclusion is reproducible, the effective rules from `az network nic list-effective-nsg` for at least one running host behind it, and the virtual network's effective security admin rules where a network manager is deployed. Record the graph `count`, `total_records`, `result_truncated` and `skip_token` values and the subscriptions swept.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when no network security group in any enabled subscription has an effective inbound Allow rule sourced from the public internet, with protocol Tcp or any, whose destination port range numerically contains 3389, after first-match-wins priority ordering over the complete inbound rule set; and no NIC carrying a public IP is left with no group on either the NIC or its subnet unless that public IP is Standard SKU. UDP/3389 openings are reported separately and do not by themselves change this verdict. An enumeration whose `result_truncated` is true, whose `count` is below `total_records`, which left a skip token unfollowed, which used `--allow-partial-scopes`, or which covered fewer subscriptions than `az account list --all` returns, is inconclusive rather than PASS.
controls.remediation: Re-scope the rule to jump-host or corporate ranges with `az network nsg rule update --nsg-name <nsg> --resource-group <rg> --name <rule> --source-address-prefixes <admin_cidr>`, or remove it and publish Remote Desktop through Azure Bastion, which brokers the session over TLS and needs no public address on the VM. Where administrators must connect directly, pair a deleted standing rule with Just-in-Time VM access so each session opens the port for a bounded window against a named source, and keep a low-priority deny on 3389 beneath it so the closed state is explicit rather than implied.
controls.caveat: Beyond the 2.1 traps — the 100-row default page and 1000-row cap, permission-filtered and eventually-consistent graph results, `--allow-partial-scopes` turning a scope failure into a partial answer, the plural field forms, an Allow-only query that cannot see the Deny that shadows it, and network manager admin rules evaluated ahead of the group and absent from the effective-rules view — three are specific here. A wide range such as `1024-65535` or `3000-4000` contains 3389 without ever naming it, so substring matching on '3389' passes the widest rules in the estate, and a destination port of `*` with protocol `*` is broader still and must fail. Portal- and marketplace-created Windows VMs ship a rule literally named `RDP` at priority 300 sourced from `*`; assessors sometimes filter out platform-looking rule names as defaults, but only `properties.defaultSecurityRules` are platform defaults — this one is in `securityRules`, is operator-owned, and is the single most common instance of this finding. Just-in-Time access cuts both ways: a sweep run inside an open window sees a legitimate short-lived allow scoped to one address and may write it up, while a standing wide-open rule is sometimes excused as a Just-in-Time artefact, so decide on the rule's source scope and description rather than on the fact that Just-in-Time is enabled somewhere in the subscription. Finally, a VM reachable through a load balancer inbound NAT rule still needs the group to permit the traffic, so a clean group is not contradicted by a public load balancer — but a Bastion subnet's own group legitimately permits 443 inbound from the internet and permits 3389 and 22 outbound to the virtual network, and neither is a finding under this control.

controls.title: No network security group opens all ports, all protocols, or database service ports to the internet
controls.objective: Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark NS-1 asks that traffic be filtered to what the workload requires. A rule with a destination port of `*` and a protocol of `*` sourced from the internet is a complete removal of the network boundary, and rules exposing database and remote-management listeners — SMB, WinRM, MSSQL, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch, memcached, the Docker daemon, VNC, Telnet and FTP — hand an attacker a directly authenticable service with no session broker in front of it.
controls.procedure: Run one `az graph query` over every enabled subscription that expands `properties.securityRules`, normalises the singular and plural source and port fields, and keeps inbound Allow rules whose source resolves to the public internet, using the same source normalisation as 2.1 including prefixes with a `/0` mask and the client-side union test for split halves. Have the query project the computed low and high bounds and an `allPorts` flag, then do the sensitive-port containment client-side over the projected bounds rather than in the query, because a wildcard port has no numeric bounds and a containment predicate written only in KQL either drops the wildcard rows or drops the bounded ones. Classify each surviving rule into three buckets and report them separately: destination port `*`, or a range spanning 0-65535, with protocol `*` (total exposure); protocol `*` with a bounded port; and a numeric range containing any member of the sensitive set {21, 23, 25, 135, 137, 138, 139, 445, 1433, 1434, 1521, 2375, 2376, 3306, 5432, 5601, 5900, 5984, 5985, 5986, 6379, 6380, 7001, 8020, 8086, 9042, 9200, 9300, 11211, 27017, 27018}. Test every element of that set against every expanded range numerically, never by string comparison. Fetch the complete priority-ordered inbound rule list for each candidate group and apply first-match-wins client-side so a lower-numbered Deny shadows a later Allow. Cross-reference each failing group's `properties.subnets` and `properties.networkInterfaces` — which live on the group, not on the rule — to state how many resources sit behind it, and check whether any of those NICs carries a public IP using the query in control 2.4: an internet-sourced rule on a group bound only to private, non-routable workloads is a lower-severity hygiene finding than the same rule in front of a routable address.
api: az graph query --first 1000 --subscriptions <sub1> <sub2> -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/networkSecurityGroups' | mv-expand rule = properties.securityRules | extend p = rule.properties | extend srcs = iff(array_length(p.sourceAddressPrefixes) > 0, p.sourceAddressPrefixes, pack_array(tostring(p.sourceAddressPrefix))) | extend prts = iff(array_length(p.destinationPortRanges) > 0, p.destinationPortRanges, pack_array(tostring(p.destinationPortRange))) | mv-expand src = srcs to typeof(string) | mv-expand prt = prts to typeof(string) | where tostring(p.direction) =~ 'Inbound' and tostring(p.access) =~ 'Allow' | where src in~ ('*','0.0.0.0/0','::/0','any','internet') or src endswith '/0' | extend lo = toint(split(prt,'-')[0]), hi = toint(iff(array_length(split(prt,'-')) > 1, split(prt,'-')[1], split(prt,'-')[0])) | extend allPorts = (prt == '*' or (lo == 0 and hi >= 65535)) | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, nsg = name, ruleName = tostring(rule.name), priority = toint(p.priority), protocol = tostring(p.protocol), src, prt, lo, hi, allPorts, subnets = array_length(properties.subnets), nics = array_length(properties.networkInterfaces), nsgId = id" -o json
az graph query --first 1000 --skip 1000 -q "<the same query, repeated while count equals --first or skip_token is populated>" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/networkSecurityGroups' | project id, name, resourceGroup, subscriptionId, subnets = properties.subnets, nics = properties.networkInterfaces" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/networkSecurityGroups' | where id in~ (<candidate nsg ids>) | mv-expand rule = properties.securityRules | extend p = rule.properties | where tostring(p.direction) =~ 'Inbound' | project id, ruleName = tostring(rule.name), priority = toint(p.priority), access = tostring(p.access), protocol = tostring(p.protocol), src = p.sourceAddressPrefix, srcs = p.sourceAddressPrefixes, prt = p.destinationPortRange, prts = p.destinationPortRanges | order by priority asc" -o json
az network nsg rule list --nsg-name <nsg> --resource-group <rg> -o table
az network nsg rule update --nsg-name <nsg> --resource-group <rg> --name <rule> --protocol Tcp --destination-port-ranges <ports> --source-address-prefixes <cidr>
controls.evidence: Per failing rule: the group's ARM id, rule name, priority, protocol, both source fields and both port fields as returned, the computed low and high bounds, and which member of the sensitive set the range was found to contain. Per failing group: the `properties.subnets` and `properties.networkInterfaces` arrays taken from the group itself, and the complete priority-ordered inbound rule list that establishes no lower-numbered Deny shadows the rule. Where the group fronts a NIC with a public IP, include that public IP resource id, its literal `ipAddress` and its SKU, so the finding carries a reachable endpoint rather than a configuration abstraction. Record the graph `count`, `total_records`, `result_truncated` and `skip_token` values and the subscriptions swept.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when no network security group in any enabled subscription has a surviving inbound Allow rule, after first-match-wins priority ordering, sourced from the public internet that either (a) has protocol `*`, or a destination port of `*`, or a range spanning 0-65535, or (b) has a destination port range numerically containing any member of the sensitive port set. Rules whose source is a specific public prefix narrower than /0, a service tag other than `Internet`, an application security group, or `VirtualNetwork`, do not fail this control. A truncated, partial-scope or short-subscription enumeration is inconclusive rather than PASS.
controls.remediation: Replace the wildcard with the specific protocol and ports the workload serves: `az network nsg rule update --nsg-name <nsg> --resource-group <rg> --name <rule> --protocol Tcp --destination-port-ranges 443 --source-address-prefixes <cidr>`. For database listeners, remove the internet-facing rule entirely and reach the service over a private endpoint (control 2.16) or from a virtual-network-integrated application tier. Where a broad rule exists only to serve a managed Azure service, replace `Internet` with the narrow service tag for that service — `AzureCloud.<region>`, `Storage.<region>`, `Sql.<region>`, `AzureMonitor` — which the platform keeps current for you, and keep a deny beneath it so the residual state is explicit.
controls.caveat: The wildcard forms are what defeat naive checks: a destination port of `*` never satisfies a numeric containment test written as `lo <= X and hi >= X`, because `toint('*')` is null and every comparison against null is false — so a scan that only parses ranges silently skips the single worst rule in the estate unless the wildcard is flagged separately first, which is why the containment is done client-side over a projected `allPorts` flag rather than inside the query. Subnet and interface associations are properties of the group, not of the rule: `array_length(rule.properties.subnets)` is always null and reports every failing group as fronting nothing, which quietly downgrades severity across the whole report. `az network nsg rule list` excludes platform rules by default and `--include-default` is a flag rather than a value-taking option, so passing it a boolean fails the command rather than filtering anything. A `sourceAddressPrefix` of `VirtualNetwork` is not internet exposure, but a peered or VPN-connected network may still carry untrusted traffic, so it belongs in the report as context and not as a pass. The service tag `Internet` means every public address including Azure's own and is exactly as broad as `0.0.0.0/0`; treating a named tag as inherently more restrictive than a prefix is a common misreading, while `AzureLoadBalancer` and `AzureCloud` are not `Internet` and must not be flagged here. A destination that is an application security group rather than a prefix does not narrow an internet source at all. Finally, this control assesses configuration: a rule matching the sensitive set may sit in front of a stopped VM or an empty subnet, which changes severity but never the verdict.

controls.title: Virtual machines are not directly addressable from the internet by a public IP
controls.objective: Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark NS-2 asks that services be exposed through a controlled front door rather than by attaching a routable address to the workload itself. A public IP bound straight to a virtual machine's network interface makes the host's whole listening surface a candidate for scanning and removes the load balancer, application gateway, firewall or Bastion where TLS termination, inspection and session brokering would otherwise happen.
controls.procedure: Enumerate every public IP in the estate with `az graph query` over `microsoft.network/publicipaddresses`, projecting `properties.ipAddress`, `properties.publicIPAllocationMethod`, the SKU name and tier, and `properties.ipConfiguration.id`, which is the ARM id of whatever the address is bound to. Classify on that id with the `contains` operator and not with `has`: `has` is a term match over a tokenised string and does not reliably match a path fragment, so a classifier written with it silently mis-buckets bindings. An id containing `/networkInterfaces/` is a direct attachment and is what this control is about; ids under `/loadBalancers/`, `/applicationGateways/`, `/azureFirewalls/`, `/bastionHosts/`, `/virtualNetworkGateways/` and `/virtualHubs/` are brokered front doors; an empty `ipConfiguration` means the address is not bound through an ip configuration at all. Resolve that last bucket rather than reporting it as unattached, because a NAT gateway holds its addresses in its own `properties.publicIpAddresses` array and leaves the address's `ipConfiguration` empty — query `microsoft.network/natgateways` and subtract those ids before calling anything unattached. Approach the same question from the other side as well, enumerating network interfaces whose ip configurations reference a public IP, so an eventually-consistent or partially-readable public IP sweep is caught by the mismatch between the two directions. Join the direct-attachment set to `microsoft.compute/virtualmachines` and `microsoft.network/networkinterfaces` so each finding names the VM, its OS type, its power state and the group guarding it, and read the effective inbound rules with `az network nic list-effective-nsg --name <nic> --resource-group <rg>` on a running host. Check whether the preventive control is actually preventive: list the policy assignments in scope, resolve the built-in definition 'Network interfaces should not have public IPs' by display name, and read the assignment's `enforcementMode` and its `effect` parameter, plus any policy exemptions covering the resources found. Then, for each direct attachment, obtain and record the owner's business justification, since some are legitimate — a self-hosted VPN concentrator, a build agent that must be reachable inbound.
api: az graph query --first 1000 --subscriptions <sub1> <sub2> -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/publicIPAddresses' | extend cfg = tostring(properties.ipConfiguration.id) | extend boundTo = case(isempty(cfg), 'unbound-ipconfig', cfg contains '/networkInterfaces/', 'nic-direct', cfg contains '/loadBalancers/', 'loadbalancer', cfg contains '/applicationGateways/', 'appgw', cfg contains '/azureFirewalls/', 'firewall', cfg contains '/bastionHosts/', 'bastion', cfg contains '/virtualNetworkGateways/', 'vpngw', cfg contains '/virtualHubs/', 'vhub', 'other') | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, name, ip = tostring(properties.ipAddress), sku = tostring(sku.name), tier = tostring(sku.tier), alloc = tostring(properties.publicIPAllocationMethod), boundTo, cfg, id" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/natGateways' | mv-expand pip = properties.publicIpAddresses | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, natgw = name, pipId = tostring(pip.id)" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/networkInterfaces' | mv-expand ipc = properties.ipConfigurations | where isnotempty(tostring(ipc.properties.publicIPAddress.id)) | extend vmId = tostring(properties.virtualMachine.id) | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, nic = name, vmId, pip = tostring(ipc.properties.publicIPAddress.id), nsg = tostring(properties.networkSecurityGroup.id), subnet = tostring(ipc.properties.subnet.id), id" -o json
az policy definition list --query "[?displayName=='Network interfaces should not have public IPs'].{id:id,name:name}" -o json
controls.evidence: The full public IP inventory with, for each address, the literal `ipAddress`, the SKU name and tier, the allocation method, the raw `ipConfiguration.id` and the resolved binding class; the NAT gateway address list used to reclassify addresses with an empty ip configuration; and the interface-side enumeration, presented alongside the address-side one so any disagreement between the two directions is visible. For every direct attachment: the interface id, the VM id, the VM's OS type and power state, the network security group id guarding the interface and its effective inbound rules from `az network nic list-effective-nsg`. For the preventive control: the resolved policy definition id, every assignment referencing it with its `enforcementMode`, its `effect` parameter value, its scope and `notScopes`, and any exemptions covering the resources found. Record the owner's written justification for each retained direct attachment, or its absence.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every public IP in every enabled subscription is bound to a brokered front door (load balancer, application gateway, Azure Firewall, Bastion, NAT gateway, VPN gateway or virtual hub) or is genuinely unbound, or — where it is bound directly to a virtual machine's interface — that binding appears in the client's written approved list with a named owner and stated purpose, and the interface's effective inbound rules admit only named source ranges with no internet-sourced allow on an administrative port. Any direct attachment absent from that list fails, as does any direct attachment whose effective inbound rules admit the internet to an administrative port. A run whose two enumeration directions disagree, or which was truncated or scope-limited, is inconclusive rather than PASS.
controls.remediation: Detach the address with `az network nic ip-config update --nic-name <nic> --resource-group <rg> --name <ipconfig> --public-ip-address ""` and re-front the workload: put inbound HTTP(S) behind an Application Gateway with a web application firewall or Azure Front Door, send egress through a NAT gateway or Azure Firewall so the VM keeps outbound reachability without an inbound address, and give administrators Azure Bastion instead of a public management port. Then make the state stick: assign the built-in definition that blocks public IPs on network interfaces at management group scope with its effect set to Deny and `enforcementMode` left at the enforcing setting, review the assignment's excluded scopes, and time-bound any exemption.
controls.caveat: Manual because no API can decide whether a given direct attachment is a deliberate, compensated design or an accident — a public IP on a VPN concentrator is correct, the identical configuration on a domain controller is critical. Five traps make the machine half unreliable on its own. First, classification is string work on `properties.ipConfiguration.id`, and the KQL `has` operator is a tokenised term match rather than a substring test, so a classifier built on it mis-buckets bindings; `contains` is the correct operator, and even then a load balancer frontend id and an interface ip configuration id differ only by their path segments, so matching on `ipConfigurations` alone drops load balancer frontends into the direct-attachment bucket and produces a report full of false positives that erodes trust in the real ones. Second, an empty `ipConfiguration` is not proof the address is unused: a NAT gateway references its addresses from its own resource, so those addresses read as unattached unless the NAT gateway list is subtracted, and an address created but never bound is still a standing reservation that becomes live exposure on the next deployment — count it and report it as an observation. Third, a VM can be internet-reachable with no public IP of its own, through a load balancer inbound NAT rule, an application gateway backend pool, or an IPv6 configuration, so an empty result here is not proof of no exposure. Fourth, the preventive control is where the comfortable false pass lives: an assignment of the right definition proves nothing if its `effect` parameter is Audit rather than Deny, if `enforcementMode` is set to not enforce, if the resource groups in question sit in `notScopes`, or if an exemption covers them — and an assignment made at subscription scope does not reach subscriptions created afterwards, which is why management group scope matters. Fifth, the SKU changes the meaning of an identical-looking attachment: a Standard-SKU address is closed to inbound traffic until a network security group allows it, whereas a Basic-SKU address is open by default; Basic-SKU public IPs reached end of life in September 2025, so any still present are both an exposure and a supportability finding, and they must never be assessed as though the Standard default applies.

controls.title: Management ports on virtual machines open only on time-boxed, approved request
controls.objective: Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark NS-7 and PA-2 favour brokered, time-limited administrative access over standing network permissions. Just-in-Time VM access keeps SSH and RDP closed in the network security group by default and inserts a scoped, expiring Allow rule at a lower priority number than the deny only when an authorised principal requests it, so the exposure window is minutes rather than the life of the VM and every opening is attributable in the activity log.
controls.procedure: Just-in-Time policies are a Microsoft.Security resource, not a network resource, and there is no first-class `az` command for them, so read them through the ARM REST surface. Enumerate the enabled subscriptions first and loop; nothing here is safe to run against whatever subscription happens to be current. For each subscription call `az rest --method get --url "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/<sub>/providers/Microsoft.Security/jitNetworkAccessPolicies?api-version=2020-01-01"`, which returns every policy in every location for that subscription in one collection. The single-policy read is resource-group scoped and its location segment is the Defender regional store (ascLocation), not necessarily the VM's own region, so `/subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/<rg>/providers/Microsoft.Security/locations/<ascLocation>/jitNetworkAccessPolicies/default` is the correct form and guessing the location from the VM is wrong — prefer the subscription-wide list. Each policy carries `properties.virtualMachines[]`; each entry has an `id` (the VM ARM id) and a `ports[]` array whose members have `number`, `protocol`, `allowedSourceAddressPrefix` or `allowedSourceAddressPrefixes`, and `maxRequestAccessDuration` as an ISO-8601 duration. `properties.requests[]` holds any live approvals. Build the covered set as the union of all `virtualMachines[].id` values across all policies in all locations in all subscriptions. Build the candidate population separately, and build it properly: one Resource Graph query lists running VMs with their NICs, a second expands `microsoft.network/networkSecurityGroups` `properties.securityRules[]` to inbound Allow rules, and the harness joins NSG to VM through the NSG's `properties.networkInterfaces[]` and `properties.subnets[]` associations. Port matching must be done in the harness, not in the query text: a rule exposes management access when `destinationPortRange` or any member of `destinationPortRanges` is `*`, is literally `22`/`3389`, or is a `low-high` range containing them, so a substring test on the projected string misses `1-65535` and over-matches `2200`. The finding is candidate minus covered. Confirm the prerequisite per subscription with `az security pricing show --name VirtualMachines --query '{tier:pricingTier,subPlan:subPlan}'` — Just-in-Time is a Defender for Servers Plan 2 capability.
api: az security pricing show --name VirtualMachines --subscription <subscription_id> --query '{tier:pricingTier,subPlan:subPlan}' -o json

az graph query --first 1000 --skip <offset> -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/virtualMachines' | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, vm = name, id, location, osType = tostring(properties.storageProfile.osDisk.osType), powerState = tostring(properties.extended.instanceView.powerState.code), nics = tostring(properties.networkProfile.networkInterfaces)" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 --skip <offset> -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/networkSecurityGroups' | mv-expand rule = properties.securityRules | extend rp = rule.properties | where tostring(rp.access) =~ 'Allow' and tostring(rp.direction) =~ 'Inbound' | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, nsg = name, ruleName = tostring(rule.name), protocol = tostring(rp.protocol), portRange = tostring(rp.destinationPortRange), portRanges = tostring(rp.destinationPortRanges), src = tostring(rp.sourceAddressPrefix), srcs = tostring(rp.sourceAddressPrefixes), priority = toint(rp.priority), nics = tostring(properties.networkInterfaces), subnets = tostring(properties.subnets), id" -o json
controls.evidence: The full `properties.virtualMachines` array from each Just-in-Time policy, keyed by subscription, resource group and ascLocation, showing per VM the ARM id and each protected port's `number`, `protocol`, `allowedSourceAddressPrefix`/`allowedSourceAddressPrefixes` and `maxRequestAccessDuration`, plus `properties.requests[]` captured at the same instant so a live approval can be told apart from a standing rule; the `pricingTier` and `subPlan` from `az security pricing show` per subscription proving the capability is licensed; and the joined candidate table — VM ARM id, NIC or subnet, NSG ARM id, rule name, priority, protocol, the raw port range strings and the raw source prefix strings — annotated as covered or uncovered by the policy union, with the parsed port decision recorded next to the raw value.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS for a subscription when every virtual machine in it that a joined NSG rule exposes on TCP/22 or TCP/3389 appears in some Just-in-Time policy in that subscription with an entry in `ports[]` for each such port, and for every one of those port entries `maxRequestAccessDuration` parses to no more than PT3H and `allowedSourceAddressPrefix` (or every member of `allowedSourceAddressPrefixes`) is neither `*`, `0.0.0.0/0`, `::/0` nor the service tag `Internet`. A subscription whose Defender for Servers plan is not Plan 2 is NOT_APPLICABLE with the observed `pricingTier`/`subPlan` recorded, not MET. A subscription where the policy list call or either Resource Graph page returned a non-zero exit, an authorisation error or a truncated page is inconclusive, not PASS.
controls.remediation: Enable Defender for Servers Plan 2 on the subscription, then create or extend the resource group's `default` Just-in-Time policy in the relevant ascLocation with `az rest --method put` against the `jitNetworkAccessPolicies/default` resource, listing each VM with its management ports, a `maxRequestAccessDuration` of PT1H to PT3H and an `allowedSourceAddressPrefix` naming the corporate egress range. Remove the corresponding standing Allow rules from the NSG afterwards: Just-in-Time inserts its own rule at a lower priority number when a request is approved, and a leftover permanent Allow makes the whole mechanism cosmetic. Restrict who can request access to the Security Admin role or a custom role granting `Microsoft.Security/locations/jitNetworkAccessPolicies/initiate/action`.
controls.caveat: The mechanism produces the most convincing false pass in this section: a policy can exist and be complete while the VM is still permanently open, because Just-in-Time only adds a time-boxed Allow above the deny — it does not remove a pre-existing standing Allow an operator left in the NSG. Assess controls 2.1 and 2.2 alongside this one and treat 'policy configured but a standing internet Allow remains' as a fail on both. Second, a live approved request temporarily rewrites the NSG, so an NSG snapshot taken during an open window shows an internet-sourced rule that is legitimate and will expire; correlate against `properties.requests[]` and the rule description before reporting it. Third, both enumeration paths silently under-report: the subscription-wide ARM list is a paged collection and `az rest` does not follow `nextLink`, so a large estate returns one page and the missing VMs read as 'no policy needed'; and `az graph query` caps at 1000 rows per call, so the sweep must page with `--skip` until short and abort rather than pass if any page errors. Fourth, `az security pricing show` reports the subscription plan, but Defender for Servers can also be enabled per-resource, so a Plan-1 subscription may still hold covered VMs and a Plan-2 subscription may hold VMs explicitly opted out. Fifth, the policy's location segment is Defender's regional store and not the VM's region, so a per-location read that iterates VM locations misses policies entirely and reports a fully covered estate as uncovered. Finally, Just-in-Time cannot protect a VM with no NIC-level or subnet-level NSG, or one reached through a Basic-SKU load balancer rule; those VMs are outside the mechanism and must be reported under a different control rather than counted as covered.

controls.title: Blob data cannot be read anonymously from any storage account
controls.objective: Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark DP-1 and IM-1 require data access to be authenticated. A storage account that permits anonymous public read lets any container or blob be published to the entire internet with a single container property change, and it is the single most common route by which Azure data is exposed — the account-level switch is the only place the capability can be removed outright.
controls.procedure: Two layers, both required, and both across every enabled subscription rather than the current one. Layer one, the account switch: one `az graph query` over `microsoft.storage/storageaccounts` projecting `properties.allowBlobPublicAccess`, `properties.allowSharedKeyAccess` and `properties.publicNetworkAccess`, paged with `--skip` until a page comes back short. Treat a null or absent `allowBlobPublicAccess` as unresolved rather than safe and resolve it per account with `az storage account show --ids <arm_id> --query 'allowBlobPublicAccess'`, addressing the account by ARM id so the call is not silently scoped to the current subscription. Also sweep `microsoft.classicstorage/storageaccounts` in the same pass: classic accounts do not carry the switch at all and are invisible to a query filtered on the modern type. Layer two, the containers: for every account where the switch is true or unresolved, list containers on the data plane with `az storage container list --account-name <acct> --auth-mode login --query "[?properties.publicAccess!=null].{name:name,level:properties.publicAccess}"`. A container's `publicAccess` is `blob` (anonymous read of blob content), `container` (anonymous read plus listing, which enumerates the whole container) or null. Where the account switch is false the container property is inert and any residual value is a hygiene observation, not exposure. Prove the negative on the wire for at least one container per account by fetching a container listing URL and a known blob URL with no credentials, keeping the response body and not just the status line: a 409 carrying `PublicAccessNotPermitted` is the proof the account switch is enforced, while a bare 404 only shows that one name did not resolve. Record `properties.allowSharedKeyAccess` alongside — an account still accepting the shared account key reaches the same data without an identity.
api: az graph query --first 1000 --skip <offset> -q "resources | where type in~ ('microsoft.storage/storageAccounts','microsoft.classicstorage/storageAccounts') | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, acct = name, type, allowBlobPublicAccess = properties.allowBlobPublicAccess, allowSharedKeyAccess = properties.allowSharedKeyAccess, publicNetworkAccess = tostring(properties.publicNetworkAccess), kind, sku = tostring(sku.name), id" -o json
az storage container list --account-name <acct> --auth-mode login --query "[?properties.publicAccess!=null].{name:name,level:properties.publicAccess}" -o json
az storage container set-permission --name <container> --account-name <acct> --auth-mode login --public-access off
controls.evidence: Per account: the ARM resource id, the resource type (modern or classic) and the effective `allowBlobPublicAccess`, `allowSharedKeyAccess` and `publicNetworkAccess` values from `az storage account show`, each recorded as an explicit true / false / absent tri-state rather than a coerced boolean. Per account where the switch is true or unresolved: the full container listing with each container's `publicAccess` level, and for at least one container the unauthenticated request's status line, response headers and body — the `x-ms-request-id` and the error code string inside the body — which is the artifact that turns a configuration reading into demonstrated exposure or a demonstrated refusal. Per account whose data-plane listing failed: the exact CLI exit code and error text, filed in the run's errors file.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, across every enabled subscription, every account of type `microsoft.storage/storageAccounts` has an effective `allowBlobPublicAccess` of literal false. Where the switch is true, PASS additionally requires that no container in that account has a `publicAccess` of `blob` or `container` and that the unauthenticated fetch returned HTTP 409 with `PublicAccessNotPermitted` or HTTP 404. Any account whose switch resolved to absent, whose container listing did not complete (data-plane role missing, account firewall refusal, or shared-key access disabled), or which is of type `microsoft.classicstorage/storageAccounts`, is inconclusive and must be reported REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW rather than PASS.
controls.remediation: Turn the capability off at the account with `az storage account update --ids <arm_id> --allow-blob-public-access false`, which makes every anonymous request fail regardless of container settings, then clean up the container properties with `az storage container set-permission --public-access off`. Where content genuinely must be public, serve it through Azure Front Door or a CDN endpoint over a private origin, or issue short-lived user-delegation SAS tokens with `az storage blob generate-sas --auth-mode login --as-user`. Enforce the account setting estate-wide with the built-in Azure Policy definition for disallowing blob public access, assigned at management group scope in Deny effect — the same definition assigned in Audit changes nothing about what a new account can do.
controls.caveat: The decisive trap is the absent property. `allowBlobPublicAccess` is not always present in the ARM payload, and its meaning when absent depends on when the account was created — accounts predating the platform default change behave as if it were true, ones created after it as if false. Code that reads the field with a `not x` test therefore marks the most dangerous accounts compliant. Read the effective value and treat absence as unresolved. Second, the container listing is a data-plane call and control-plane Reader is not enough: without `Storage Blob Data Reader` the call fails, and a script that treats a non-zero exit as 'no public containers' converts a permission error into a pass. Third, if the account's network rules are set to deny (control 2.8) the same call fails from the assessor's address for a completely different reason; distinguish the two by error code, never merge them. Fourth, `container` and `blob` are not equivalent — `container` also allows listing, so an attacker needs no blob-name guessing. Fifth, `curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}'` throws away the body that carries the error code, and a bare 404 is ambiguous between 'anonymous access off' and 'that blob does not exist', so the negative must be proven from the body of a container-listing request. Sixth, a Resource Graph sweep that stops at the first 1000 rows, or that filters only on `microsoft.storage/storageAccounts`, leaves the remainder of a large estate and every classic account out of the population entirely, and an absent resource reads as a clean one. Finally, anonymous public access is only one credential-free path: a long-lived account-key SAS, or an account still allowing shared-key authentication, reaches the same data without a login, so `allowSharedKeyAccess` is recorded here even though it sits outside this control's verdict.

controls.title: Storage endpoints refuse plaintext connections and legacy TLS versions
controls.objective: Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark DP-3 requires data in transit to be encrypted with current protocol versions.
