A storage account that accepts HTTP allows account keys and SAS tokens to be replayed off the wire, and one that still negotiates TLS 1.0 or 1.1 exposes the session to downgrade and to the known weaknesses of those versions — both are per-account settings that no client-side configuration can compensate for.
controls.procedure: Answer both properties for the whole estate in one paged `az graph query` over `microsoft.storage/storageaccounts`, projecting `properties.supportsHttpsTrafficOnly` and `properties.minimumTlsVersion`. Resource Graph is the right instrument precisely because it spans every readable subscription; `az storage account list` sees only the current one. Neither field is guaranteed present, so treat an absent value as unresolved and resolve it per account with `az storage account show --ids <arm_id> --query '{https:enableHttpsTrafficOnly,tls:minimumTlsVersion}'` — the ARM and Resource Graph property is `supportsHttpsTrafficOnly` while the CLI's own object model surfaces it as `enableHttpsTrafficOnly`, and the name has moved between CLI versions, so query both keys and record which one answered rather than assuming. `minimumTlsVersion` is a string enum: `TLS1_0`, `TLS1_1` and `TLS1_2` are accepted everywhere and `TLS1_3` only on recent API versions and regions; map each to an ordinal for comparison and treat any unrecognised or null value as unresolved rather than as a fail or a pass. Corroborate on the wire where the account is reachable: a plaintext request to `http://<acct>.blob.core.windows.net/` should be rejected with HTTP 400 and an `AccountRequiresHttps` error in the body, and a TLS 1.1 handshake should not complete. Repeat the wire check against every service endpoint the account exposes — blob, file, queue, table, dfs and web — since the settings are account-wide but the observable proof is per endpoint. Read the file service separately with `az storage account file-service-properties show`, because the account TLS floor governs REST and not the SMB channel, whose permitted versions, authentication methods and channel encryption live in `properties.protocolSettings.smb`. Cover Data Lake Storage Gen2 accounts (`isHnsEnabled` true) in the same sweep; they are the same resource type and are routinely missed by tooling that filters on `kind == 'StorageV2'`.
api: az graph query --first 1000 --skip <offset> -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.storage/storageAccounts' | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, acct = name, httpsOnly = properties.supportsHttpsTrafficOnly, minTls = tostring(properties.minimumTlsVersion), hns = properties.isHnsEnabled, kind, primaryEndpoints = tostring(properties.primaryEndpoints), id" -o json
az storage account file-service-properties show --account-name <acct> --resource-group <rg> --query 'protocolSettings.smb' -o json
az storage account update --ids <storage_account_arm_id> --https-only true --min-tls-version TLS1_2
controls.evidence: Per account: ARM resource id plus the effective secure-transfer boolean and `minimumTlsVersion` string exactly as returned, naming which property key answered, with absence recorded distinctly from false and from an unrecognised value. Where the endpoint is reachable from the assessor: the status line, headers and body of the plaintext request (the `AccountRequiresHttps` error code being the artifact, not the status code alone), and the full `openssl s_client` transcript for the TLS 1.1 attempt including the local OpenSSL version banner and the alert or error returned, timestamped — the local version matters because it determines whether the failure came from Azure or from the assessor's own client. For accounts exposing the file endpoint, the `protocolSettings.smb` object with its `versions`, `authenticationMethods` and `channelEncryption` values.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, across every enabled subscription, every storage account has an effective secure-transfer flag of literal true and a `minimumTlsVersion` whose mapped ordinal is at least that of `TLS1_2`. An account where either property is absent or unrecognised in the Resource Graph response and could not be resolved by `az storage account show --ids` is inconclusive, not PASS. A wire check that did not complete — endpoint unreachable, account firewall refusal, or a local TLS stack that will not offer TLS 1.1 — is recorded as not-performed and does not by itself satisfy the PASS condition, which rests on the resolved property values.
controls.remediation: Set both in one call: `az storage account update --ids <arm_id> --https-only true --min-tls-version TLS1_2`. Before enforcing TLS 1.2 on a busy account, find the legacy callers first — the `StorageRead` and `StorageWrite` diagnostic log categories record the negotiated TLS version per request, so a 30-day query over the account's log destination names exactly which clients will break. Tighten the SMB channel separately with `az storage account file-service-properties update --account-name <acct> --resource-group <rg> --versions SMB3.1.1 --channel-encryption AES-256-GCM`. Assign the built-in Azure Policy definitions for secure transfer and for minimum TLS version at management group scope in Deny effect, since the same definitions in Audit will report a non-compliant new account without preventing it.
controls.caveat: Several ways to record a false pass here. First, the property-name mismatch: ARM and Resource Graph call it `supportsHttpsTrafficOnly`, the CLI object model calls it `enableHttpsTrafficOnly`, and a query written against the wrong one returns null for every account — a truthiness test then reads that as universally non-compliant while a `!= false` test reads it as universally compliant. Second, the subscription trap: `az storage account list` and any JMESPath filter over it cover only the current subscription, so an estate-wide claim built that way is clean by construction for every account elsewhere; scope with Resource Graph or address accounts by `--ids`. Third, string comparison of `minimumTlsVersion` gives no protection against null, and an account created before the property existed can return nothing while still negotiating TLS 1.0 — resolve absence explicitly instead of defaulting it, and do not fail an account merely for returning a newer value such as `TLS1_3`. Fourth, the TLS 1.1 probe is the classic self-inflicted false pass: OpenSSL 3.x refuses TLS 1.1 at its default security level, so the handshake fails on the assessor's machine and the transcript looks like server-side enforcement — pass `-cipher 'DEFAULT@SECLEVEL=0'` (or use a client that will actually offer TLS 1.1) and record the client version, or mark the wire check not-performed. Fifth, the account setting governs the REST endpoints; a client reaching the account through a vanity CNAME, a CDN or Front Door terminates TLS elsewhere, so take the wire proof against the canonical `*.blob.core.windows.net` name. Sixth, the TLS floor does not govern SMB on the file endpoint, so an account at TLS1_2 can still accept SMB 2.1 with unencrypted channels, which is why `protocolSettings.smb` is read alongside. Finally, neither property applies to `Microsoft.ClassicStorage/storageAccounts`; if classic accounts exist they must be reported separately as unmanageable legacy exposure rather than omitted from the population.

controls.title: Storage accounts deny network access by default and allow only named networks
controls.objective: Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark NS-2 asks that PaaS data services be reachable only from approved networks. A storage account whose network rules default to Allow is reachable from every address on the internet, so a leaked SAS token or account key becomes immediately usable from anywhere; a default of Deny turns the same leaked credential into something an attacker must also be inside an approved network or private endpoint to use.
controls.procedure: Query the whole estate once with a paged `az graph query` over `microsoft.storage/storageaccounts`, projecting `properties.publicNetworkAccess`, `properties.networkAcls.defaultAction`, `properties.networkAcls.bypass` and the lengths of `properties.networkAcls.ipRules`, `properties.networkAcls.virtualNetworkRules` and `properties.networkAcls.resourceAccessRules`. Two properties interact and both must be read: `publicNetworkAccess` of `Disabled` closes the public endpoint entirely regardless of the ACL and is the strongest state; `SecuredByPerimeter` hands enforcement to a Network Security Perimeter and is only as strong as that perimeter's association mode; `Enabled` or absent means the `networkAcls` govern. Within `networkAcls`, `defaultAction` of `Deny` is the required state and `Allow` fails outright. For accounts at Deny, enumerate the allowances: expand `ipRules[].value` and compare each against the engagement's approved-ranges input file, expand `virtualNetworkRules[].id` to name the subnets and record each rule's `state`, and read `bypass`, a comma-separated subset of `AzureServices`, `Logging`, `Metrics` or the literal `None`. For accounts at `SecuredByPerimeter`, resolve the perimeter association and its access mode with the `az network perimeter` commands from the `nsp` extension — an association in learning mode observes and does not block. Confirm each account's effective state with `az storage account show --ids <arm_id> --query '{pna:publicNetworkAccess,acl:networkAcls}'` and establish private connectivity from Resource Graph over `microsoft.network/privateendpoints`, reading both `properties.privateLinkServiceConnections[]` and `properties.manualPrivateLinkServiceConnections[]` and each connection's `privateLinkServiceConnectionState.status`, so that a denied public endpoint can be told apart from a broken one.
api: az graph query --first 1000 --skip <offset> -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.storage/storageAccounts' | extend acl = properties.networkAcls | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, acct = name, publicNetworkAccess = tostring(properties.publicNetworkAccess), defaultAction = tostring(acl.defaultAction), bypass = tostring(acl.bypass), ipRules = array_length(acl.ipRules), vnetRules = array_length(acl.virtualNetworkRules), resourceRules = array_length(acl.resourceAccessRules), id" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 --skip <offset> -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.storage/storageAccounts' | mv-expand r = properties.networkAcls.ipRules | project subscriptionId, acct = name, allowedIp = tostring(r.value), action = tostring(r.action), id" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 --skip <offset> -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/privateEndpoints' | mv-expand conn = properties.privateLinkServiceConnections, manual = properties.manualPrivateLinkServiceConnections | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, pe = name, target = tostring(coalesce(conn.properties.privateLinkServiceId, manual.properties.privateLinkServiceId)), groupIds = tostring(coalesce(conn.properties.groupIds, manual.properties.groupIds)), status = tostring(coalesce(conn.properties.privateLinkServiceConnectionState.status, manual.properties.privateLinkServiceConnectionState.status)), id" -o json
az storage account network-rule list --account-name <acct> --resource-group <rg> -o json
az storage account update --ids <storage_account_arm_id> --default-action Deny --bypass AzureServices
controls.evidence: Per account: the ARM resource id together with the literal `publicNetworkAccess` string and the whole `networkAcls` object as returned — `defaultAction`, `bypass`, every `ipRules[].value` and `action`, every `virtualNetworkRules[].id` with its `state`, and every `resourceAccessRules` entry with its `tenantId` and `resourceId`, the tenant id compared against the assessed tenant. Where a private endpoint targets the account, its resource id, `groupIds` and connection status and the private DNS zone group attached to it. Where `publicNetworkAccess` is `SecuredByPerimeter`, the perimeter resource id, the profile and the association's access mode recorded literally. Accounts at `defaultAction: Deny` with zero allowances are listed separately, since they are reachable only by private endpoint or bypass and that reachability must be shown rather than assumed.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS for an account when either `publicNetworkAccess` equals `Disabled`, or `networkAcls.defaultAction` equals `Deny` and every `ipRules[].value` appears in the engagement's approved-ranges input file with a prefix length of /24 or longer (a bare address counts as /32) and every `virtualNetworkRules[].id` names a subnet in a virtual network inside the assessed tenant with `state` of `Succeeded`. `defaultAction` of `Allow`, an absent `networkAcls` object, or any `ipRules[].value` not present in the approved-ranges file, fails. `publicNetworkAccess` of `SecuredByPerimeter` is PASS only where the resolved perimeter association reports an enforced access mode; a learning-mode association fails. The control is PASS overall only when every account in every enabled subscription passes and no Resource Graph page errored or truncated.
controls.remediation: Switch the default and keep the platform paths you actually need: `az storage account update --ids <arm_id> --default-action Deny --bypass AzureServices`, then add each legitimate source explicitly with `az storage account network-rule add --account-name <acct> --resource-group <rg> --ip-address <cidr>` or `--subnet <subnet_id>`. For accounts that should have no public surface, prefer `--public-network-access Disabled` plus a private endpoint with a linked private DNS zone group, which removes the public endpoint rather than filtering it. Sequence the change carefully: add the rules first, verify the workload still connects, then flip the default action. Where a Network Security Perimeter is used, move the association out of learning mode once traffic has been observed, because learning mode logs and permits.
controls.caveat: The headline trap is that `defaultAction: Deny` is not the same as closed. `bypass` defaults to `AzureServices`, which admits a large set of first-party services acting on your behalf, and `resourceAccessRules` can name specific resources including ones in another tenant; both are legitimate and both widen the account beyond the IP and VNet rules an assessor reads, so describing a Deny account as 'restricted to two subnets' while its bypass is `AzureServices` overstates the posture. Second, `publicNetworkAccess` and `defaultAction` override each other in opposite directions — `Allow` plus `Disabled` is closed, `Deny` plus `Enabled` is filtered rather than closed — and reading either field alone gets one of those two cases wrong. Third, `SecuredByPerimeter` is the quiet false pass: it reads as the strongest value in the enum while a perimeter association in learning mode blocks nothing at all, so the value must be resolved to the association's access mode before it is credited. Fourth, network rules govern the data-plane endpoints (blob, file, queue, table, dfs) and not control-plane operations, and they do not evaluate identity, so a network-restricted account is not an access-controlled account. Fifth, Azure rejects `/31` and `/32` prefixes and private ranges in `ipRules` — a single address is supplied bare — so a rule list that looks conveniently narrow may simply be the narrowest form the platform accepts, and a public /24 is still 256 hosts. Sixth, a private-endpoint query that reads only `privateLinkServiceConnections[]` misses manually approved connections, and one run through a subscription-scoped `az network private-endpoint list` misses every endpoint outside the current subscription, both of which turn a compensating control into an apparent absence. Finally, this restriction is what breaks the container enumeration in control 2.6 from an outside vantage: run the data-plane checks from an allowed address, or record them as inconclusive rather than clean.

controls.title: Storage encryption uses a customer-managed key the tenant can revoke
controls.objective: Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark DP-5 distinguishes platform-managed from customer-managed keys. All Azure Storage is encrypted at rest either way; the security difference is control — a customer-managed key held in Key Vault or Managed HSM means the tenant can rotate it, audit every unwrap in the vault log, and revoke it to render the data cryptographically unreadable, which is the only mechanism that makes an emergency de-provisioning of a storage account meaningful.
controls.procedure: Read the encryption block for every account in one paged `az graph query` over `microsoft.storage/storageaccounts`, projecting `properties.encryption.keySource`, the `keyVaultProperties` fields `keyName`, `keyVaultUri`, `keyVersion`, `currentVersionedKeyIdentifier` and `lastKeyRotationTimestamp`, `properties.encryption.requireInfrastructureEncryption`, the per-service `properties.encryption.services` map, and `identity.type` with `identity.userAssignedIdentities`. A `keySource` of `Microsoft.Storage` is the platform key and fails this control; `Microsoft.Keyvault` is the customer-managed state — note the lower-case `v`, which a string comparison against `Microsoft.KeyVault` will miss. For each customer-managed account, resolve the key the pointer names and prove the binding is alive rather than merely present. Read the vault with `az keyvault show --name <vault> --query '{purge:properties.enablePurgeProtection,softDelete:properties.enableSoftDelete,rbac:properties.enableRbacAuthorization}'`; Azure will not bind a customer key to a vault without purge protection, so a customer-managed account pointing at an unprotected vault is a signal the pointer is stale rather than a signal the platform relaxed. Read the key itself — `az keyvault key show --vault-name <vault> --name <key>` for a vault, `--hsm-name <hsm>` for a Managed HSM, which is a different endpoint the vault form cannot reach — and take `key.kty`, `key.key_ops`, `attributes.enabled`, `attributes.expires` and `attributes.notBefore`; rotation is read from `az keyvault key rotation-policy show`, not from an update timestamp. Then prove the account's identity can still unwrap: on an RBAC vault, `az role assignment list --assignee <account_principal_id> --scope <key_or_vault_scope> --include-inherited`, because the grant is usually made at vault or resource-group scope and a key-scoped query without inheritance returns nothing; on a legacy vault, read `properties.accessPolicies` and look for `wrapKey`, `unwrapKey` and `get`. Version pinning is read from the pointer: an absent `keyVersion` with a populated `currentVersionedKeyIdentifier` means the account follows the latest version automatically, the preferred state. Finally read `properties.encryption.services.<blob|file|queue|table>.keyType`: only `Account` puts that service under the customer key, and for queue and table the account-scoped key type can only be chosen when the account is created.
api: az graph query --first 1000 --skip <offset> -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.storage/storageAccounts' | extend enc = properties.encryption | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, acct = name, keySource = tostring(enc.keySource), keyName = tostring(enc.keyVaultProperties.keyName), keyVaultUri = tostring(enc.keyVaultProperties.keyVaultUri), keyVersion = tostring(enc.keyVaultProperties.keyVersion), currentKeyId = tostring(enc.keyVaultProperties.currentVersionedKeyIdentifier), infraEnc = enc.requireInfrastructureEncryption, services = tostring(enc.services), identityType = tostring(identity.type), principalId = tostring(identity.principalId), id" -o json
az keyvault key rotation-policy show --vault-name <vault> --name <key> -o json
controls.evidence: Per account: the ARM resource id and the whole `properties.encryption` object as returned — `keySource`, the full `keyVaultProperties` including `keyName`, `keyVaultUri`, `keyVersion`, `currentVersionedKeyIdentifier` and `lastKeyRotationTimestamp`, `requireInfrastructureEncryption`, and the `services` map with each service's `enabled`, `keyType` and `lastEnabledTime` — plus `identity.type` and the identity's principal id. For customer-managed accounts: the referenced vault's purge-protection, soft-delete and RBAC-mode values; the key's type, key operations, enabled flag and expiry, and its rotation policy; and the role assignment (with the scope it was found at and whether it was inherited) or the access-policy entry granting that principal wrapKey and unwrapKey. Where any Key Vault read failed, the exact error, filed in the errors file — the binding is then unverified, not verified.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS for an account when `properties.encryption.keySource` equals `Microsoft.Keyvault` compared case-insensitively, `keyVaultProperties.currentVersionedKeyIdentifier` is non-empty and resolves to a key that exists with `attributes.enabled` true and either no `attributes.expires` or an expiry in the future, the referenced vault reports `enablePurgeProtection` true, and the account's identity principal holds wrapKey and unwrapKey on that key through a role assignment found at key, vault, resource-group or subscription scope, or through an access policy. `keySource` of `Microsoft.Storage` fails. An account whose key, vault or grant could not be read because the assessing principal lacks Key Vault access is inconclusive, not PASS. The control is evaluated over every storage account in every enabled subscription except accounts whose ARM id appears in the engagement's documented exemption input file, which are reported as excluded with the file's justification quoted.
controls.remediation: Give the account a managed identity with `az storage account update --ids <arm_id> --assign-identity`, grant that principal `Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User` over the key or vault (or wrapKey/unwrapKey/get in an access policy on a legacy vault), then bind the key with `az storage account update --ids <arm_id> --encryption-key-source Microsoft.Keyvault --encryption-key-vault <vault_uri> --encryption-key-name <key>`. Omit the key version so the account follows automatic rotation, and set a rotation policy on the key so the version actually changes. For the highest-assurance workloads enable infrastructure encryption, a second platform-managed layer beneath the customer key — but only at account creation, since the property is immutable afterwards. Enforce with the built-in Azure Policy definition requiring customer-managed keys on storage accounts, assigned at management group scope in Deny effect; the audit-effect assignment will not stop the next account from being created on the platform key.
controls.caveat: Level 2 because a customer-managed key adds a real availability dependency: if the key is deleted, expired, disabled or the vault firewall blocks the account, the storage account becomes unreadable — which is the point of the control and also its principal operational risk. The traps. First, `keySource` is `Microsoft.Storage` on the overwhelming majority of accounts and that data is still encrypted at rest, so this must be reported as a key-custody finding and never as 'unencrypted storage', which is factually wrong and damages the report. Second, the enum is spelled `Microsoft.Keyvault`; a case-sensitive comparison against `Microsoft.KeyVault` marks every compliant account as failing and invites the assessor to 'fix' the check by inverting it. Third, a customer-managed binding can be present and dead — the key disabled, past `expires`, or the grant removed — and none of that changes `keySource`, so the pointer must be resolved rather than trusted. Fourth, if the assessing principal has ARM Reader but no Key Vault data-plane or management access, `az keyvault key show` fails while `az storage account show` succeeds, and a script that ignores the second failure records a healthy binding it never verified; that account is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW. Fifth, the grant is normally made at vault or resource-group scope, so `az role assignment list --scope <key>` without `--include-inherited` returns empty and produces a confident false finding in the other direction. Sixth, a key held in a Managed HSM is not readable through `--vault-name` at all; the wrong flag yields a not-found that reads like a broken binding. Seventh, `requireInfrastructureEncryption` is immutable after creation, so any remediation promising to enable it on an existing account is not executable and the finding must say so. Finally, `keySource` at the account does not mean every service is covered: queue and table remain on a service-managed key unless their `services[].keyType` is `Account`, which can only be chosen at creation time.

controls.title: Managed disks, snapshots and images encrypt with a customer-managed disk encryption set
controls.objective: Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark DP-5 applied to compute storage. Managed disks are encrypted with a platform key by default; binding them to a disk encryption set backed by a Key Vault key gives the tenant rotation, an auditable unwrap trail and the ability to revoke — and it must extend to the snapshots and images derived from those disks, which are the artifacts most often copied into another subscription or exported over a SAS URL.
controls.procedure: Sweep the derived artifacts together with the live ones, because a customer-managed disk whose snapshot uses the platform key leaks the same bytes. One paged `az graph query` covers `microsoft.compute/disks`, `microsoft.compute/snapshots` and `microsoft.compute/images`, projecting `properties.encryption.type`, `properties.encryption.diskEncryptionSetId` and, for disks, `properties.diskState`, `managedBy` and `properties.diskSizeGB`. The `encryption.type` values are `EncryptionAtRestWithPlatformKey` (fails), `EncryptionAtRestWithCustomerKey` (customer key only) and `EncryptionAtRestWithPlatformAndCustomerKeys` (double encryption, the strongest). Gallery image versions need a separate pass: their encryption is not a single top-level property but is declared per published region under `properties.publishingProfile.targetRegions[].encryption.osDiskImage.diskEncryptionSetId` and the parallel `dataDiskImages[]` entries, so read them with `az sig image-version show` (or `az sig image-version list` per gallery and image definition) and evaluate every target region, since one unencrypted replica is a full copy. Enumerate the disk encryption sets from Resource Graph rather than the subscription-scoped list command, then read each one's `properties.activeKey.sourceVault.id`, `properties.activeKey.keyUrl`, `properties.rotationToLatestKeyVersionEnabled`, `properties.encryptionType` and `identity.principalId`, and confirm that identity still holds wrapKey and unwrapKey on the key with `az role assignment list --assignee <principal> --include-inherited`, since a revoked grant leaves the pointer intact while the set is non-functional. Separately record VMs where `properties.securityProfile.encryptionAtHost` is not literally true, because the customer key on the managed disk does not cover the VM's temporary disk or the host cache unless encryption at host is on. Finally list unattached disks (`properties.diskState` of `Unattached`) and any disk in `ActiveSAS` as their own populations: the first holds data nobody is watching, the second is being exported right now.
api: az graph query --first 1000 --skip <offset> -q "resources | where type in~ ('microsoft.compute/disks','microsoft.compute/snapshots','microsoft.compute/images') | extend enc = properties.encryption | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, type, name, encType = tostring(enc.type), desId = tostring(enc.diskEncryptionSetId), diskState = tostring(properties.diskState), managedBy = tostring(managedBy), sizeGb = properties.diskSizeGB, adeSettings = tostring(properties.encryptionSettingsCollection), id" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 --skip <offset> -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/diskEncryptionSets' | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, des = name, keyUrl = tostring(properties.activeKey.keyUrl), vault = tostring(properties.activeKey.sourceVault.id), rotate = properties.rotationToLatestKeyVersionEnabled, encType = tostring(properties.encryptionType), principalId = tostring(identity.principalId), id" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 --skip <offset> -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/virtualMachines' | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, vm = name, encryptionAtHost = properties.securityProfile.encryptionAtHost, securityType = tostring(properties.securityProfile.securityType), osDiskDes = tostring(properties.storageProfile.osDisk.managedDisk.diskEncryptionSet.id), id" -o json
controls.evidence: Per disk, snapshot and image: the ARM resource id, the literal `properties.encryption.type` string, the `diskEncryptionSetId` where present, the disk state, the `managedBy` VM id and the size in GB. Per gallery image version: the version id and, for every entry in `publishingProfile.targetRegions[]`, the region name and the OS and data disk `diskEncryptionSetId` values or their absence. Per disk encryption set: name, `activeKey.keyUrl` including the version segment or its absence, `activeKey.sourceVault.id`, `rotationToLatestKeyVersionEnabled`, `encryptionType`, the identity principal id, and the role assignment proving that identity can still unwrap, recorded with the scope it was found at. Per VM: `encryptionAtHost` as an explicit true / false / absent tri-state. The reconciliation count of the Resource Graph sweep against `az disk list` for at least one subscription, so the sweep's completeness is itself evidenced.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, across every enabled subscription, every resource of type `microsoft.compute/disks`, `microsoft.compute/snapshots` and `microsoft.compute/images` has `properties.encryption.type` equal to `EncryptionAtRestWithCustomerKey` or `EncryptionAtRestWithPlatformAndCustomerKeys` with a non-empty `diskEncryptionSetId` that resolves to an existing disk encryption set whose identity principal holds wrapKey and unwrapKey on the key named in `activeKey.keyUrl`, in a vault reporting `enablePurgeProtection` true; and every gallery image version has a non-empty `diskEncryptionSetId` for the OS disk image in every entry of `publishingProfile.targetRegions[]`. Any such resource at `EncryptionAtRestWithPlatformKey`, including unattached disks and orphaned snapshots, fails. A run in which any Resource Graph page errored or returned exactly the page limit without being paged to exhaustion is inconclusive, not PASS.
controls.remediation: Create a disk encryption set against a purge-protected vault key, grant its managed identity `Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User`, then bind existing disks with `az disk update --ids <disk_arm_id> --disk-encryption-set <des_id> --encryption-type EncryptionAtRestWithCustomerKey` — the disk must be detached or the VM deallocated for the change, so schedule it. Turn on `rotationToLatestKeyVersionEnabled` on the set so key rotation propagates without touching every disk. Enable encryption at host on the VM sizes that support it to cover the temp disk and host cache; the subscription feature must be registered first with `az feature register --namespace Microsoft.Compute --name EncryptionAtHost` and the VM must be deallocated for the update. Re-publish gallery image versions with a disk encryption set named for every target region. Delete unattached disks and stale snapshots outright rather than re-encrypting them, and revoke any active export SAS with `az disk revoke-access`. Enforce with the built-in Azure Policy definitions requiring a disk encryption set on disks and on OS and data disks at VM creation, assigned in Deny effect at management group scope.
controls.caveat: Level 2 because binding a disk encryption set requires downtime on existing disks and introduces a hard availability dependency on the vault. The recurring false pass is scope: an estate reporting 100% customer-managed disks while every snapshot and every gallery image version still carries the platform key has not met the objective, because a snapshot is a full copy of the disk and can be exported with a SAS URL — and gallery image versions in particular will not appear in a query over `microsoft.compute/disks`, `snapshots` and `images`, so they must be read through the gallery API and evaluated per target region. Restore point collections hold disk data on the same footing and should be reported alongside if present. Second, `encryptionAtHost` is a different mechanism from the disk encryption set: a VM with a customer-managed OS disk still writes a temp disk and host cache outside that key unless it is on, and the property is absent rather than false on VMs where it was never configured — treat absence as not-enabled and say so explicitly. Third, do not conflate this with the older in-guest BitLocker/dm-crypt disk encryption: the two are different features, are largely mutually exclusive on the same disk, and an assessor who reads `properties.encryptionSettingsCollection` while the control is about `properties.encryption` will report the wrong thing about the same resource — both are projected above so the two can be told apart rather than swapped. Fourth, `az disk-encryption-set list` and `az disk list` see only the current subscription, so an estate conclusion built on them is clean by construction everywhere else; enumerate from Resource Graph and page with `--skip` until a page comes back short, treating a page that returns exactly the limit as unfinished rather than complete. Fifth, the disk encryption set pointer can outlive its grant: the set still resolves, the disks still report a customer key, and nothing can be unwrapped — check the role assignment with `--include-inherited`, since the grant is usually held at vault scope. Finally, Resource Graph's `properties` for compute types is eventually consistent, so a disk created minutes before the sweep may be missing; reconcile the count against `az disk list` for at least one subscription and record the reconciliation.

controls.title: Key vaults survive deletion attempts through soft delete and purge protection
controls.objective: Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark DP-6 and BR-2. Without purge protection an attacker or a mistaken automation holding vault-delete rights can permanently destroy the keys that encrypt storage accounts, managed disks and databases, making the encrypted data unrecoverable — a single-command destructive action with no undo. Purge protection makes the deletion honour the retention window unconditionally, so the keys can be restored and the blast radius of a compromised operator is bounded.
controls.procedure: Enumerate the subscription set first with `az account list --query "[?state=='Enabled']"` so the sweep is provably estate-wide rather than whatever subscription happens to be the CLI default. Cover both vault families: `microsoft.keyvault/vaults` and `microsoft.keyvault/managedhsms` are distinct resource types and a query for the first misses every Managed HSM in the estate. Run one `az graph query` (needs the `resource-graph` extension) projecting `properties.enableSoftDelete`, `properties.softDeleteRetentionInDays`, `properties.enablePurgeProtection`, `properties.enableRbacAuthorization` and `properties.publicNetworkAccess`; Managed HSM carries the first three and `publicNetworkAccess` but not `enableRbacAuthorization`, so a null there is a type difference and not a finding. Resource Graph caps a page at 1000 rows, so page with `--first 1000 --skip N` until a short page returns and record the total — a truncated result set that is read as a complete one is the quietest way to miss the failing vaults. The critical reading rule is that `enablePurgeProtection` comes back as `true` when on and is absent from the payload when off — the platform does not emit `false` — so the test must be 'not equal to true', never 'equal to false'. Confirm per vault with `az keyvault show --name <vault> --query 'properties.enablePurgeProtection'`, which returns `null` for the off state. Soft delete can no longer be turned off on new vaults and reads true almost everywhere, so the meaningful readings are the purge-protection flag and the retention window, which is settable between 7 and 90 days. Then check what the vaults actually hold, because a vault with no keys is a lower-priority finding than one holding the disk encryption set key from control 2.10: list keys, secrets and certificates with `az keyvault key list --vault-name <vault>` (a Managed HSM takes `--hsm-name`, not `--vault-name`) and its `secret`/`certificate` siblings, noting these are data-plane calls needing a Key Vault data role and network reachability. Finally inspect the recycle bin with `az keyvault list-deleted`, once with `--resource-type vault` and once with `--resource-type hsm` — vaults already soft-deleted and pending purge are evidence of past deletion events, and their names stay reserved.
api: az graph query --first 1000 --skip 0 -q "resources | where type in~ ('microsoft.keyvault/vaults','microsoft.keyvault/managedHSMs') | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, vault = name, type, softDelete = properties.enableSoftDelete, retentionDays = properties.softDeleteRetentionInDays, purgeProtection = properties.enablePurgeProtection, rbac = properties.enableRbacAuthorization, publicNetworkAccess = tostring(properties.publicNetworkAccess), id" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 -q "resources | where type in~ ('microsoft.keyvault/vaults','microsoft.keyvault/managedHSMs') | where isnull(properties.enablePurgeProtection) or tostring(properties.enablePurgeProtection) !~ 'true' | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, vault = name, type, id" -o json
controls.evidence: Per vault and per Managed HSM: the ARM resource id, the subscription id, and the raw `enableSoftDelete`, `softDeleteRetentionInDays` and `enablePurgeProtection` values, with the purge-protection field recorded as the literal `true` or as absent — never coerced to a boolean false, because that distinction is the whole check. The Resource Graph page accounting (rows returned per page and the point at which paging stopped), so the reader can see the sweep was not truncated at 1000. Alongside each vault, the count of keys, secrets and certificates it holds and whether any of them is referenced by a storage account's customer-managed key, a disk encryption set or a SQL server TDE protector, which establishes the blast radius. The `az keyvault list-deleted` output for both resource types with each entry's deletion and scheduled purge dates.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, across every subscription returned by `az account list` with state `Enabled`, every `microsoft.keyvault/vaults` and `microsoft.keyvault/managedhsms` resource returns `properties.enablePurgeProtection` equal to the literal true, `properties.enableSoftDelete` equal to true, and `properties.softDeleteRetentionInDays` of at least 7 — at least 90 for any vault whose key is referenced as a storage account's `encryption.keyVaultProperties.keyVaultUri`, a disk encryption set's `activeKey`, or a SQL server's TDE protector. A vault where `enablePurgeProtection` is absent or null FAILS. The control is INCONCLUSIVE, never PASS, for any subscription where the Resource Graph result hit the 1000-row page cap without pagination or where the ARM read returned an authorisation error. A vault whose key inventory could not be read because the caller lacks a data-plane role or is blocked by the vault firewall remains assessable on this control, since both flags are control-plane properties.
controls.remediation: Turn it on with `az keyvault update --name <vault> --resource-group <rg> --enable-purge-protection true`, and `az keyvault update-hsm --hsm-name <hsm> --resource-group <rg> --enable-purge-protection true` for Managed HSM, which `az keyvault update` does not accept. The change is deliberately irreversible — once purge protection is on it cannot be turned off for the life of the vault — so confirm the retention window first: the window is fixed when soft delete is established and an attempt to change `--retention-days` on an existing vault is commonly rejected or ignored, which means a vault that needs 90 days generally has to be recreated. Plan for name reservation, since a deleted vault's name stays reserved for the whole retention period. Restrict who can delete vaults at all by removing `Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/delete` from operator roles and keeping vault management in a resource group with a `CanNotDelete` lock. Assign the built-in Azure Policy definitions for soft delete and purge protection at management group scope so new vaults inherit both, and assign them in Deny effect — the same definitions in Audit effect change nothing about what gets created.
controls.caveat: The absent-versus-false asymmetry is the exact false pass this control exists to catch: ARM omits `enablePurgeProtection` entirely when it is off, so a filter written as `properties.enablePurgeProtection == false` matches nothing and the assessment reports a clean estate while none of the vaults are protected. Write the test as 'not equal to true' and treat null as a fail. Second, soft delete is now enforced by the platform on new vaults and always reads true, which makes the control look satisfied on the strength of the wrong field; purge protection is the one carrying the security property. Third, Managed HSM is a separate resource type with its own flags and its own CLI verbs — a sweep filtered on `microsoft.keyvault/vaults` misses it, and Managed HSMs typically hold the most sensitive keys in the tenant. Fourth, Resource Graph pages at 1000 rows and `az graph query` returns exactly what it was asked for, so an unpaged sweep of a large estate silently assesses a prefix of it; and Resource Graph only spans subscriptions in the tenant of the current token, so a second tenant needs a second `az login`. Fifth, the irreversibility has an operational consequence that belongs in the finding: an environment that creates and destroys vaults per deployment will find its names locked for the retention period, which is usually why purge protection was left off, so pair the remediation with a naming convention that tolerates reservation. Sixth, purge protection protects the vault contents from purge, not from a key being disabled, expired or rotated by whoever holds the data-plane role, so it is not a substitute for restricting those roles.

controls.title: Key vault data planes reject traffic from unapproved networks
controls.objective: Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark NS-2 and IM-8. A key vault's data plane is a public HTTPS endpoint by default, so a leaked token, a stolen managed-identity assertion or an SSRF against a workload reaches the vault from anywhere on the internet. Restricting the vault to named virtual networks and addresses, or to a private endpoint only, means such a credential must also be used from inside the perimeter to be worth anything.
controls.procedure: Query both vault types in one `az graph query`, paging with `--first 1000 --skip N`, projecting `properties.publicNetworkAccess`, `properties.networkAcls.defaultAction`, `properties.networkAcls.bypass`, the `ipRules` and `virtualNetworkRules` arrays, and an explicit presence flag for the `networkAcls` object itself. Read the two governing fields together: `publicNetworkAccess` of `Disabled` removes the public endpoint outright and is the target state for a vault backing encryption keys; where it is `Enabled` or absent, `networkAcls.defaultAction` decides, and `Deny` is required. When the `networkAcls` block is entirely absent the effective behaviour is unrestricted — an absent ACL is the open state, not an inherited safe one. Where `defaultAction` is `Deny`, expand `ipRules[].value` and `virtualNetworkRules[].id` to name every allowance, and read `bypass`, which is `AzureServices` or `None`; `AzureServices` admits the trusted first-party service set (deployment engine, Disk Encryption, Backup and others) and is usually necessary but must be stated rather than left implicit. Then verify the compensating path with a Resource Graph query over `microsoft.network/privateendpoints` rather than `az network private-endpoint list`, which only ever sees the current subscription: expand the connection array and keep connections whose `groupIds` contain `vault` (or `managedhsm`), recording `privateLinkServiceConnectionState.status`. For each such endpoint list its DNS zone group with `az network private-endpoint dns-zone-group list`, because a private endpoint without `privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net` linked to the consuming VNet leaves clients resolving the public name. Finally confirm the vault is logging its data plane: `az monitor diagnostic-settings list --resource <vault_resource_id>` should show a setting carrying the `AuditEvent` category. Inspect that response's raw shape before filtering it — depending on the CLI version it is either a bare array or an object with a `value` array, and a `--query` written for the wrong shape returns empty for a correctly configured vault.
api: az graph query --first 1000 --skip 0 -q "resources | where type in~ ('microsoft.keyvault/vaults','microsoft.keyvault/managedHSMs') | extend acl = properties.networkAcls | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, vault = name, type, publicNetworkAccess = tostring(properties.publicNetworkAccess), aclPresent = isnotnull(acl), defaultAction = tostring(acl.defaultAction), bypass = tostring(acl.bypass), ipRules = array_length(acl.ipRules), vnetRules = array_length(acl.virtualNetworkRules), id" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/privateEndpoints' | mv-expand c = properties.privateLinkServiceConnections | where tostring(c.properties.groupIds) has 'vault' or tostring(c.properties.groupIds) has 'managedhsm' | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, pe = name, target = tostring(c.properties.privateLinkServiceId), groups = tostring(c.properties.groupIds), status = tostring(c.properties.privateLinkServiceConnectionState.status), subnet = tostring(properties.subnet.id), id" -o json
az network private-endpoint dns-zone-group list --endpoint-name <pe> --resource-group <rg> -o json
controls.evidence: Per vault: the ARM resource id, the literal `publicNetworkAccess` string (recorded as absent where the provider returns nothing), and the whole `networkAcls` object with `defaultAction`, `bypass`, every `ipRules[].value` and every `virtualNetworkRules[].id` with its `ignoreMissingVnetServiceEndpoint` flag — and where `networkAcls` is absent entirely, that absence recorded explicitly as the finding rather than as a null to be skipped. Per private endpoint serving a vault: its resource id, connection status, `groupIds`, host subnet, and the DNS zone group response with the zone name it links plus that zone's virtual-network link count. The raw diagnostic-settings response (unfiltered, so its shape is visible) showing whether the `AuditEvent` category is enabled and where it lands. For any vault the assessor could not read, the ARM error code, so a firewall block is not filed as an empty configuration.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, in every subscription returned by `az account list` with state `Enabled`, every key vault and Managed HSM satisfies at least one of: (a) `properties.publicNetworkAccess` equals `Disabled`; or (b) `properties.networkAcls.defaultAction` equals `Deny` and every `ipRules[].value` is a prefix of /24 or longer that appears on the operator-supplied approved-ranges input, and every `virtualNetworkRules[].id` names a specific subnet resource id. FAIL when the `networkAcls` object is absent, when `defaultAction` is `Allow`, or when `publicNetworkAccess` is `Enabled` or absent and no `Deny` ACL is present. Record separately, without altering this verdict, whether an Approved private endpoint targets the vault and whether its DNS zone group is non-empty and links `privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net`; an empty zone group is reported as its own observation. INCONCLUSIVE where the ACL could not be read or where the Resource Graph sweep was truncated at the page cap.
controls.remediation: Set the default and add the legitimate sources explicitly: `az keyvault update --name <vault> --resource-group <rg> --default-action Deny --bypass AzureServices`, then `az keyvault network-rule add --name <vault> --resource-group <rg> --subnet <subnet_id>` for each consuming subnet and `--ip-address <cidr>` for operator ranges. For vaults holding encryption keys go further and set `--public-network-access Disabled`, create a private endpoint with `az network private-endpoint create --group-id vault`, and attach a private DNS zone group for `privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net` linked to every VNet whose clients need the vault. Sequence it as add-rules, verify, then flip the default, and keep the deployment pipeline's own egress address in the allow list or the next deployment fails. Managed HSM does not accept `az keyvault network-rule`; use `az keyvault update-hsm` for its public-access and ACL settings. Assign the built-in Azure Policy definitions restricting key vault public network access at management group scope in Deny effect, since the same definitions in Audit effect will report the drift and permit it.
controls.caveat: An absent `networkAcls` block is the open state and is easy to read as a missing value to be skipped; a filter that only inspects vaults where `networkAcls` exists reports the completely unrestricted vaults as unassessed at best and clean at worst, which is why the query projects an explicit presence flag. Second, `bypass: AzureServices` is on by default and is a genuine allowance — a vault described as 'restricted to one subnet' while its bypass admits the first-party service set is being described inaccurately, and some of those services can be driven from outside the vault owner's control. Third, network restriction is not authorisation: a vault reachable only from one subnet still hands its secrets to any principal in the tenant holding a Key Vault Secrets User role or a legacy access policy, so pair this with the RBAC-versus-access-policy reading from `enableRbacAuthorization`. Fourth, `az network private-endpoint list` is scoped to the single current subscription, so a hub-and-spoke estate whose endpoints live in a connectivity subscription will show zero endpoints and the vault will be judged on the wrong evidence — enumerate endpoints through Resource Graph. Fifth, the private endpoint half fails silently in the most consequential way: a Connected endpoint with no private DNS zone group means clients resolve the public hostname and the traffic never enters the private path, so listing the zone group is not optional. Sixth, `az monitor diagnostic-settings list` has returned both a bare array and a `{value: [...]}` envelope across CLI versions; a `--query` written for the other shape yields an empty result that reads as 'no audit logging' or, if inverted, as 'nothing to report'. Seventh, tightening the vault will break the assessor's own data-plane calls from control 2.11 when run from an outside vantage — distinguish a `Forbidden` caused by the firewall from one caused by missing roles using the returned error code, and record either as inconclusive rather than as an empty inventory.

controls.title: Database servers are not reachable from the whole internet
controls.objective: Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark NS-2. An Azure SQL logical server, a managed instance, or a PostgreSQL or MySQL flexible server that keeps public network access on with a permissive firewall rule presents its authentication surface to every scanner on the internet, where credential stuffing, brute force and any pre-authentication protocol flaw are unmitigated by network position. The intended state is a disabled public endpoint with a private endpoint, or at minimum a firewall enumerating specific addresses.
controls.procedure: Cover every managed database engine in the estate, not just Azure SQL: `microsoft.sql/servers`, `microsoft.sql/managedinstances`, `microsoft.dbforpostgresql/flexibleservers`, `microsoft.dbformysql/flexibleservers`, `microsoft.documentdb/databaseaccounts` and `microsoft.cache/redis` each carry their own public-access model under a different property path. Start with a single paged `az graph query` that coalesces the dynamic properties before stringifying them — `coalesce(properties.publicNetworkAccess, properties.network.publicNetworkAccess)` — because SQL, Cosmos DB and Redis expose `properties.publicNetworkAccess` while the PostgreSQL and MySQL flexible servers nest it under `properties.network.publicNetworkAccess`. Managed instance is the exception that no coalesce catches: it has no `publicNetworkAccess` and its public data endpoint is `properties.publicDataEndpointEnabled`, a boolean, so project it explicitly. Then enumerate firewall rules per server with the CLI — `az sql server firewall-rule list --resource-group <rg> --server <server>`, `az postgres flexible-server firewall-rule list`, `az mysql flexible-server firewall-rule list` — iterating the server list across every enabled subscription with `--subscription`. A Resource Graph query over `microsoft.sql/servers/firewallrules` may be run as a fast first pass, but Resource Graph's coverage of child proxy types is not guaranteed and this one is frequently absent, so an empty result there means 'not enumerated' and must be settled with the per-server CLI call. Two rule shapes matter and mean entirely different things: start `0.0.0.0` with end `0.0.0.0` is the marker permitting all Azure-hosted traffic including other tenants' subscriptions, while start `0.0.0.0` with end `255.255.255.255` permits the literal internet. Flag both, separately. Convert every other rule's start and end to integers and flag any range spanning more than 256 addresses. Also read `properties.restrictOutboundNetworkAccess` and the `virtualNetworkRules` child collection on SQL servers, the `ipRules` and `isVirtualNetworkFilterEnabled` fields on Cosmos DB accounts (whose own `0.0.0.0` entry is a portal-access marker, not a firewall rule), and cross-reference private endpoints through Resource Graph for connections whose `groupIds` include `sqlServer`, `postgresqlServer`, `mysqlServer`, `Sql` or `redisCache`.
api: az graph query --first 1000 --skip 0 -q "resources | where type in~ ('microsoft.sql/servers','microsoft.dbforpostgresql/flexibleServers','microsoft.dbformysql/flexibleServers','microsoft.documentdb/databaseAccounts','microsoft.cache/redis') | extend pna = tostring(coalesce(properties.publicNetworkAccess, properties.network.publicNetworkAccess)) | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, srv = name, type, publicNetworkAccess = pna, id" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.sql/managedInstances' | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, srv = name, type, publicDataEndpoint = properties.publicDataEndpointEnabled, subnet = tostring(properties.subnetId), id" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.sql/servers/firewallRules' | extend startIp = tostring(properties.startIpAddress), endIp = tostring(properties.endIpAddress) | extend kind = case(startIp == '0.0.0.0' and endIp == '0.0.0.0', 'allow-all-azure-services', startIp == '0.0.0.0' and endIp == '255.255.255.255', 'allow-entire-internet', 'scoped') | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, rule = name, startIp, endIp, kind, id" -o json
az sql server firewall-rule list --resource-group <rg> --server <server> --subscription <sub> -o json
az sql server vnet-rule list --resource-group <rg> --server <server> -o json
az postgres flexible-server firewall-rule list --resource-group <rg> --name <server> -o json
az mysql flexible-server firewall-rule list --resource-group <rg> --name <server> -o json

az graph query --first 1000 -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/privateEndpoints' | mv-expand c = properties.privateLinkServiceConnections | extend groups = tostring(c.properties.groupIds) | where groups has 'sql' or groups has 'postgresqlServer' or groups has 'mysqlServer' or groups has 'redisCache' | project subscriptionId, pe = name, target = tostring(c.properties.privateLinkServiceId), groups, status = tostring(c.properties.privateLinkServiceConnectionState.status)" -o json
controls.evidence: Per server: ARM resource id, engine type, and the literal public-access value from whichever property that engine uses, recorded together with the property path it was read from — including `publicDataEndpointEnabled` for managed instances. Per firewall rule: the rule name, the raw `startIpAddress` and `endIpAddress` strings, the computed integer span, and the classification (allow-all-Azure-services, allow-entire-internet, or scoped), together with which command enumerated it, so a rule set that came only from the Resource Graph child-type query is distinguishable from one confirmed per server. Per server, the virtual network rules with their subnet ids and `ignoreMissingVnetServiceEndpoint` flags, and any private endpoint connection with its `groupIds` and status. Where the assessor can reach the endpoint, a TCP connect result against 1433, 5432, 3306, 6380 or the Cosmos endpoint from an address that is not on the allow list, which converts a configuration reading into demonstrated reachability, with the source address and timestamp recorded.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, in every subscription returned by `az account list` with state `Enabled`, every managed database server either has its engine's public-access property equal to `Disabled` (for `microsoft.sql/managedinstances`, `publicDataEndpointEnabled` equal to false), or has public access enabled with a firewall-rule set enumerated by the per-server CLI call in which no rule has start `0.0.0.0` with end `255.255.255.255`, no rule has start `0.0.0.0` with end `0.0.0.0`, and every remaining rule spans at most 256 addresses and matches an entry on the operator-supplied approved-ranges input. Any server whose rule set could not be enumerated — including one for which only the Resource Graph child-type query was run and returned nothing — is INCONCLUSIVE, never PASS.
controls.remediation: Close the public endpoint with `az sql server update --name <server> --resource-group <rg> --enable-public-network false` and create a private endpoint with `--group-id sqlServer` plus a private DNS zone group for `privatelink.database.windows.net`. Where public access must remain, delete the broad rules with `az sql server firewall-rule delete` and replace them with per-address entries, and use virtual network rules referencing the application subnet instead of IP rules wherever the client runs in Azure. Remove the all-Azure-services marker — it admits every Azure tenant, not only yours. For the flexible-server engines prefer VNet-integrated (private access) networking, which has no public firewall at all, over public access plus rules; note this is chosen at server creation and cannot be switched afterwards. Assign the built-in Azure Policy definitions denying public network access on SQL, PostgreSQL and MySQL servers at management group scope, in Deny effect rather than Audit, so a permissive server cannot be created in the first place.
controls.caveat: The `0.0.0.0`-to-`0.0.0.0` rule is the trap that produces both false passes and false reassurance: it does not mean 'no addresses' and it does not mean 'my subscription' — it enables access from all Azure-hosted resources in any tenant, so an attacker with any Azure subscription is already past the network control and only the credential stands between them and the data. A parser that treats it as a degenerate empty range skips it entirely. Second, firewall rules are inert while `publicNetworkAccess` is `Disabled`, so reporting a private-only server as failing on a stale rule is a false positive, while a server at `Enabled` with zero rules is unreachable today but one rule away from exposure — state both accurately rather than collapsing them. Third, the property path differs per engine and managed instance has no `publicNetworkAccess` at all, so a single-path query returns null for a large share of the estate and a truthiness test then reads null as compliant. Fourth, firewall rules are child proxy resources: they do not appear in the parent server's `properties`, and Resource Graph does not reliably index `microsoft.sql/servers/firewallrules`, so an ARG-only sweep can return zero rows for an estate riddled with open rules — treat an empty child-type result as unenumerated and settle it per server. Fifth, the per-server CLI loop inherits whatever subscription is currently active unless `--subscription` is passed on every call, which is how a sweep that looks estate-wide silently reports on one subscription. Sixth, a private endpoint whose connection state is `Pending`, `Rejected` or `Disconnected` carries no traffic, and one without a private DNS zone group leaves clients on the public name — check both before crediting it as the compensating control.

controls.title: Database connections require TLS 1.2 or higher
controls.objective: Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark DP-3. Database clients authenticate with credentials on every connection, so a server that still negotiates TLS 1.0 or 1.1, or permits an unencrypted connection at all, exposes those credentials and the query results to downgrade and interception on any path the traffic crosses — and unlike an application tier, the protocol floor is a single server-side property with no client-side compensation.
controls.procedure: The property name, the location and the value vocabulary all differ per engine, so read each explicitly and never fold them into one column. For `microsoft.sql/servers` and `microsoft.sql/managedinstances` project `properties.minimalTlsVersion`, whose values are the strings `1.0`, `1.1`, `1.2`, `None` and, where the platform and CLI version accept it, `1.3` — `None` means no floor is enforced, which is the worst state and reads deceptively like a benign unset. For `microsoft.documentdb/databaseaccounts` project `properties.minimalTlsVersion` as well, but note the vocabulary is entirely different: Cosmos DB uses the enum values `Tls`, `Tls11` and `Tls12`, so a comparison against the string `1.2` never matches and every Cosmos account fails or passes for the wrong reason. For `microsoft.cache/redis` project `properties.minimumTlsVersion` — a different spelling — together with `properties.enableNonSslPort`, since a cache with the non-SSL port on accepts plaintext on 6379 regardless of the TLS floor. For `microsoft.dbforpostgresql/flexibleservers` and `microsoft.dbformysql/flexibleservers` the transport requirement is not a resource property at all and Resource Graph does not carry it: read `require_secure_transport` with `az postgres flexible-server parameter show` and `az mysql flexible-server parameter show`, and the version floor as `ssl_min_protocol_version` on PostgreSQL and `tls_version` on MySQL. Run the resource-property half as one paged `az graph query` projecting each engine's own field into its own column, then loop the parameter-based engines per server across every enabled subscription. Where the endpoint is reachable, corroborate on the wire — but use a client that speaks the engine's protocol: `openssl s_client -starttls postgres` and `-starttls mysql` exist, whereas there is no `mssql` value for `-starttls`, so an Azure SQL wire check needs a TDS-aware tool such as `nmap -p 1433 --script ssl-enum-ciphers` or a driver pinned to TLS 1.1.
api: az graph query --first 1000 --skip 0 -q "resources | where type in~ ('microsoft.sql/servers','microsoft.sql/managedInstances','microsoft.documentdb/databaseAccounts','microsoft.cache/redis') | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, srv = name, type, sqlOrCosmosMinTls = tostring(properties.minimalTlsVersion), redisMinTls = tostring(properties.minimumTlsVersion), nonSslPort = properties.enableNonSslPort, id" -o json

az sql server list --subscription <sub> --query "[?minimalTlsVersion==null || minimalTlsVersion=='None' || minimalTlsVersion=='1.0' || minimalTlsVersion=='1.1'].{name:name,rg:resourceGroup,tls:minimalTlsVersion}" -o json
az postgres flexible-server parameter show --resource-group <rg> --server-name <server> --name require_secure_transport --query '{name:name,value:value,source:source}' -o json
az postgres flexible-server parameter show --resource-group <rg> --server-name <server> --name ssl_min_protocol_version --query '{name:name,value:value,source:source}' -o json
az mysql flexible-server parameter show --resource-group <rg> --server-name <server> --name require_secure_transport --query '{name:name,value:value,source:source}' -o json
az mysql flexible-server parameter show --resource-group <rg> --server-name <server> --name tls_version --query '{name:name,value:value,source:source}' -o json
controls.evidence: Per server: the ARM resource id, the engine type, the exact property or parameter name the value came from, and the literal value as returned — `1.2` for Azure SQL, `Tls12` for Cosmos DB, and so on, never normalised, because the normalisation is where the comparison bug hides. For the flexible-server engines, the parameter response including its `source` field of `system-default` or `user-override`, since an inherited default is a weaker evidenced state than an explicit one. For Redis, the `enableNonSslPort` boolean alongside the TLS floor. Where a wire check was run, the full transcript with the tool, the flags, the exit status and the timestamp — and where no wire check was possible, that fact recorded rather than omitted.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, in every subscription returned by `az account list` with state `Enabled`, every managed database server enforces a 1.2-or-higher floor through its own mechanism: `properties.minimalTlsVersion` in {`1.2`, `1.3`} for `microsoft.sql/servers` and `microsoft.sql/managedinstances`; `properties.minimalTlsVersion` equal to `Tls12` for `microsoft.documentdb/databaseaccounts`; `properties.minimumTlsVersion` of `1.2` or higher with `properties.enableNonSslPort` equal to false for `microsoft.cache/redis`; `require_secure_transport` equal to `ON`/`on` with `ssl_min_protocol_version` in {`TLSv1.2`, `TLSv1.3`} for PostgreSQL flexible servers; and `require_secure_transport` equal to `ON` with `tls_version` listing only `TLSv1.2` and/or `TLSv1.3` for MySQL flexible servers. Any of `None`, `1.0`, `1.1`, `Tls`, `Tls11`, `OFF`, null or an absent property FAILS. A flexible server for which the per-server parameter calls were not run is INCONCLUSIVE, never PASS, because Resource Graph cannot see those parameters.
controls.remediation: For Azure SQL, `az sql server update --name <server> --resource-group <rg> --minimal-tls-version 1.2`, which takes effect on new connections without downtime. For Cosmos DB, `az cosmosdb update --minimal-tls-version Tls12`. For Redis, `az redis update --name <cache> --resource-group <rg> --set enableNonSslPort=false minimumTlsVersion=1.2`. For the flexible-server engines set `require_secure_transport` to `ON` and pin `ssl_min_protocol_version` or `tls_version` with `az postgres flexible-server parameter set` / `az mysql flexible-server parameter set`, noting that some of these are static parameters requiring a server restart before they take effect. Before enforcing, identify legacy clients: for Azure SQL the connection audit and the `sys.dm_exec_connections` view record the negotiated protocol, and old ODBC, JDBC and .NET Framework versions are the usual casualties. Assign the built-in Azure Policy definitions requiring a minimum TLS version at management group scope in Deny effect so new servers cannot be created below the floor.
controls.caveat: `None` is the false-pass value: a non-empty, plausible-looking string meaning no floor is enforced, so a check written as 'flag when the value is 1.0 or 1.1' passes the least secure servers in the estate, and a null passes them too — enumerate the acceptable values and fail everything else. Second, the vocabularies differ across engines even where the property name matches: Cosmos DB returns `Tls12` while Azure SQL returns `1.2`, so a single string comparison marks every compliant Cosmos account as failing or, if written as an inequality, marks `Tls11` as compliant. Third, the property name differs too — `minimalTlsVersion` on SQL and Cosmos DB against `minimumTlsVersion` on Redis — and a single-name query returns null for the other engines, which then read as unassessed or, under a truthiness test, as compliant. Fourth, the MySQL and PostgreSQL flexible servers do not expose this as a resource property at all; it lives in the server parameter set, which Resource Graph does not carry, so a sweep built only on Resource Graph cannot settle those engines, and an assessment reporting 'all databases enforce TLS 1.2' on that basis has simply not looked at them. Fifth, the parameter response distinguishes `system-default` from `user-override`, and a system default can move under you on a version upgrade, so only an explicitly set value is evidenced. Sixth, the wire check is a false-pass generator in its own right: `openssl s_client -starttls mssql` is not a valid option and returns a usage error, a firewalled port returns a connection failure, and both look identical to 'the server refused TLS 1.1' unless the exit status and stderr are read — treat any non-handshake failure as inconclusive, not as evidence of enforcement. Seventh, a version floor says nothing about cipher suites or about whether the client validates the server certificate: a client connecting with `TrustServerCertificate=true` or `sslmode=require` rather than `verify-full` gets encryption without authentication, which is a client-side exposure this control cannot see.

controls.title: Database servers record an auditable trail of data-plane activity to a durable destination
controls.objective: Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark LT-3 and LT-4. Without server-level auditing there is no record of who connected, what was queried or what was exported, so a credential compromise or a bulk read is undetectable and unprovable after the fact. The trail must also land somewhere durable and separately governed — a log written nowhere, or written to a storage account the database administrator can delete, is not evidence.
controls.procedure: Iterate the server inventory from a paged `az graph query` over `microsoft.sql/servers` and `microsoft.sql/managedinstances`, and pass `--subscription` on every subsequent CLI call so the loop cannot collapse onto the default subscription. Read the audit policy per logical server with `az sql server audit-policy show --resource-group <rg> --name <server>`; the response carries `state` (`Enabled` or `Disabled`), `storageEndpoint`, `retentionDays`, `isAzureMonitorTargetEnabled` and `auditActionsAndGroups`. An Enabled state alone settles nothing: the policy must have a live destination. Where `storageEndpoint` is populated, confirm the account still exists and check its own posture against controls 2.6 to 2.8. Where `isAzureMonitorTargetEnabled` is true, records only flow if a diagnostic setting carrying the `SQLSecurityAuditEvents` category exists — and that setting is attached to the server's `master` database, not to the server resource, so call `az monitor diagnostic-settings list --resource "<server_id>/databases/master"` and inspect the raw response shape before filtering it. Verify `auditActionsAndGroups` actually covers the meaningful groups (successful and failed database authentication, batch completed, and the schema and permission change groups) rather than an empty or token set. Then check database-level policies, which supplement rather than replace the server policy, with `az sql db audit-policy show`. Managed instance has no `az sql mi audit-policy` verb: read its server-level policy through the ARM API with `az rest` against the instance's `auditingSettings/default`. For the PostgreSQL and MySQL flexible servers the equivalent is the `pgaudit.log` / `audit_log_enabled` parameter set plus a diagnostic setting on the server resource. Finally prove the destination is receiving data rather than merely configured, by querying the workspace for recent records or listing recent blobs under the storage endpoint's audit container.
api: az graph query --first 1000 --skip 0 -q "resources | where type in~ ('microsoft.sql/servers','microsoft.sql/managedInstances') | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, srv = name, type, id" -o json

az sql server audit-policy show --resource-group <rg> --name <server> --subscription <sub> --query '{state:state,storage:storageEndpoint,retention:retentionDays,monitor:isAzureMonitorTargetEnabled,actions:auditActionsAndGroups}' -o json
az sql db audit-policy show --resource-group <rg> --server <server> --name <database> -o json
az postgres flexible-server parameter show --resource-group <rg> --server-name <server> --name pgaudit.log -o json
az mysql flexible-server parameter show --resource-group <rg> --server-name <server> --name audit_log_enabled -o json

az monitor log-analytics query --workspace <workspace_customer_id_guid> --analytics-query "union isfuzzy=true (AzureDiagnostics | where Category == 'SQLSecurityAuditEvents'), (SQLSecurityAuditEvents) | summarize n = count(), last = max(TimeGenerated) by _ResourceId" -o json
az storage blob list --account-name <audit_account> --container-name sqldbauditlogs --auth-mode login --num-results 20 -o json
az sql server audit-policy update --resource-group <rg> --name <server> --state Enabled --log-analytics-target-state Enabled --log-analytics-workspace-resource-id <workspace_resource_id>
controls.evidence: Per server: the full audit-policy response with `state`, `storageEndpoint`, `retentionDays`, `isAzureMonitorTargetEnabled` and the complete `auditActionsAndGroups` array — the array itself, not a count. Where Azure Monitor is the target, the raw diagnostic-settings response taken against the `master` database showing whether the `SQLSecurityAuditEvents` category is enabled and which workspace, event hub or storage account it targets, plus the resource path the call was made against so a reader can see it was not the server resource. The proof-of-flow artifact: a Log Analytics result giving a non-zero record count and a recent `max(TimeGenerated)` for the server's resource id, or a recent blob listing under the storage endpoint's audit container, with the query window stated. Per database, any database-level policy that differs from the server policy. For managed instances, the `auditingSettings/default` response body and the API version used.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, in every subscription returned by `az account list` with state `Enabled`, every SQL logical server and managed instance has an audit policy with `state` equal to `Enabled`; a resolvable destination — either a `storageEndpoint` naming an account that still exists, or `isAzureMonitorTargetEnabled` true together with a diagnostic setting on `<server_id>/databases/master` whose enabled categories include `SQLSecurityAuditEvents`; an `auditActionsAndGroups` array containing at least the successful and failed database authentication groups and the batch-completed group; and at least one record observed at the destination within the last 24 hours of the queried window. Where the destination is storage, `retentionDays` must be at least 90 or exactly 0, where 0 denotes unlimited retention. A server whose diagnostic settings were read against the server resource instead of its `master` database, or whose destination could not be queried, is INCONCLUSIVE, never PASS.
controls.remediation: Enable server-level auditing to a workspace the database team cannot alter: `az sql server audit-policy update --resource-group <rg> --name <server> --state Enabled --log-analytics-target-state Enabled --log-analytics-workspace-resource-id <workspace_id>`. Prefer Log Analytics or an Event Hub over a storage account, since a workspace in a separate, restricted subscription removes an administrator's ability to delete their own trail. Keep the policy at server level rather than per database so new databases inherit it. If a storage destination is required, set retention explicitly and lock the container with an immutability policy, and make sure the storage firewall still admits the SQL service or the writes fail silently. For managed instances configure `auditingSettings/default` through ARM or the portal, since the CLI has no managed-instance audit verb. Assign the built-in Azure Policy definition that deploys SQL auditing at management group scope with a DeployIfNotExists effect, so new servers are configured on creation rather than merely reported.
controls.caveat: The dominant false pass is `state: Enabled` with nowhere to write. A policy can report Enabled with `isAzureMonitorTargetEnabled` true while no diagnostic setting exists, in which case not one audit record is produced — and because the setting hangs off the server's `master` database, an assessor who calls `az monitor diagnostic-settings list --resource <server_id>` gets an empty list for a correctly configured server and a wrong verdict in either direction. Always target `<server_id>/databases/master`. Second, `retentionDays: 0` means unlimited, so a naive `retentionDays >= 90` test flags the best-configured servers as failing; special-case zero. Third, the proof-of-flow query itself has a false-negative trap: SQL audit records land in the `AzureDiagnostics` table only when the diagnostic setting uses Azure-diagnostics mode, and in the dedicated `SQLSecurityAuditEvents` table when it uses resource-specific mode, so a query against one table alone returns nothing for a healthy server — union both. Fourth, a database-level audit policy does not replace the server-level one and the two coexist: reading only the database level under-reports coverage, while reading only the server level misses a database whose own policy points somewhere else. Fifth, the storage destination may name an account that was deleted or has since been firewalled against the SQL service, which leaves the policy Enabled while every write fails; resolving the endpoint and proving recent arrivals is the only check that catches it. Sixth, an `auditActionsAndGroups` array that is empty or holds one trivial group satisfies every structural check while capturing nothing worth having, so inspect its contents rather than its presence. Seventh, `az sql server audit-policy show` runs against whatever subscription is currently active unless `--subscription` is supplied, which turns an apparently estate-wide sweep into a single-subscription one that reports the rest as clean by omission.

controls.title: PaaS data services are reached over private endpoints rather than service endpoints
controls.objective: Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark NS-2. A service endpoint keeps traffic on the Microsoft backbone and lets the resource's firewall trust a subnet, but the resource keeps a public IP and stays reachable from anywhere the firewall permits — and crucially a service endpoint does not stop a workload from reaching a resource in someone else's tenant, so it does not prevent exfiltration to an attacker-controlled storage account. A private endpoint gives the resource a private address inside the VNet, which lets the public endpoint be disabled entirely and makes the connection the only path in.
controls.procedure: Build both inventories and compare them per data service.
