For private endpoints, run a paged `az graph query` over `microsoft.network/privateendpoints`, expanding `properties.privateLinkServiceConnections[]` to project `properties.privateLinkServiceId` (the target resource), `properties.groupIds` (the sub-resource, such as `blob`, `vault`, `sqlServer`) and `properties.privateLinkServiceConnectionState.status`, plus the endpoint's `properties.subnet.id` and `properties.customDnsConfigs`. Run the same expansion a second time over `properties.manualPrivateLinkServiceConnections[]`, which a query reading only the automatic array misses entirely. For service endpoints, query `microsoft.network/virtualnetworks`, expanding `properties.subnets[]` and then `properties.serviceEndpoints[]` to get every subnet-to-service pairing, and read `properties.serviceEndpointPolicies` on each subnet, which is the only mechanism constraining a service endpoint to specific target resources. Because `mv-expand` drops rows whose array is empty, run a companion query listing every subnet regardless, so subnets with no service endpoints are known to have been looked at rather than merely absent. Then join both inventories against the data-service inventory from controls 2.8, 2.12 and 2.13 to classify each storage account, key vault and database server as private-endpoint-fronted with public access disabled, private-endpoint-fronted with public access still enabled, service-endpoint-only, or publicly reachable. For every private endpoint, list its DNS zone groups with `az network private-endpoint dns-zone-group list` and confirm the matching `privatelink.*` zone exists and is linked to the VNets whose clients use it, with `az network private-dns link vnet list`. Also read each hosting subnet's `privateEndpointNetworkPolicies`. Finally, a human judges each service-endpoint-only and publicly-reachable case against the data classification, against whether the resource type and SKU offer Private Link at all, and against the DNS architecture.
api: az graph query --first 1000 --skip 0 -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/privateEndpoints' | mv-expand c = properties.privateLinkServiceConnections | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, pe = name, kind = 'auto', target = tostring(c.properties.privateLinkServiceId), groups = tostring(c.properties.groupIds), status = tostring(c.properties.privateLinkServiceConnectionState.status), subnet = tostring(properties.subnet.id), id" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/privateEndpoints' | mv-expand c = properties.manualPrivateLinkServiceConnections | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, pe = name, kind = 'manual', target = tostring(c.properties.privateLinkServiceId), groups = tostring(c.properties.groupIds), status = tostring(c.properties.privateLinkServiceConnectionState.status), subnet = tostring(properties.subnet.id), id" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/virtualNetworks' | mv-expand sn = properties.subnets | mv-expand se = sn.properties.serviceEndpoints | project subscriptionId, resourceGroup, vnet = name, subnet = tostring(sn.name), service = tostring(se.service), policies = array_length(sn.properties.serviceEndpointPolicies), id" -o json

az graph query --first 1000 -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/virtualNetworks' | mv-expand sn = properties.subnets | project subscriptionId, vnet = name, subnet = tostring(sn.name), seCount = array_length(sn.properties.serviceEndpoints), pePolicy = tostring(sn.properties.privateEndpointNetworkPolicies)" -o json
az network private-endpoint dns-zone-group list --endpoint-name <pe> --resource-group <rg> -o json
az network private-dns zone list --query "[?starts_with(name,'privatelink')].{name:name,rg:resourceGroup,links:numberOfVirtualNetworkLinks,records:numberOfRecordSets}" -o json
az network private-dns link vnet list --zone-name <privatelink_zone> --resource-group <rg> -o json
az network vnet subnet show --name <subnet> --vnet-name <vnet> --resource-group <rg> --query '{se:serviceEndpoints,pol:serviceEndpointPolicies,pePolicy:privateEndpointNetworkPolicies}' -o json
az network private-endpoint dns-zone-group create --endpoint-name <pe> --resource-group <rg> --name <zg> --private-dns-zone <zone_id> --zone-name privatelink-blob-core-windows-net
controls.evidence: The two joined inventories: every private endpoint — from both the automatic and the manual connection arrays, each labelled with which array it came from — with its target resource id, `groupIds`, connection status, host subnet, DNS zone group and the linked `privatelink.*` zone together with that zone's virtual-network link list; and every subnet-to-service-endpoint pairing with whether a service endpoint policy constrains it and what that policy names. The companion subnet listing showing which subnets have no service endpoints, so absence is evidenced rather than inferred from a dropped row. Per data service, the resulting classification carried alongside the public-access property already collected for controls 2.8, 2.12 and 2.13. For each service-endpoint-only or publicly-reachable case, the reviewer's recorded decision, the data classification applied, and the reason a private endpoint was not used — including where the resource type or SKU offers none.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, for every resource on the reviewer-supplied in-scope list of sensitive data services (the human input this control depends on), all of the following hold mechanically: at least one private endpoint targets that resource id with `privateLinkServiceConnectionState.status` equal to `Approved`, taken from the union of the automatic and manual connection arrays; `az network private-endpoint dns-zone-group list` for that endpoint returns a non-empty group naming the correct `privatelink.*` zone for the sub-resource; that zone has a virtual-network link to every VNet on the reviewer-supplied consuming-VNet list; and the resource's own public-access property is `Disabled`. FAIL when any of those is false. Report separately, and without changing the verdict, every subnet that has service endpoints with `array_length(serviceEndpointPolicies)` of zero or null, as an unconstrained egress path. INCONCLUSIVE where the in-scope list was not supplied, where a Resource Graph sweep hit the page cap, or where the DNS zone group could not be read.
controls.remediation: Create the endpoint and its DNS in one flow: `az network private-endpoint create --name <pe> --resource-group <rg> --vnet-name <vnet> --subnet <subnet> --private-connection-resource-id <target_id> --group-id <sub_resource> --connection-name <conn>`, then `az network private-endpoint dns-zone-group create` against the matching zone (`privatelink.blob.core.windows.net`, `privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net`, `privatelink.database.windows.net`), and link that zone to every VNet whose clients resolve the name. Disable the resource's public network access afterwards, since a private endpoint alongside an open public endpoint adds a path without removing one. Where service endpoints must remain and the target is Azure Storage, attach a service endpoint policy naming the permitted resource ids so a workload cannot use the endpoint to reach a foreign tenant's account; for service types that policies do not cover, the equivalent containment has to come from egress firewalling with FQDN rules instead. Centralise the `privatelink.*` zones in a hub subscription and link the spokes to them, rather than creating a zone per spoke, which is the usual cause of split resolution.
controls.caveat: Manual because the target state depends on data classification, on which resource types and SKUs offer Private Link at all, and on the DNS architecture — a human has to decide which resources are in scope and whether a service-endpoint-only path is an accepted risk, and no API returns that judgement. The automated half still has five concrete traps. First, a private endpoint with no DNS zone group is the classic silent failure: the connection exists and reports Approved while clients keep resolving the resource's public name and every byte takes the public path, so the endpoint appears in every inventory and does nothing — an empty `dns-zone-group list` is the finding. Second, connections created out-of-band land in `properties.manualPrivateLinkServiceConnections` rather than `privateLinkServiceConnections`, so a query expanding only the latter reports zero endpoints for a resource that has one, and a manual connection sitting at `Pending` or `Rejected` carries no traffic at all. Third, service endpoints are routinely reported as equivalent protection; they are not, because the resource keeps its public IP and, without a service endpoint policy, the subnet can reach every account of that service type in every tenant over the same optimised path, which is an exfiltration channel rather than a control — and service endpoint policies cover only a narrow set of services (Azure Storage in general availability), so for most services the policy remedy simply does not exist and the honest finding is that the path is unconstrained. Fourth, `mv-expand` over an empty or absent array drops the row entirely, so a subnet with no service endpoints and a VNet with no such subnets vanish from the result, and a reader counting rows concludes the estate is clean when it was never enumerated — hence the companion subnet query. Fifth, an older subnet with `privateEndpointNetworkPolicies` set to `Enabled` applies NSG and route rules to the endpoint's private IP and can break it in ways invisible in the endpoint's own status. Finally, a private endpoint terminates in one VNet: peers and on-premises networks reach it only if the private DNS zone is linked and routes exist, so one endpoint is not estate-wide coverage and the zone's virtual-network link list — not the endpoint's status — is what evidences reach.

controls.title: Every subscription streams its control-plane activity log into a central Log Analytics workspace
controls.objective: The activity log is the only record of who changed what through Azure Resource Manager, and it is queryable for 90 days before it disappears. A subscription-scoped diagnostic setting that ships it to a Log Analytics workspace is what turns that transient feed into durable, joinable evidence, and it is the precondition for almost every other control in this section (MCSB LT-3, LT-5).
controls.procedure: Establish the denominator before assessing anything. `az account list --all --query "[].{id:id,name:name,state:state,tenantId:tenantId}" -o json` returns only the subscriptions this credential holds a role on, so it is a claim about the credential, not about the tenant. Obtain a second, independent count from the management-group tree with `az graph query -q "resourcecontainers | where type =~ 'microsoft.resources/subscriptions' | project subscriptionId, name, tenantId, state = tostring(properties.state)" --management-groups <root-mg-id> --first 1000`. Run that query WITHOUT `--allow-partial-scopes` first, so a scope the principal cannot read raises an error rather than being silently dropped from the result set; only add the flag when you also record which scopes were skipped. Any subscription present in the graph result and absent from `az account list --all` is unassessed, not compliant. For each subscription whose `state` is `Enabled`, run `az monitor diagnostic-settings subscription list --subscription <sub-id>`; the CLI returns a `value[]` array whose elements have the ARM `properties` bag flattened, so read `workspaceId`, `storageAccountId`, `eventHubAuthorizationRuleId` and each entry of `logs[]` (`category`, `enabled`) directly on the element rather than under a `properties` path. Resolve every referenced workspace with `az monitor log-analytics workspace show --ids <workspace-resource-id>` to prove it still exists and sits in a subscription you also enumerated; a dangling workspace id is an unresolvable destination, not a passing one. Entra ID is a separate control plane reached with a separate credential and separate roles, so read the directory-log export through the ARM shim for the tenant: `az rest --method get --url "https://management.azure.com/providers/microsoft.aadiam/diagnosticSettings?api-version=2017-04-01-preview"`, and confirm the AuditLogs and SignInLogs categories are enabled against a workspace. Follow paging by hand: ARM list responses carry `nextLink` and Microsoft Graph responses carry `@odata.nextLink`, and `az rest` returns exactly one page and follows neither, so a collector that reads only the first response silently under-counts.
api: az graph query -q "resourcecontainers | where type =~ 'microsoft.resources/subscriptions' | project subscriptionId, name, tenantId, state = tostring(properties.state)" --management-groups <root-mg-id> --first 1000
controls.evidence: For each subscription id: every subscription diagnostic-setting object, each with its name, `workspaceId`, and the `logs[]` array showing `category` and `enabled` per category, plus the resolved workspace resource id, name, region and `customerId`. Record the subscription count from `az account list --all` beside the count from the management-group graph query, and record whether `--allow-partial-scopes` was used together with any scope the graph call reported as skipped, so an under-enumerated run is visible in the artefact rather than inferred. For the tenant, record the `microsoft.aadiam/diagnosticSettings` response with the enabled state of AuditLogs and SignInLogs and the workspace they target, and note which credential and directory role were used to read it.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, for every subscription whose `state` is `Enabled` in the denominator, `az monitor diagnostic-settings subscription list` returns at least one setting whose `workspaceId` is non-empty AND resolves through `az monitor log-analytics workspace show --ids`, and whose `logs[]` shows `enabled: true` for the Administrative, Security and Policy categories at minimum. A subscription with zero settings, a setting that targets only a storage account or an event hub, a setting whose `workspaceId` does not resolve, or a setting whose Administrative category is `enabled: false`, is a FAIL for that subscription. PARTIALLY_MET when the condition holds for some subscriptions and not others — name them. REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW, never MET, when the `az account list --all` count is lower than the management-group graph count, when the graph query at the root management group could not be executed at all, or when the graph call was run with `--allow-partial-scopes` and reported skipped scopes.
controls.remediation: Per subscription: `az monitor diagnostic-settings subscription create --name activity-to-law --location <region> --workspace <workspace-resource-id> --logs '[{"category":"Administrative","enabled":true},{"category":"Security","enabled":true},{"category":"ServiceHealth","enabled":true},{"category":"Alert","enabled":true},{"category":"Policy","enabled":true},{"category":"Recommendation","enabled":true},{"category":"ResourceHealth","enabled":true},{"category":"Autoscale","enabled":true}]'`. Then assign the built-in policy that configures subscription activity logs to a workspace at the management-group root so newly created subscriptions inherit it instead of being onboarded by hand — the assignment must carry the DeployIfNotExists effect with `enforcementMode: Default`, because an assignment left on an audit-only effect or on `enforcementMode: DoNotEnforce` reports non-compliance forever and configures nothing. Grant the assignment's managed identity Monitoring Contributor and Log Analytics Contributor at that scope, then run a remediation task to backfill existing subscriptions. Configure the Entra ID diagnostic setting separately, from the tenant control plane, to send AuditLogs, SignInLogs and the non-interactive and service-principal sign-in categories to the same workspace.
controls.caveat: Five ways this reads clean when it is not. First, the denominator: `az account list` only shows subscriptions the signed-in principal has a role on, so a Reader scoped to two subscriptions in a fifty-subscription tenant assesses 4% of the estate and reports no failures. Second, the management-group walk is only an independent denominator if the principal holds Reader at the root management group — Azure Resource Graph is itself permission-filtered, so a principal with the same narrow scope returns the same short list twice and the cross-check silently agrees with itself; treat two matching small numbers in a large tenant as unverified, and record the root management group the query was actually run against. `--allow-partial-scopes` compounds this by turning an unreadable scope into a quietly shorter result instead of an error. Third, subscription diagnostic settings are not indexed by Azure Resource Graph, so there is no single-query shortcut; the per-subscription call is mandatory, and a loop that swallows an authorization error produces an empty list indistinguishable from a subscription that genuinely has no setting — every failed call must be recorded as unknown. Fourth, the legacy log-profile mechanism is retired, so a tenancy that still relies on one has no subscription diagnostic setting and genuinely is not exporting, even though operators remember configuring it. Fifth, and most often missed: Entra ID sign-in and audit logs are not part of the ARM activity log at all — they are a different control plane, reached with a different credential and different roles, and a subscription that passes this control can still have zero visibility of directory sign-ins and role activations.

controls.title: Log data survives long enough to investigate a breach discovered months later
controls.objective: Intrusions are typically found long after the fact, so the retention of the destination — not the fact that logs are being shipped — decides whether an investigation is possible. Interactive retention must cover routine hunting and total retention must cover the realistic dwell time between compromise and discovery (MCSB LT-6).
controls.procedure: List every workspace across the estate in one call: `az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.operationalinsights/workspaces' | project id, name, subscriptionId, resourceGroup, location, sku = tostring(properties.sku.name), retentionInDays = toint(properties.retentionInDays)" --first 1000`, paging with `--skip` until a page returns fewer rows than `--first`. For each workspace that is the destination of a setting found in 3.1, 3.3 or 3.4, read the effective per-table retention, because a table-level value overrides the workspace default: `az monitor log-analytics workspace table list --resource-group <rg> --workspace-name <ws> --query "[].{table:name,plan:plan,interactive:retentionInDays,total:totalRetentionInDays,inherited:retentionInDaysAsDefault}" -o table`. Note the field paths carefully — this command flattens the ARM `properties` bag, so `retentionInDays`, `totalRetentionInDays` and `plan` sit at the top level of each element and a JMESPath expression written as `properties.retentionInDays` evaluates to null for every table. Pay particular attention to AzureActivity, AzureDiagnostics, SigninLogs, AuditLogs, AZKVAuditLogs and the firewall rule tables. Read the workspace-level context too — `az monitor log-analytics workspace show --resource-group <rg> --workspace-name <ws> --query "{retention:retentionInDays,sku:sku.name,capping:workspaceCapping}"` — where `workspaceCapping.dailyQuotaGb` of -1 means uncapped and any other value means ingestion stops for the day once it is reached. Where a diagnostic setting also targets a storage account, read what deletes those blobs: `az storage account management-policy show --account-name <sa> --resource-group <rg>` for lifecycle rules, and `az storage container immutability-policy show --account-name <sa> --container-name <container> --resource-group <rg>` plus `az storage container legal-hold show --account-name <sa> --container-name <container> --resource-group <rg>` for tamper resistance.
api: az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.operationalinsights/workspaces' | project id, name, subscriptionId, resourceGroup, location, sku = tostring(properties.sku.name), retentionInDays = toint(properties.retentionInDays)" --first 1000

az monitor log-analytics workspace table list --resource-group <rg> --workspace-name <ws> --query "[].{table:name,plan:plan,interactive:retentionInDays,total:totalRetentionInDays,inherited:retentionInDaysAsDefault}" -o table
az storage container immutability-policy show --account-name <sa> --container-name insights-activity-logs --resource-group <rg>
controls.evidence: Per workspace: resource id, sku name, workspace-level `retentionInDays`, `workspaceCapping.dailyQuotaGb` with `workspaceCapping.dataIngestionStatus`, and the per-table listing showing `plan`, `retentionInDays`, `totalRetentionInDays` and `retentionInDaysAsDefault` for every table that receives activity, sign-in, resource or security data. Per storage destination: the lifecycle management policy JSON with every rule's `enabled` flag, `delete` action and day threshold, and the immutability policy with its `immutabilityPeriodSinceCreationInDays` and its `state` (Locked or Unlocked), plus the legal-hold tags. Record explicitly any workspace referenced by a diagnostic setting that could not be read because it lives outside the assessed scope.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every workspace receiving activity, sign-in or security data reports, on each of those tables, an effective interactive `retentionInDays` of at least 90 and a `totalRetentionInDays` of at least 365, and no storage-account destination has an enabled lifecycle rule deleting the log containers, their versions or their snapshots sooner than 365 days. A table whose own `retentionInDays` is below the threshold FAILs even when the workspace-level value is above it, because the table value wins. A table whose `plan` is Basic or Auxiliary FAILs the interactive requirement by construction, since those plans pin interactive retention at 30 days. `totalRetentionInDays` is the whole lifetime including the interactive period, not an amount added to it, so compare it against 365 directly. Where the tamper-resistance requirement is being claimed, only an immutability policy whose `state` is `Locked` satisfies it; an Unlocked policy is a preference, not a control. A workspace referenced by a setting but unreadable in the assessed scope makes the control REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW for that destination rather than MET.
controls.remediation: Raise the workspace default with `az monitor log-analytics workspace update --resource-group <rg> --workspace-name <ws> --retention-time 90`, then set retention explicitly on the tables that matter: `az monitor log-analytics workspace table update --resource-group <rg> --workspace-name <ws> --name AzureActivity --retention-time 90 --total-retention-time 730` (interactive accepts 4–730 days, total accepts 4–2556). Keep security-relevant tables on the Analytics plan; moving one to Basic or Auxiliary to save money silently caps its interactive retention at 30 days and restricts how it can be queried. For storage destinations, replace any short lifecycle delete rule and apply a time-based immutability policy to the log containers, then lock it once the period is agreed so that an attacker holding a storage data role cannot shorten it. Do not rely on the retention field that used to live on the diagnostic setting itself.
controls.caveat: The classic false pass is reading the workspace-level `retentionInDays` and stopping: any table can carry its own value, so a workspace that says 730 can hold AzureActivity at 30. The second is a query bug that produces the same silence — because the CLI flattens `properties`, a `--query` written against `properties.retentionInDays` returns null for every table, and a comparison against null does not trip a numeric threshold test, so the whole estate reads as having no short-retention tables. Third: the retention field that older diagnostic settings carry for storage destinations is retired and inert — a setting that still shows a 365-day retention policy is deleting nothing and keeping nothing, and blob lifetime is now governed solely by storage lifecycle management. Fourth: a workspace with a daily ingestion cap drops data once the cap is hit, so retention can be perfect while whole days are missing; read `workspaceCapping.dailyQuotaGb` (-1 means uncapped) and `workspaceCapping.dataIngestionStatus`. Fifth: an Unlocked immutability policy can be shortened or removed by the same identity an attacker would already need, so it does not survive the threat it is there for. Sixth: a workspace living in a subscription outside the assessed scope cannot be read, and the collector must record that as unknown rather than assuming a 30-day default or assuming compliance.

controls.title: Diagnostics-capable resources actually emit resource logs, and the estate coverage is measured against a real denominator
controls.objective: A subscription with no diagnostic settings anywhere generates no findings from log analysis, which reads exactly like a subscription with nothing wrong. Coverage must therefore be expressed as a fraction of the resources that are capable of emitting logs, not as the absence of bad log entries (MCSB LT-3, LT-5).
controls.procedure: Build the denominator first with a tenant-wide inventory query: `az graph query -q "resources | where type in~ ('microsoft.keyvault/vaults','microsoft.storage/storageaccounts','microsoft.sql/servers/databases','microsoft.network/applicationgateways','microsoft.network/azurefirewalls','microsoft.web/sites','microsoft.containerservice/managedclusters','microsoft.dbforpostgresql/flexibleservers','microsoft.apimanagement/service','microsoft.recoveryservices/vaults') | project id, name, type, subscriptionId, resourceGroup, location" --first 1000 --skip 0`, incrementing `--skip` by 1000 until a page returns fewer rows than `--first`; cross-check the total against `az graph query -q "resources | where type in~ (...) | summarize count()"` so a truncated page loop cannot masquerade as a small estate. A fast pre-filter exists — `az graph query -q "insightsresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.insights/diagnosticsettings' | project id, resourceId = tostring(split(id,'/providers/microsoft.insights/diagnosticSettings/')[0]), workspaceId = tostring(properties.workspaceId), logs = properties.logs" --first 1000` — but treat it as an index, not as proof. For every resource in the denominator, ask the platform which categories it can emit with `az monitor diagnostic-settings categories list --resource <resource-id>`, reading each element of the returned `value[]` for `categoryType` (Logs or Metrics) and `categoryGroups`; then read what is configured with `az monitor diagnostic-settings list --resource <resource-id>`, which returns a bare array whose elements carry `workspaceId`, `logs[]`, `metrics[]` and `logAnalyticsDestinationType` at the top level. Corroborate against policy, but read the assignment before the compliance number: `az policy assignment list --disable-scope-strict-match --scope /providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/<root-mg-id> --query "[].{name:name,policy:policyDefinitionId,enforcement:enforcementMode,params:parameters}"` shows whether the diagnostic-settings initiatives are assigned with a deploying effect and with `enforcementMode: Default`, and only then does `az policy state summarize --management-group <root-mg-id> --from <iso8601> --to <iso8601>` give a meaningful non-compliant count.
api: az graph query -q "resources | where type in~ ('microsoft.keyvault/vaults','microsoft.storage/storageaccounts','microsoft.sql/servers/databases','microsoft.network/applicationgateways','microsoft.network/azurefirewalls','microsoft.web/sites','microsoft.containerservice/managedclusters','microsoft.dbforpostgresql/flexibleservers','microsoft.apimanagement/service','microsoft.recoveryservices/vaults') | project id, name, type, subscriptionId, resourceGroup, location" --first 1000 --skip 0

az graph query -q "insightsresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.insights/diagnosticsettings' | project id, resourceId = tostring(split(id,'/providers/microsoft.insights/diagnosticSettings/')[0]), workspaceId = tostring(properties.workspaceId), logs = properties.logs" --first 1000 --skip 0
controls.evidence: A coverage table with one row per resource in the denominator: resource id, type, subscription id, whether `az monitor diagnostic-settings categories list` reported any element with `categoryType: Logs`, the names of the diagnostic settings returned, the `workspaceId` each targets, and whether the setting enables a `categoryGroup` of `allLogs` or `audit` or names individual categories with `enabled: true`. Publish the coverage fraction and the count of resources with zero settings explicitly, alongside the number of subscriptions the graph query actually reached, the row count returned against the `summarize count()` total, and the list of resources whose `categories list` or `diagnostic-settings list` call errored — those are unknown, not covered and not uncovered. Record for each relevant policy assignment its effect parameter and its `enforcementMode`.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every resource in the denominator whose `categories list` includes at least one element with `categoryType: Logs` has at least one diagnostic setting with a non-empty `workspaceId` and either the `allLogs` or `audit` category group enabled, or every Logs category present with `enabled: true`. Resources that can only emit Metrics are excluded from the denominator. Any resource with zero diagnostic settings FAILs. PARTIALLY_MET when coverage is incomplete, with the uncovered resource ids listed. REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW for any resource whose enumeration calls errored, and for the estate as a whole when the graph row count is short of the `summarize count()` total, since a truncated inventory makes the coverage fraction meaningless.
controls.remediation: For an individual resource: `az monitor diagnostic-settings create --name diag-to-law --resource <resource-id> --workspace <workspace-resource-id> --logs '[{"categoryGroup":"allLogs","enabled":true}]' --metrics '[{"category":"AllMetrics","enabled":true}]'`. Do not remediate resource by resource at scale: assign the per-resource-type deploy-if-not-exists diagnostic-settings policies, or the bundled initiative, at the management-group root with `az policy assignment create --name diag-to-law --scope /providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/<root-mg-id> --policy-set-definition <initiative-id> --mi-system-assigned --location <region> --params '{"logAnalytics":{"value":"<workspace-resource-id>"}}'`, leaving `enforcementMode` at Default and the effect parameter at DeployIfNotExists rather than an audit-only value. Grant the assignment identity Monitoring Contributor and Log Analytics Contributor at that scope, then backfill existing resources with `az policy remediation create --name diag-backfill --management-group <root-mg-id> --policy-assignment <assignment-id> --resource-discovery-mode ReEvaluateCompliance`. Prefer the `allLogs` category group so categories the provider adds later are collected without a policy change.
controls.caveat: This control exists because of one specific false pass: an empty response from `az monitor diagnostic-settings list` means 'no setting configured', and a script that only inspects the settings it finds will never notice the resources that have none. The verdict must be computed against the inventory denominator, never against the list of settings found. Azure Resource Graph is subject to the caller's read permissions, so a principal whose Reader assignment covers three resource groups returns a small, fully covered estate and looks perfect — print the subscription count the query reached beside `az account list --all`, and remember the graph caps a page at 1000 rows, so an unpaged loop shrinks the denominator rather than erroring. `insightsresources` is a convenience index whose coverage is not guaranteed for every resource type, so neither its silence nor its rows are authoritative; confirm every negative with the per-resource call, and never treat an errored call as a covered resource. The policy corroboration has its own trap in both directions: an initiative assigned with an audit-only effect, or with `enforcementMode: DoNotEnforce`, produces compliance records and deploys nothing, so a healthy-looking assignment list is not remediation; and policy compliance is evaluated on a roughly daily cycle with `az policy state summarize` defaulting to a short recent window, so a freshly created resource shows as compliant simply because it has not been evaluated yet, while a policy exemption removes a resource from the non-compliant count without changing its configuration at all. Finally, a setting can exist while shipping only Metrics, or shipping logs to an event hub or storage account and not to a workspace, and an explicit category list silently omits categories the provider adds later, whereas `allLogs` does not.

controls.title: Key Vault data-plane access is recorded, because the activity log never shows secret retrieval
controls.objective: Reading a secret, unwrapping a key or signing with a certificate is a data-plane operation that leaves no trace in the ARM activity log. Only the vault's own AuditEvent resource log records who retrieved which secret, which is the sole evidence available after a credential theft (MCSB LT-3, DP-8).
controls.procedure: Enumerate both vault families across every subscription in one query, because they are distinct resource types: `az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.keyvault/vaults' or type =~ 'microsoft.keyvault/managedhsms' | project id, name, type, subscriptionId, resourceGroup, location, rbacAuth = tostring(properties.enableRbacAuthorization)" --first 1000`, paging with `--skip` until a page returns fewer rows than `--first`. For each returned id run `az monitor diagnostic-settings list --resource <vault-id>` — a bare array whose elements carry `logs[]`, `workspaceId` and `logAnalyticsDestinationType` at the top level — and inspect `logs[]` for a `category` of `AuditEvent` with `enabled: true`, or a `categoryGroup` of `audit` or `allLogs` with `enabled: true`. Confirm the destination workspace id is non-empty and resolves via `az monitor log-analytics workspace show --ids <workspace-resource-id>`; take the workspace `customerId` GUID from that same response, because the data-plane query command needs the GUID and not the ARM resource id. Record `enableRbacAuthorization` per vault, since it determines which caller identity fields appear in the audit rows and therefore how the evidence is read. Then corroborate that the pipe is live by querying across both possible table layouts, since a setting with `logAnalyticsDestinationType: Dedicated` writes to the resource-specific table and NOT to AzureDiagnostics: `az monitor log-analytics query --workspace <workspace-customer-id-guid> --analytics-query "union isfuzzy=true (AzureDiagnostics | where ResourceProvider == 'MICROSOFT.KEYVAULT'), (AZKVAuditLogs) | summarize last = max(TimeGenerated), events = count() by _ResourceId" --timespan P7D`. For a managed HSM, read its own `logAnalyticsDestinationType` to determine which table its rows land in rather than assuming the vault table applies.
api: az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.keyvault/vaults' or type =~ 'microsoft.keyvault/managedhsms' | project id, name, type, subscriptionId, resourceGroup, location, rbacAuth = tostring(properties.enableRbacAuthorization)" --first 1000 --skip 0

az monitor log-analytics query --workspace <workspace-customer-id-guid> --analytics-query "union isfuzzy=true (AzureDiagnostics | where ResourceProvider == 'MICROSOFT.KEYVAULT'), (AZKVAuditLogs) | summarize last = max(TimeGenerated), events = count() by _ResourceId" --timespan P7D
controls.evidence: One row per vault and managed HSM: resource id, resource type, the diagnostic-setting name, the AuditEvent entry (or the `audit`/`allLogs` category group) with its `enabled` value, the `logAnalyticsDestinationType`, the destination `workspaceId` and whether it resolved, and the most recent AuditEvent timestamp and event count observed in the workspace for that resource across both table layouts. Record vaults with zero settings explicitly, record the total vault and managed-HSM counts returned by the graph query so the denominator is visible, and record any vault whose enumeration or workspace query errored as unknown.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every `microsoft.keyvault/vaults` and `microsoft.keyvault/managedhsms` resource in the denominator has at least one diagnostic setting whose `workspaceId` is non-empty and resolvable and which enables AuditEvent, either directly as a `category` with `enabled: true` or through the `audit` or `allLogs` category group with `enabled: true`. The verdict is decided on configuration alone. Any vault or managed HSM with no setting, with a setting that enables only metrics, or with a setting whose only destination is a storage account or event hub, FAILs. The row-count query is recorded as corroborating evidence and never decides the verdict, because zero rows cannot be mechanically distinguished from a vault that genuinely saw no data-plane access in the window; a configured vault with zero rows over seven days is reported as an observation for follow-up. PARTIALLY_MET when some vaults pass and others do not, naming them; REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW for any vault whose enumeration failed.
controls.remediation: `az monitor diagnostic-settings create --name kv-audit --resource <vault-id> --workspace <workspace-resource-id> --logs '[{"categoryGroup":"allLogs","enabled":true}]' --metrics '[{"category":"AllMetrics","enabled":true}]'`, repeated for every managed HSM as well as every vault. Deploy this through a deploy-if-not-exists policy assigned at the management-group root, with `enforcementMode: Default` and a deploying effect rather than an audit-only one, so new vaults are onboarded at creation rather than at the next audit; confirm the policy's managed identity holds Monitoring Contributor plus Log Analytics Contributor on the target scope, otherwise remediation tasks fail while the assignment still reports activity.
controls.caveat: Managed HSM is a different resource type from a vault; a query filtered on `microsoft.keyvault/vaults` alone silently drops the highest-value key store in the estate and reports a clean result for the vaults that remain. The second trap is the corroborating query itself: when a setting uses `logAnalyticsDestinationType: Dedicated`, rows land in AZKVAuditLogs and never appear in AzureDiagnostics, so a check written against AzureDiagnostics alone reports a correctly configured vault as a dead pipe — and, if that query were allowed to drive the verdict, would mark a compliant estate non-compliant while telling a reader nothing about the vaults that really are unlogged. A vault protected by a firewall or a private endpoint still needs AuditEvent explicitly: network isolation is not logging, and a denied data-plane request is only visible if the log is on. Because AuditEvent is the sole record of secret retrieval, the alerting control in 3.11 gives no coverage here at all — it watches control-plane changes to the vault, which is a separate feed from data-plane access. Ingestion latency runs to roughly ten minutes, so 'no recent rows' on a vault created minutes ago is not evidence of misconfiguration, while 'no rows in seven days' on a busy production vault is a strong signal that the setting points at a workspace nobody reads.

controls.title: Network flow records are captured for every virtual network carrying workload traffic
controls.objective: Flow logs are the only record of which addresses actually talked to which, and they are what turns a suspected compromise into a scoped one. Coverage has to be measured against virtual networks and subnets, because traffic through a subnet with no attached security group produces no security-group flow log at all (MCSB LT-4).
controls.procedure: Flow logs are regional Network Watcher child resources, so build the region list from the estate rather than from a guess: `az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/virtualnetworks' or type =~ 'microsoft.network/networksecuritygroups' | summarize vnets = countif(type =~ 'microsoft.network/virtualnetworks'), nsgs = countif(type =~ 'microsoft.network/networksecuritygroups') by subscriptionId, location" --first 1000`. Enumerate the virtual networks with their subnets so the denominator is a list of subnets and not a count of security groups: `az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/virtualnetworks' | mv-expand subnet = properties.subnets | project id, name, subscriptionId, location, subnetName = tostring(subnet.name), ipConfigs = array_length(subnet.properties.ipConfigurations), delegations = array_length(subnet.properties.delegations)" --first 1000`. Check where a Network Watcher exists at all with `az network watcher list --query "[].{name:name,location:location,rg:resourceGroup,provisioning:provisioningState}" -o table`, since a region with no watcher can hold no flow log. Then, for each subscription and each region that appears in the inventory, run `az network watcher flow-log list --location <region> --subscription <sub-id>` and, for each entry, `az network watcher flow-log show --location <region> --name <flow-log-name> --subscription <sub-id>`. The show command flattens the ARM properties bag, so read `enabled`, `provisioningState`, `targetResourceId` (the VNet, subnet, NIC or security group it is bound to), `storageId`, `format.version`, `retentionPolicy.enabled` with `retentionPolicy.days`, and `flowAnalyticsConfiguration.networkWatcherFlowAnalyticsConfiguration` with its `enabled`, `workspaceResourceId` and `trafficAnalyticsInterval` directly on the object. Resolve every `storageId` and read that account's network rules, because a flow log bound to a firewalled storage account stays `enabled: true` and writes nothing. Join the `targetResourceId` values back to the VNet and subnet inventory to compute which subnets no flow log covers.
api: az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/virtualnetworks' | mv-expand subnet = properties.subnets | project id, name, subscriptionId, location, subnetName = tostring(subnet.name), ipConfigs = array_length(subnet.properties.ipConfigurations), delegations = array_length(subnet.properties.delegations)" --first 1000 --skip 0

az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/networkwatchers/flowlogs' | project id, subscriptionId, location, enabled = tostring(properties.enabled), state = tostring(properties.provisioningState), target = tostring(properties.targetResourceId), storage = tostring(properties.storageId), retention = toint(properties.retentionPolicy.days)" --first 1000
controls.evidence: One row per virtual network and subnet: VNet id, subnet name, region, whether the subnet holds any IP configurations or delegations, and either the flow-log object covering it (name, `targetResourceId`, `enabled`, `provisioningState`, `retentionPolicy.enabled`, `retentionPolicy.days`, storage account id and whether it resolved, traffic-analytics `enabled` and `workspaceResourceId`) or an explicit 'no flow log' marker. Record the set of regions enumerated per subscription beside the set of regions in which network resources exist, and beside the set of regions that actually have a Network Watcher, so a partial regional sweep is visible in the evidence rather than inferred. Record the network rules of every destination storage account.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every subnet whose `ipConfigurations` array is non-empty or which carries a delegation or a private endpoint is covered by a flow log — bound either to that subnet or to its parent virtual network — with `enabled: true`, `provisioningState: Succeeded`, `retentionPolicy.enabled: true` and `retentionPolicy.days >= 90`, whose `storageId` resolves to an existing account that permits writes from the flow-log service, and with traffic analytics `enabled: true` pointing at a workspace assessed under 3.2. A flow log object that exists with `enabled: false`, with a `provisioningState` other than Succeeded, or with `retentionPolicy.enabled: false` regardless of the day count, FAILs. PARTIALLY_MET when some subnets are covered and others are not, naming them. A region that contains network resources but for which `az network watcher flow-log list` was never run, errored, or has no Network Watcher deployed, makes the control REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW for that region rather than MET.
controls.remediation: Create virtual-network-scoped flow logs so coverage does not depend on a security group being attached: `az network watcher flow-log create --name <vnet>-flowlog --location <region> --vnet <vnet-resource-id> --storage-account <storage-resource-id> --retention 90 --enabled true --traffic-analytics true --workspace <workspace-resource-id> --interval 10`. The destination must be a general-purpose v2 account in the same region as the flow log, and if that account has a firewall it needs a rule admitting the flow-log service, otherwise the resource provisions and never writes. Migrate any security-group-scoped flow logs to virtual-network scope, since the security-group flow log mechanism is on a published retirement path — confirm the current retirement date from the vendor's announcement before quoting one in a report. Enforce with a deploy-if-not-exists policy at the management-group root, with a deploying effect and `enforcementMode: Default`, so new virtual networks are enrolled at creation.
controls.caveat: The single-region run is the standard false pass: flow logs live in the Network Watcher resource group of the target's own region, `az network watcher flow-log list` is per `--location`, and a sweep of one region over a five-region estate reports the four unenumerated regions as nothing rather than as unknown. A region that never had a Network Watcher created returns an empty list for the same reason, and an authorization failure returns an empty list too, so the collector has to distinguish 'no flow logs' from 'could not look'. The second trap is the denominator: counting security-group-scoped flow logs against the number of security groups scores 100% while every subnet with no security group attached — precisely the unfiltered ones — contributes no flow records at all, which is why the denominator must be virtual networks and their populated subnets. Third, a retention day count is inert unless `retentionPolicy.enabled` is true, and the storage account must be general-purpose v2 in the same region for retention to apply at all. Fourth, `enabled: true` is a statement of intent, not of delivery: a flow log whose storage account was deleted, whose account firewall blocks the service, or whose `provisioningState` is Failed still reads as enabled, so resolve the destination and require a Succeeded state. Fifth, security-group flow logs are being retired in favour of virtual-network flow logs, so an estate that passes today on the legacy mechanism carries a dated dependency worth reporting even when the verdict is MET.

controls.title: Defender for Cloud protection is switched on for the resource types actually deployed in each subscription
controls.objective: Defender plans are what generate security alerts and vulnerability findings for servers, storage, containers, databases, key vaults and Resource Manager itself. They are billed and enabled per subscription and are not inherited down the management-group tree, so a single unprotected subscription is a hole with no alerting at all (MCSB LT-1, LT-2).
controls.procedure: Determine which plans are relevant per subscription from the actual inventory rather than enabling everything blindly: `az graph query -q "resources | summarize count() by subscriptionId, type" --first 1000` tells you which subscriptions hold virtual machines, storage accounts, SQL servers, App Service sites, AKS clusters, container registries, key vaults, Cosmos DB accounts, API Management services and open-source relational databases. Confirm the Microsoft.Security resource provider is registered in each subscription with `az provider show --namespace Microsoft.Security --subscription <sub-id> --query registrationState`, because an unregistered provider makes the pricing call fail rather than report Free. Then, per subscription, read the plan state: `az security pricing list --subscription <sub-id> --query "value[].{plan:name,tier:pricingTier,subPlan:subPlan,freeTrial:freeTrialRemainingTime}" -o table`, and take the raw ARM form `az rest --method get --url "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/<sub-id>/providers/Microsoft.Security/pricings?api-version=2024-01-01"` whenever a capability claim depends on the per-plan `extensions[]` array, whose elements carry `name` and an `isEnabled` value that is the STRING "True" or "False". Cross-check for resource-level opt-outs beneath a Standard subscription: servers expose `az rest --method get --url "https://management.azure.com/<vm-resource-id>/providers/Microsoft.Security/pricings/virtualMachines?api-version=2024-01-01"`, while a storage account's per-account override is a different resource entirely — `az rest --method get --url "https://management.azure.com/<storage-account-id>/providers/Microsoft.Security/defenderForStorageSettings/current?api-version=2022-12-01-preview"` — so the server pattern must not be reused for storage.
api: az graph query -q "resources | summarize count() by subscriptionId, type | order by subscriptionId asc" --first 1000
controls.evidence: A matrix of subscription id against plan name recording `pricingTier`, `subPlan`, `freeTrialRemainingTime` and every element of `extensions[]` with its `name` and `isEnabled` string, and beside each row the count of resources of the corresponding type in that subscription taken from the graph inventory. Include the CloudPosture plan state for every subscription, the Microsoft.Security registration state per subscription, and the resource-level pricing or Defender-for-Storage responses for any sampled resource that overrides the subscription tier. Record any subscription whose pricing call errored as unknown rather than as Free or Standard.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, for every subscription in the denominator, each plan whose corresponding resource type has at least one instance in that subscription reports `pricingTier: Standard`, and the CloudPosture plan reports `pricingTier: Standard` in every subscription regardless of inventory. Where a subPlan governs the capability being claimed, the subPlan string must match it: VirtualMachines must report `subPlan: P2` for agentless machine scanning and file integrity monitoring, and StorageAccounts must report `subPlan: DefenderForStorageV2` for malware scanning and sensitive-data discovery. Where a capability is claimed at extension granularity, the matching element of `extensions[]` must carry `isEnabled` equal to the string "True" — compare the string, since "False" is a non-empty value that a truthiness test accepts. A plan returned with `pricingTier: Free` for a type that is in use is a FAIL, as is a resource-level override that puts an in-use resource back on Free beneath a Standard subscription. PARTIALLY_MET when only some subscriptions or some types are covered. REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW for any subscription where Microsoft.Security is unregistered or the pricing call errored.
controls.remediation: `az security pricing create --name VirtualMachines --tier Standard --subscription <sub-id> --subplan P2`, repeated for CloudPosture, StorageAccounts (with `--subplan DefenderForStorageV2`), SqlServers, SqlServerVirtualMachines, AppServices, Containers, KeyVaults, Arm, OpenSourceRelationalDatabases, CosmosDbs and Api as the inventory requires — the former separate container-registry and Kubernetes plans have been folded into the single Containers plan, so onboarding scripts that still target them are configuring nothing. Where a capability rather than a plan is required, set it explicitly through the `--extensions` argument or the ARM pricings body so the extension records `isEnabled: "True"`. Drive all of this from a policy assignment at the management-group root with a remediation task rather than subscription by subscription, so newly created subscriptions arrive protected; verify the assignment's managed identity holds Security Admin at that scope and that the assignment carries a deploying effect with `enforcementMode: Default`.
controls.caveat: `az security pricing list` returns every plan name whether or not it is enabled, so a long response is not evidence of protection — the verdict must key on `pricingTier`, never on the presence of the entry. Plans do not inherit from a management group: a subscription created after the last review is Free by default and generates no alerts, which is the most common way an estate that passed once quietly stops being covered, and it is invisible to any assessment whose subscription denominator is the credential's own role assignments. A subscription can report Standard while individual servers are opted out through resource-level pricing, or while a storage account carries its own DefenderForStorageSettings override, so a subscription-only read is a false pass on those resources — and the storage override lives at a different API path from the server one, so a collector that reuses the server URL gets an error it may log as 'no override'. `freeTrialRemainingTime` means the plan is genuinely on but unbilled, which is compliant now and a scheduled failure later. The `extensions[]` array is the quietest failure of all in two ways: a plan can read Standard with the capability extension disabled, and `isEnabled` is the string "False", which any truthiness check treats as enabled — compare it as a string. Finally, the wrong subPlan hides the same gap at plan level: Servers P1 reports Standard while agentless scanning, file integrity monitoring and premium vulnerability assessment are simply absent, and the legacy per-transaction storage plan reports Standard without malware scanning; and a plan such as Api can be Standard while no API is actually onboarded to it, so the plan state is a necessary and not a sufficient condition.

controls.title: Defender's collection components are provisioned automatically and are actually bound to a collection rule
controls.objective: An enabled plan only produces findings if something is collecting from the workload: agentless disk scanning, the Defender for Endpoint sensor, and the Azure Monitor Agent bound to a data collection rule that actually reaches a destination. Manual per-machine onboarding drifts within weeks, so provisioning has to be automatic and its result has to be verified on the machines themselves (MCSB LT-1, AM-2).
controls.procedure: Enumerate subscriptions first so the check cannot silently cover only the CLI's default one: `az account list --all --query "[?state=='Enabled'].id" -o tsv`, then loop. Per subscription read the plan and its per-plan extension state, which is where modern provisioning lives: `az rest --method get --url "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/<sub-id>/providers/Microsoft.Security/pricings/VirtualMachines?api-version=2024-01-01"`, recording `properties.pricingTier` and every entry of `properties.extensions[]` (`AgentlessVmScanning`, `MdeDesignatedSubscription`, `FileIntegrityMonitoring`) with its `isEnabled` value — that field is the string `"True"`/`"False"`, not a boolean, so compare it as a string. Repeat for the `CloudPosture` plan (`AgentlessVmScanning`, `AgentlessDiscoveryForKubernetes`, `SensitiveDataDiscovery`) and for `Containers`. Read the tenant integrations with `az security setting list --subscription <sub-id>` and `az security setting show --name WDATP --subscription <sub-id>`, taking `properties.enabled`. Then verify the outcome on the fleet rather than trusting the setting. `az graph` ships in the `resource-graph` extension (`az extension add --name resource-graph`), returns at most 1000 rows per call and does not page for you, so drive it with `--first 1000` plus an increasing `--skip` until a short page returns: `az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/virtualmachines/extensions' or type =~ 'microsoft.hybridcompute/machines/extensions' | extend extType = tostring(properties.type) | where extType in~ ('AzureMonitorWindowsAgent','AzureMonitorLinuxAgent','MDE.Windows','MDE.Linux') | extend machineId = strcat_array(array_slice(split(id,'/'), 0, 8), '/') | project id, machineId, extType, publisher = tostring(properties.publisher), state = tostring(properties.provisioningState), subscriptionId" --first 1000`. Use `in~` rather than `has_any`: `has` tokenises on the dot and matches `MDE.Windows` far too loosely. Compare the distinct `machineId` values against the machine inventory query. For every machine carrying an Azure Monitor Agent, resolve what it is actually bound to: `az monitor data-collection rule association list --resource <machine-resource-id>`, then for each association that carries a `dataCollectionRuleId` run `az monitor data-collection rule show --ids <data-collection-rule-id>` and confirm the rule has a non-empty `dataSources` block and a `destinations` block.
api: az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/virtualmachines' or type =~ 'microsoft.hybridcompute/machines' | project id, name, type, subscriptionId, powerState = tostring(properties.extended.instanceView.powerState.code), arcStatus = tostring(properties.status)" --first 1000 --skip 0

az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/virtualmachines/extensions' or type =~ 'microsoft.hybridcompute/machines/extensions' | extend extType = tostring(properties.type) | where extType in~ ('AzureMonitorWindowsAgent','AzureMonitorLinuxAgent','MDE.Windows','MDE.Linux') | extend machineId = strcat_array(array_slice(split(id,'/'), 0, 8), '/') | project id, machineId, extType, state = tostring(properties.provisioningState), subscriptionId" --first 1000
az monitor data-collection rule association list --resource <machine-resource-id>
controls.evidence: Per subscription: the `VirtualMachines` and `CloudPosture` pricing objects showing `pricingTier` and each `extensions[]` entry's `isEnabled` string, and the `WDATP` security setting object with its `enabled` value. Per machine: the machine resource id, its power state or Arc connection status, whether an Azure Monitor Agent or Defender for Endpoint extension is present with `provisioningState: Succeeded`, and for each data collection rule association returned, whether it carries a populated `dataCollectionRuleId` or only a `dataCollectionEndpointId`, plus the resolved rule's `dataSources` and `destinations`. Report the covered-machine fraction with the uncovered machine ids named, and state how many subscriptions the enumeration actually reached.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when all of the following hold in every enabled subscription containing at least one virtual machine or Arc-enabled server: the `VirtualMachines` pricing object reads `pricingTier: Standard`; every extension the organisation relies on in that plan reads `isEnabled: "True"` (string compare); the `WDATP` security setting reads `enabled: true`; every machine whose power state is running or whose Arc status is Connected has at least one Defender for Endpoint or Azure Monitor Agent extension in `provisioningState: Succeeded`; and every machine carrying an Azure Monitor Agent extension has at least one data collection rule association with a populated `dataCollectionRuleId` whose referenced rule has a non-empty `dataSources` and at least one entry under `destinations`. A machine with the agent installed and zero rule associations FAILs, and so does one whose only association carries `dataCollectionEndpointId` alone, because neither collects anything. A subscription with zero machines is NOT_APPLICABLE with the inventory count stated.
controls.remediation: Enable the plan extensions in place rather than per machine: PUT the pricing object back with `pricingTier: Standard` and the required `extensions[]` entries enabled — `az rest --method put --url "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/<sub-id>/providers/Microsoft.Security/pricings/VirtualMachines?api-version=2024-01-01" --body @pricing.json` — and turn on the Defender for Endpoint integration with `az security setting update --name WDATP --enabled true`, falling back to a PUT against `https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/<sub-id>/providers/Microsoft.Security/settings/WDATP?api-version=2022-05-01` where the installed CLI does not expose that flag. Deploy the Azure Monitor Agent together with its data collection rule associations through a policy initiative assigned at the management-group root with a remediation task, so new and rebuilt machines are onboarded by the platform rather than by hand, and assign the same initiative at the scope that contains the Arc-enabled servers.
controls.caveat: The single biggest false pass is an agent with no data collection rule association: the extension reads `Succeeded`, the machine looks onboarded, and not one byte is collected. Two near misses behave the same way — an association that carries only a `dataCollectionEndpointId` rather than a rule id, and a rule whose `dataSources` do not include the events the control depends on — so resolve the rule, never count the association. The legacy auto-provisioning switch is a second trap: the monitoring agent it provisioned has been retired, so a subscription reporting auto-provisioning on is describing a mechanism that no longer collects anything, and the meaningful state now lives in the per-plan `extensions[]` array. An extension can read `isEnabled: "True"` while `pricingTier` is `Free`, where it is inert, so read both; and because `isEnabled` is a string, a truthiness test on it passes for `"False"` too. Agentless disk scanning runs on a cadence of up to a day, so a machine built this morning is legitimately unassessed and must not be scored as a failure. Finally, Resource Graph returns only what the calling principal can read and caps at 1000 rows per call, so an under-privileged or unpaged run produces a small fleet with perfect coverage — enumerate subscriptions explicitly instead of relying on the CLI's default subscription, and report the count reached.

controls.title: Security alerts are routed to a monitored mailbox and to the subscription owners
controls.objective: Alerts that nobody receives are not a detective control. Each subscription needs a security contact with alert notifications on, a severity floor low enough to include the alerts the organisation intends to act on, and role-based notification so ownership does not depend on one address staying valid (MCSB IR-2).
controls.procedure: Enumerate every enabled subscription first — `az account list --all --query "[?state=='Enabled'].id" -o tsv` — because contacts are a subscription-scoped resource that does not inherit from a management group, and a run against the CLI's default subscription will report the estate from a sample of one. Per subscription: `az rest --method get --url "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/<sub-id>/providers/Microsoft.Security/securityContacts?api-version=2020-01-01-preview"`, falling back to `az security contact list --subscription <sub-id>` where the CLI shape is sufficient. For the contact named `default`, read `properties.emails`, `properties.phone`, `properties.alertNotifications` (its `state` and `minimalSeverity`) and `properties.notificationsByRole` (its `state` and `roles[]`). Because the older api-version returns `alertNotifications` as a bare string and 2020-01-01-preview and later return an object, record the api-version you used alongside the response and parse accordingly. Establish who the role-based notification actually reaches with `az role assignment list --scope /subscriptions/<sub-id> --role Owner`, and where an Owner is a group, expand it: `az rest --method get --url "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/groups/<group-id>/members?\$select=id,displayName,mail"`. Confirm the contact addresses are real distribution points rather than individuals by resolving each against the directory: `az rest --method get --url "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/groups?\$filter=mail eq '<address>'"` and the equivalent `/users` query. Those Graph calls are the Entra control plane and need a Microsoft Graph token, not a Resource Manager one; `az rest` does not follow `@odata.nextLink`, so loop on that property yourself for any list that pages.
api: az role assignment list --scope /subscriptions/<sub-id> --role Owner --query "[].{principalId:principalId,principal:principalName,type:principalType}" -o json
controls.evidence: Per subscription: the full security-contacts response including the api-version used, the `emails` value, the `alertNotifications` state and `minimalSeverity`, and the `notificationsByRole` state with its `roles[]` list. Alongside it, the Owner role assignments on that subscription with principal type, the expanded membership of any Owner group, and the directory lookup result for each contact address showing whether it resolves to a group, a user, or nothing at all. State the number of subscriptions enumerated and the number that returned a contact.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every enabled subscription has a security contact named `default` with a non-empty `emails` value, `alertNotifications.state` equal to `On` with `minimalSeverity` of `High` or lower, and `notificationsByRole.state` equal to `On` with `Owner` present in `roles[]`, and at least one principal holds Owner at that subscription scope. A subscription with no contact object, an empty `emails` value, notifications off, role notification off, or zero Owner assignments FAILs. PARTIALLY_MET when some subscriptions comply and others do not — name them.
controls.remediation: PUT the contact object directly, which is the shape-stable route and the only one that reliably carries every field: `az rest --method put --url "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/<sub-id>/providers/Microsoft.Security/securityContacts/default?api-version=2020-01-01-preview" --body '{"properties":{"emails":"soc@<org>;secops-oncall@<org>","alertNotifications":{"state":"On","minimalSeverity":"Medium"},"notificationsByRole":{"state":"On","roles":["Owner"]}}}'`. Where the installed CLI exposes the fields, `az security contact create --name default --emails "soc@<org>" --subscription <sub-id>` is equivalent, but confirm the created object's shape afterwards because the CLI's parameters have changed across versions. Point the address at a monitored distribution list or ticket-queue mailbox, never at a named individual, and set the severity floor to include Medium where the team has capacity to triage it. Automate creation via a policy assignment at the management-group root so new subscriptions inherit the contact.
controls.caveat: Contacts are per subscription and do not inherit, so a newly created subscription silently regresses the estate and a run against one default subscription reports nothing about the rest. Parser fragility is a real false pass here: older api-versions return `alertNotifications` as the string `On`, newer ones return an object with `state` and `minimalSeverity`, and a check written against one shape reports the other as disabled or, worse, as truthy because a non-empty object is truthy. A `minimalSeverity` of `High` is a valid configuration that nonetheless suppresses every Medium alert, so it passes a naive presence check while matching a much narrower intent than the report will imply. Role-based notification is the subtler trap: it reaches whoever holds Owner at that moment, so a subscription whose only Owner is a dynamic-membership group whose rule currently resolves to zero members satisfies every field of this check and notifies nobody — expand the group and count the members. The API cannot tell you whether anyone reads the mailbox, whether the address still resolves, or whether mail filtering bins the notification, so verify one delivery out of band. Finally, notifications only carry alerts that a Defender plan produced, so a subscription that passes this control while failing 3.6 receives nothing at all.

controls.title: Changes to policy assignments and to role assignments raise an alert in every subscription
controls.objective: Removing a policy assignment and granting oneself a role are the two edits that convert a foothold into durable control of a subscription, and both are ordinary, quiet Resource Manager writes. An activity log alert on those operations, wired to an action group with a live receiver, is what makes them noisy (MCSB PA-1, PA-7, LT-5).
controls.procedure: Enumerate the subscriptions in scope with `az account list --all --query "[?state=='Enabled'].id" -o tsv`, since the control is satisfied or failed per subscription. Collect every alert rule in the tenant with one inventory query — activity log alerts are ordinary ARM resources and are indexed: `az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.insights/activitylogalerts' | project id, name, subscriptionId, enabled = tobool(properties.enabled), scopes = properties.scopes, condition = properties.condition, actionGroups = properties.actions.actionGroups" --first 1000` and page with `--skip` until a short page returns. For each rule of interest confirm the detail with `az monitor activity-log alert show --name <name> --resource-group <rg> --subscription <sub-id>` and walk `condition.allOf[]` for a clause on `category` equal to `Administrative` together with clauses on `operationName` covering `Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/write`, `Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/delete`, `Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write` and `Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/delete` — an `anyOf` list of operation names counts as coverage. While walking the conditions, record any further clause that narrows the rule (an equality on `resourceGroup`, `resourceId`, `caller` or `level`), because such a clause shrinks the rule below the subscription. Resolve every referenced action group with `az monitor action-group show --name <ag> --resource-group <rg>` and require `enabled: true` with at least one receiver holding a delivery address. List suppressions with `az monitor alert-processing-rule list --subscription <sub-id>`, since one can mute a correctly configured rule without editing it. Where the organisation alerts from the workspace instead, accept `az monitor scheduled-query list --subscription <sub-id>` rules whose query filters `AzureActivity` on those `OperationNameValue` strings and which carry an action group.
api: az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.insights/activitylogalerts' | project id, name, subscriptionId, enabled = tobool(properties.enabled), scopes = properties.scopes, condition = properties.condition, actionGroups = properties.actions.actionGroups" --first 1000
controls.evidence: Per subscription: the alert rule id and name, `enabled: true`, the `scopes[]` array showing the subscription resource id, every `condition.allOf[]` clause including any that narrows the rule, and for each referenced action group its id, `enabled` flag and receiver list with delivery targets. Add the alert processing rules in force on that subscription so a suppression is visible. Where no qualifying rule exists, record the subscription id explicitly as uncovered rather than omitting it.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every enabled subscription contains at least one activity log alert with `enabled: true`, a `scopes[]` entry exactly equal to `/subscriptions/<sub-id>`, conditions matching all four operations (policyAssignments write and delete, roleAssignments write and delete — spread over one rule or several), no additional condition clause narrowing the rule by `resourceGroup`, `resourceId` or `caller`, at least one action group that resolves and is itself `enabled: true` with a non-empty receiver list, and no alert processing rule in `Suppression` mode whose scope covers that rule. A rule scoped only to a resource group, a rule with an empty `actionGroups[]`, or a rule pointing at an action group that is disabled or has no receivers, does not satisfy the control for that subscription.
controls.remediation: Per subscription: `az monitor action-group create --name secops-ag --resource-group <rg> --short-name secops --action email soc soc@<org>` then `az monitor activity-log alert create --name authz-changes --resource-group <rg> --scope /subscriptions/<sub-id> --condition "category=Administrative and operationName=Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write" --action-group <action-group-id>`, repeated for the delete operation and for the two policyAssignment operations, or a single PUT of the rule with the four operation names in an `anyOf` block. Because the rule cannot span subscriptions, deploy it from a policy assignment or template assigned at the management-group root so each subscription materialises its own copy, and hold the alert rules in a resource group nobody but the platform team can write to. Alert separately on the Entra directory audit stream for tenant role grants, which this rule cannot see.
controls.caveat: An activity log alert's scope must sit inside a single subscription, so there is no management-group-wide rule to find: one carefully built rule in the hub subscription leaves every other subscription uncovered, and an assessment that stops at 'a rule exists somewhere in the tenant' is a false pass by construction. The second trap is the far end of the pipe — a rule can be enabled while its action group is disabled, holds no receivers, or points at a decommissioned webhook — so the action group must be resolved, not counted. Third, PIM activations issue the same `Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write` operation, so these rules are noisy in a PIM estate and the usual tuning is a `caller` or `resourceGroup` clause that quietly excludes exactly the grants this control exists to catch; read every clause, not just the operation names. Fourth, an alert processing rule in `Suppression` mode mutes a perfectly configured alert without altering it, so list those rules explicitly. Fifth and most important: Entra ID directory role assignments, including Global Administrator and Privileged Role Administrator, are not Resource Manager operations and never appear in the activity log at all. This control covers Azure RBAC only; tenant-level privilege grants need the Entra diagnostic setting from 3.1 plus alerting on the directory audit stream, which is a different control plane and a different credential.

controls.title: Network security group and rule changes raise an alert
controls.objective: A single inbound rule permitting management ports from the internet is enough to expose an estate, and it is a one-line change that looks routine in a change log. Alerting on security-group and security-rule writes and deletes puts a human in the loop within minutes rather than at the next review (MCSB NS-1, NS-7, LT-5).
controls.procedure: Take the inventory of network security groups first, because it decides which subscriptions the control even applies to and stops an empty estate reading as a clean one: `az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/networksecuritygroups' | summarize nsgCount = count() by subscriptionId" --first 1000`. Reuse the tenant-wide rule inventory: `az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.insights/activitylogalerts' | project id, name, subscriptionId, enabled = tobool(properties.enabled), scopes = properties.scopes, condition = properties.condition, actionGroups = properties.actions.actionGroups" --first 1000`, paging with `--skip`. For each subscription, look for `condition.allOf[]` clauses on `operationName` covering `Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/write`, `Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/delete`, `Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/securityRules/write` and `Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/securityRules/delete`, confirm `enabled: true`, confirm the `scopes[]` entry is the subscription resource id, and resolve each action group with `az monitor action-group show`. List `az monitor alert-processing-rule list` for suppressions. Sanity-check the result against what the activity log actually contains over the last month, which also proves the alert would have had something to fire on: `az monitor log-analytics query --workspace <workspace-guid> --analytics-query "AzureActivity | where OperationNameValue startswith 'MICROSOFT.NETWORK/NETWORKSECURITYGROUPS' | summarize count() by OperationNameValue, Caller, SubscriptionId" --timespan P30D` — the `--workspace` argument is the workspace customer id GUID, not its resource id, and a zero-row result only means something if that subscription's activity log is known to be flowing into that workspace.
api: az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/networksecuritygroups' | summarize nsgCount = count() by subscriptionId" --first 1000

az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.insights/activitylogalerts' | project id, name, subscriptionId, enabled = tobool(properties.enabled), scopes = properties.scopes, condition = properties.condition, actionGroups = properties.actions.actionGroups" --first 1000

az monitor log-analytics query --workspace <workspace-guid> --analytics-query "AzureActivity | where OperationNameValue startswith 'MICROSOFT.NETWORK/NETWORKSECURITYGROUPS' | summarize count() by OperationNameValue, Caller, SubscriptionId" --timespan P30D
controls.evidence: Per subscription: the network security group count from the inventory query, the alert rule id, `enabled: true`, the `scopes[]` entry equal to the subscription resource id, the condition clauses naming both the parent security-group and the child security-rule operations, the resolved action group with its `enabled` flag and receivers, and any alert processing rule that covers the alert. Add the 30-day `AzureActivity` summary of those operation names as corroboration, together with the fact of whether that subscription's Administrative log is routed to the queried workspace.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every enabled subscription holding at least one network security group has an activity log alert with `enabled: true`, a `scopes[]` entry equal to `/subscriptions/<sub-id>`, conditions covering both the `networkSecurityGroups` and the `networkSecurityGroups/securityRules` operations for write and delete, routing to an action group that resolves with `enabled: true` and a non-empty receiver list, and no `Suppression`-mode alert processing rule covering it. A subscription whose inventory count is zero is NOT_APPLICABLE with that count stated. Missing coverage of the `securityRules` child operations alone is a FAIL, because that is where the exposure is created.
