controls.remediation: `az monitor activity-log alert create --name nsg-changes --resource-group <rg> --scope /subscriptions/<sub-id> --condition "category=Administrative and operationName=Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/securityRules/write" --action-group <action-group-id>`, repeated for the delete operation and for the two parent `networkSecurityGroups` operations, or one PUT of the rule carrying all four in an `anyOf` block. Deploy the rule per subscription from a management-group policy assignment so subscriptions that hold no security groups today are still covered when they acquire one, and complement it with a policy in Deny — not Audit — on inbound rules that allow management ports from any source, so the control does not depend on someone reading the alert.
controls.caveat: A subscription with zero network security groups is NOT_APPLICABLE only for as long as that stays true; if the alert is not deployed by policy, the first security group created there arrives unmonitored and the assessment that recorded NOT_APPLICABLE reads in the report as though nothing were wrong. Alerting on security-group writes also does not cover the ways effective network exposure changes without touching a security group: detaching a group from a subnet is a `Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/subnets/write`, changing application security group membership is a NIC write, and Azure Firewall, Front Door, Application Gateway WAF and route table changes belong to entirely different resource providers — a report presenting this control as network change monitoring overstates it. The corroborating workspace query is itself a false-pass source: zero rows over thirty days reads as 'no changes' when it usually means the subscription's Administrative activity log was never routed to that workspace, so confirm the diagnostic setting before drawing any conclusion from an empty result. Alert processing rules can suppress a correctly configured alert without altering the rule, so list them. The same scope constraint as 3.9 applies — the rule cannot span subscriptions, so a hub-only rule leaves the spokes uncovered. Finally, the alert fires on the write regardless of whether the resulting rule is dangerous, so a high-churn environment usually mutes it within weeks; check the action group receivers are still live and that the rule has not been left enabled with an empty action list.

controls.title: Key Vault configuration and permission changes raise an alert
controls.objective: The fastest route to every secret in a subscription is to grant yourself access to the vault rather than to break into it. Alerting on vault create, update and delete, and on the permission change that fits each vault's authorization model, gives near-real-time notice of that move (MCSB DP-8, PA-7, LT-5).
controls.procedure: Inventory the vaults and their authorization models first, because the model decides which permission operation is the one that matters, and because a subscription with no vaults must be recorded as such rather than as clean: `az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.keyvault/vaults' | project id, name, subscriptionId, rbac = tostring(properties.enableRbacAuthorization)" --first 1000`, and separately `az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.keyvault/managedhsms' | project id, name, subscriptionId" --first 1000`. Treat an empty or absent `rbac` value as the access-policy model — the property is null on vaults created before it existed, and `tostring(null)` is the empty string, not `false`. From the tenant-wide alert inventory (`az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.insights/activitylogalerts' | project id, name, subscriptionId, enabled = tobool(properties.enabled), scopes = properties.scopes, condition = properties.condition, actionGroups = properties.actions.actionGroups" --first 1000`, paged with `--skip`), look per subscription for conditions covering `Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/write` and `Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/delete`. For access-policy vaults additionally require coverage of `Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/accessPolicies/write`; for RBAC vaults require that the role-assignment coverage from 3.9 is present in the same subscription, since permission grants on those vaults are `Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write` at vault scope. Where managed HSMs exist, require `Microsoft.KeyVault/managedHSMs/write` and `Microsoft.KeyVault/managedHSMs/delete` as well. Resolve every action group with `az monitor action-group show` and require it to be enabled with at least one receiver. To document who holds vault access today, run `az role assignment list --scope <vault-resource-id> --include-inherited`; note that `principalName` is resolved through Microsoft Graph and comes back empty when the principal lacks directory read, so key the output on `principalId`.
api: az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.keyvault/vaults' | project id, name, subscriptionId, rbac = tostring(properties.enableRbacAuthorization)" --first 1000
az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.keyvault/managedhsms' | project id, name, subscriptionId" --first 1000

az graph query -q "resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.insights/activitylogalerts' | project id, name, subscriptionId, enabled = tobool(properties.enabled), scopes = properties.scopes, condition = properties.condition, actionGroups = properties.actions.actionGroups" --first 1000
controls.evidence: Per subscription holding vaults: the vault inventory with each vault's authorization model as read (including where the property was absent), the managed HSM inventory, the alert rule id, `enabled: true`, the subscription-scoped `scopes[]` entry, the condition clauses naming the vault write and delete operations plus the `accessPolicies/write` operation wherever an access-policy vault exists, and the resolved enabled action group with its receivers. Add the per-vault role assignments keyed on `principalId`, noting whether directory names could be resolved, so the reviewer can see which permission operation was required for each vault.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every enabled subscription containing at least one Key Vault has an activity log alert with `enabled: true`, a `scopes[]` entry equal to `/subscriptions/<sub-id>`, conditions covering `Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/write` and `Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/delete`, and an action group that resolves with `enabled: true` and a non-empty receiver list; additionally covering `Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/accessPolicies/write` in any subscription holding a vault whose `enableRbacAuthorization` is `false`, absent or empty; and additionally covering `Microsoft.KeyVault/managedHSMs/write` and `Microsoft.KeyVault/managedHSMs/delete` in any subscription holding a managed HSM. A subscription whose vaults are all RBAC-model satisfies the permission half of this control only if 3.9 passed for that same subscription. A subscription with zero vaults and zero managed HSMs is NOT_APPLICABLE with the counts stated.
controls.remediation: `az monitor activity-log alert create --name keyvault-changes --resource-group <rg> --scope /subscriptions/<sub-id> --condition "category=Administrative and operationName=Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/write" --action-group <action-group-id>`, plus the delete operation, plus `Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/accessPolicies/write` for access-policy vaults and the `managedHSMs` operations where those exist. Migrate vaults to the RBAC authorization model so permission changes surface in one place and are covered by the role-assignment alert, and pair the alert with soft delete and purge protection so an alerted deletion is also a recoverable one. Deploy the rule per subscription from a management-group policy assignment so a subscription that acquires its first vault is already covered.
controls.caveat: The dominant false pass is model drift: a vault migrated to the RBAC authorization model never emits `accessPolicies/write` again, so an accessPolicies-only alert is a dead rule that still reads as configured, while the real grant appears as a role assignment at vault scope that only 3.9 catches. The inverse also bites — an estate assessed as RBAC-covered may still hold legacy access-policy vaults — and the property that distinguishes them is null on older vaults, so a check comparing it to the string `false` silently classifies them as RBAC and drops the accessPolicies requirement. A second false pass is the delivery route of the change itself: `az keyvault set-policy` emits `accessPolicies/write`, but the same policy edited through a full ARM template deployment of the vault emits `Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/write` instead, so an accessPolicies-only condition misses template-driven grants entirely — cover both operations. Nothing in this control sees the data plane: retrieving every secret from a vault the attacker already has access to is a data-plane operation appearing only in the `AuditEvent` log from 3.4, so passing here says nothing about exfiltration. Managed HSMs use a separate operation namespace and are invisible to a vaults-only condition. And as in 3.9 and 3.10, the rule cannot span subscriptions, the action group must be resolved rather than assumed, and an alert processing rule can suppress the whole thing without touching the rule.

controls.title: Defender recommendations are triaged, owned and time-bound rather than accumulating
controls.objective: Secure score and the benchmark assessments are only worth anything if unhealthy findings are being worked, exempted with a stated reason, or formally accepted by a named owner with a date. The judgement this control needs — is the residual risk acceptable, is the exemption legitimate — is not something an API can settle (MCSB GS-1, PV-2, LT-1).
controls.procedure: Pull the whole tenant's assessment state in one query rather than per subscription, paging with `--skip` because Resource Graph caps each call at 1000 rows: `az graph query -q "securityresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.security/assessments' | extend status = tostring(properties.status.code), sev = tostring(properties.metadata.severity), assessmentName = tostring(properties.displayName) | summarize count() by subscriptionId, status, sev, assessmentName | order by subscriptionId asc, sev asc" --first 1000`. Read the score itself with `az graph query -q "securityresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.security/securescores' | project subscriptionId, current = todouble(properties.score.current), max = todouble(properties.score.max), percentage = todouble(properties.score.percentage)" --first 1000`, or per subscription with `az security secure-scores show --name ascScore --subscription <sub-id>`. Establish whether the benchmark initiative is even assigned, because an unassigned subscription produces no assessments at all: `az policy assignment list --scope /subscriptions/<sub-id> --disable-scope-strict-match --query "[].{name:name,policyDefinitionId:policyDefinitionId,enforcement:enforcementMode,scope:scope}" -o json` — the flag is essential, since without it the listing returns only assignments made at that exact scope and an initiative assigned at the management-group root is invisible, producing a spurious 'not assigned' finding, while its absence in the other direction hides an inherited assignment you were relying on. List everything that has been made to disappear: `az policy exemption list --scope /subscriptions/<sub-id> --disable-scope-strict-match -o json`, reading each exemption's `exemptionCategory`, `expiresOn` and `description`, and `az graph query -q "securityresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.security/assessments/governanceassignments' | project id, subscriptionId, owner = tostring(properties.owner), dueDate = tostring(properties.remediationDueDate)" --first 1000`. Then read the ticketing system or risk register for each accepted item and judge whether the acceptance is current, owned and justified — that last step is the human one.
api: az graph query -q "securityresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.security/assessments' | extend status = tostring(properties.status.code), sev = tostring(properties.metadata.severity) | summarize count() by subscriptionId, status, sev" --first 1000

az graph query -q "securityresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.security/securescores' | project subscriptionId, current = todouble(properties.score.current), max = todouble(properties.score.max), percentage = todouble(properties.score.percentage)" --first 1000

az graph query -q "securityresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.security/assessments/governanceassignments' | project id, subscriptionId, owner = tostring(properties.owner), dueDate = tostring(properties.remediationDueDate)" --first 1000
controls.evidence: Per subscription: the secure score current, max and percentage; the count of assessments by status and severity; the list of High-severity assessments in `Unhealthy` state with their display names and affected resource counts; the policy exemptions in force with their `exemptionCategory`, `expiresOn` and `description`; and the governance assignments showing owner and remediation due date. Record whether the benchmark initiative was found at the subscription scope or inherited from an ancestor, and how many subscriptions the enumeration reached. Alongside the API evidence, the risk-register or ticket reference for each accepted finding and the date of the last triage — these are the human-supplied artefacts and must be cited, not summarised.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS requires both a mechanical condition and a documentary one, and both must be recorded. Mechanically: every enabled subscription returns at least one `microsoft.security/assessments` row and has the benchmark initiative assigned at its own scope or inherited from an ancestor; the count of assessments with `status.code` equal to `Unhealthy` and `metadata.severity` equal to `High` that have no matching governance assignment carrying a non-empty `owner` and a `remediationDueDate` in the future is zero; and every policy exemption whose scope covers a security assessment has a non-empty `description` and an `expiresOn` in the future. Documentarily: each remaining accepted finding carries a dated risk-acceptance reference naming a person. Any High-severity `Unhealthy` assessment with no owner, or any exemption with no expiry, is a FAIL. A subscription returning zero assessments is not a pass — it is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW pending confirmation of whether the initiative is assigned and the Defender resource provider registered.
controls.remediation: Assign the cloud security benchmark initiative at the management-group root so every current and future subscription is assessed, then configure governance rules in Defender for Cloud that attach an owner and a due date to every High-severity recommendation automatically. Replace open-ended exemptions with time-bound ones carrying a justification, and review them on expiry rather than renewing by default. Track the score trend per subscription over time; a flat score with rising resource counts means new resources are arriving unprotected.
controls.caveat: Manual because no API can decide whether a risk acceptance is legitimate, whether the named owner is still in the role, or whether an exemption reflects a genuine compensating control rather than a convenient way of clearing the dashboard; the API supplies the inventory, a human supplies the verdict on each accepted item. Several concrete false passes must be named in the report. First, a subscription with no benchmark initiative assigned returns no assessments and therefore no unhealthy findings — it scores as clean precisely because nothing was ever evaluated — and the listing that would have revealed this returns nothing unless `--disable-scope-strict-match` is passed, so the inherited management-group assignment is invisible and the tool reports the wrong thing in either direction. Second, an assessment type simply does not appear when the plan that generates it was never enabled or the relevant resource type is absent, so an estate with Defender for SQL off shows zero SQL findings, which is indistinguishable from zero SQL problems unless the plan state from 3.6 is reported beside it. Third, exemptions and `NotApplicable` statuses are removed from the score calculation, so secure score rises when findings are hidden and a high percentage can coexist with a critical unremediated exposure — always report unhealthy High-severity counts beside the percentage, never the percentage alone. Fourth, secure score is weighted by control rather than by resource, so a control failing on one resource and a control failing on four hundred can cost the same points, which makes the number a poor proxy for exposure. Fifth, `securityresources` returns only what the calling principal can read and caps at 1000 rows per call, so an under-privileged or unpaged run produces a small, tidy estate — state how many subscriptions the query actually reached and whether every page was consumed.
